You do not meet a man but frowns; our bloods / No more obey the heavens than our courtiers / Still seem as does the King's.
Every man you meet is frowning. Our moods follow the King's as closely as the courtiers' faces do.

His daughter, and the heir of's kingdom, whom / He purpos'd to his wife's sole son—a widow / That late he married—hath referr'd herself / Unto a poor but worthy gentleman. She's wedded; / Her husband banish'd; she imprison'd. All / Is outward sorrow, though I think the King / Be touch'd at very heart.

His daughter, heir to his kingdom, whom he meant to marry to his new wife's only son (the Queen is a widow he married recently), has given herself to a poor but worthy gentleman. She's married; her husband is banished, and she's a prisoner. Everyone looks sad, though I think only the King is truly hurt to the heart.

He that hath lost her too. So is the Queen, / That most desir'd the match. But not a courtier, / Although they wear their faces to the bent / Of the King's looks, hath a heart that is not / Glad at the thing they scowl at.

And the man who lost her too, and the Queen, who wanted the match most. But no courtier, however much they shape their faces to match the King's looks, isn't secretly glad about what they pretend to scowl at.

He that hath miss'd the Princess is a thing / Too bad for bad report; and he that hath her— / I mean that married her, alack, good man! / And therefore banish'd—is a creature such / As, to seek through the regions of the earth / For one his like, there would be something failing / In him that should compare. I do not think / So fair an outward and such stuff within / Endows a man but he.

The man who failed to win the Princess is too bad to describe, and the man who has her (I mean the one who married her, poor good man, and was banished for it) is someone without equal: search the whole earth for his match and any rival would fall short. I don't think any man but he combines such good looks with such inner worth.
I do extend him, sir, within himself; / Crush him together rather than unfold / His measure duly.
I'm only stretching him to his true size, sir. If anything I'm shrinking him rather than showing his full measure.

I cannot delve him to the root; his father / Was call'd Sicilius, who did join his honour / Against the Romans with Cassibelan, / But had his titles by Tenantius, whom / He serv'd with glory and admir'd success, / So gain'd the sur-addition Leonatus; / And had, besides this gentleman in question, / Two other sons, who, in the wars o' th' time, / Died with their swords in hand; for which their father, / Then old and fond of issue, took such sorrow / That he quit being; and his gentle lady, / Big of this gentleman, our theme, deceas'd / As he was born. The King he takes the babe / To his protection, calls him Posthumus Leonatus, / Breeds him and makes him of his bed-chamber, / Puts to him all the learnings that his time / Could make him the receiver of; which he took, / As we do air, fast as 'twas minist'red, / And in's spring became a harvest, liv'd in court— / Which rare it is to do—most prais'd, most lov'd, / A sample to the youngest; to th' more mature / A glass that feated them; and to the graver / A child that guided dotards. To his mistress, / For whom he now is banish'd—her own price / Proclaims how she esteem'd him and his virtue; / By her election may be truly read / What kind of man he is.

I can't trace his roots far. His father was Sicilius, who fought for honour alongside Cassibelan against the Romans but got his titles from Tenantius, whom he served with glory and great success, and so earned the extra name Leonatus. Besides this gentleman, he had two other sons, who died sword in hand in the wars of the time. Their father, old and devoted to his children, grieved so much that he died, and his gentle wife, pregnant with this gentleman, died as he was born. The King took the baby under his protection, named him Posthumus Leonatus, brought him up, made him a gentleman of his bedchamber, and gave him every kind of learning his age could offer. He took it in as fast as we breathe air and was ripe for harvest in his youth. He lived at court, which is rare, and was praised and loved by all: a model to the young, a mirror for the mature to dress themselves by, and to the old, a child who guided their foolish age. As for his lady, for whom he is now banished, her own worth shows how highly she valued him and his virtue. You can read what kind of man he is from her choice.
I honour him / Even out of your report. But pray you tell me, / Is she sole child to th' King?
I honour him just from your account. But tell me, is she the King's only child?

His only child. / He had two sons—if this be worth your hearing, / Mark it—the eldest of them at three years old, / I' th' swathing clothes the other, from their nursery / Were stol'n; and to this hour no guess in knowledge / Which way they went.

His only child now. He had two sons (this is worth hearing, mark it): the older at three years old, the other still in baby clothes, were stolen from their nursery, and to this day nobody knows which way they went.
That a king's children should be so convey'd, / So slackly guarded, and the search so slow / That could not trace them!
That a king's children could be stolen like that, so carelessly guarded, and the search so slow that it couldn't trace them!
Howsoe'er 'tis strange, / Or that the negligence may well be laugh'd at, / Yet is it true, sir.
However strange it is, and however laughable the negligence, it's true, sir.
We must forbear; here comes the gentleman, / The Queen, and Princess.
We must stop talking. Here comes the gentleman, with the Queen and the Princess.

No, be assur'd you shall not find me, daughter, / After the slander of most stepmothers, / Evil-ey'd unto you. You're my prisoner, but / Your gaoler shall deliver you the keys / That lock up your restraint. For you, Posthumus, / So soon as I can win th' offended King, / I will be known your advocate. Marry, yet / The fire of rage is in him, and 'twere good / You lean'd unto his sentence with what patience / Your wisdom may inform you.

No, daughter, you can be sure you won't find me treating you with the evil eye that stepmothers are famous for. You're my prisoner, but your jailer will hand you the keys that lock you up. As for you, Posthumus, as soon as I can soften the angry King, I'll be known as your champion. But right now he's burning with rage, and you'd do well to accept his sentence with as much patience as your good sense allows.
Please your Highness, / I will from hence to-day.
If it please your Highness, I'll leave today.
You know the peril. / I'll fetch a turn about the garden, pitying / The pangs of barr'd affections, though the King / Hath charg'd you should not speak together.
You know the danger. I'll take a walk round the garden, feeling for the pain of forbidden love, even though the King has ordered that you mustn't talk together.

O dissembling courtesy! How fine this tyrant / Can tickle where she wounds! My dearest husband, / I something fear my father's wrath, but nothing— / Always reserv'd my holy duty—what / His rage can do on me. You must be gone; / And I shall here abide the hourly shot / Of angry eyes, not comforted to live / But that there is this jewel in the world / That I may see again.

Oh, false kindness! How sweetly this tyrant can tickle while she wounds! My dearest husband, I'm a little afraid of my father's anger, but (saving the duty I owe him) I'm not afraid of anything his rage can do to me. You must go, and I must stay here and endure the constant fire of angry looks, with no comfort in living except that this jewel, you, is somewhere in the world for me to see again.

My queen! my mistress! / O lady, weep no more, lest I give cause / To be suspected of more tenderness / Than doth become a man. I will remain / The loyal'st husband that did e'er plight troth; / My residence in Rome at one Philario's, / Who to my father was a friend, to me / Known but by letter; thither write, my queen, / And with mine eyes I'll drink the words you send, / Though ink be made of gall.

My queen, my lady! Don't cry any more, or I'll show more tenderness than a man should. I'll stay the most loyal husband who ever made a vow. I'll be living in Rome at the house of a man called Philario, a friend of my father's whom I know only by letter. Write to me there, my queen, and I'll drink in your words with my eyes, even if the ink is bitter gall.

Be brief, I pray you. / If the King come, I shall incur I know not / How much of his displeasure. [Aside] Yet I'll move him / To walk this way. I never do him wrong / But he does buy my injuries, to be friends; / Pays dear for my offences.

Be quick, please. If the King comes I'll be in more trouble than I can say. (Aside) Still, I'll get him to walk this way. Whenever I wrong him, he pays for my injuries to make friends again; he pays dearly for my offences.
Should we be taking leave / As long a term as yet we have to live, / The loathness to depart would grow. Adieu!
If we spent the rest of our lives saying goodbye, the pain of parting would only grow. Goodbye!

Nay, stay a little. / Were you but riding forth to air yourself, / Such parting were too petty. Look here, love: / This diamond was my mother's; take it, heart; / But keep it till you woo another wife, / When Imogen is dead.

No, wait a moment. If you were only riding out for some air, a goodbye like this would be too small. Look, love: this diamond was my mother's. Take it, my heart, but keep it until you court another wife, after Imogen is dead.
How, how? Another? / You gentle gods, give me but this I have, / And sear up my embracements from a next / With bonds of death! Remain, remain thou here
What? Another wife? Kind gods, let me keep the one I have, and seal me off from embracing anyone else with the bonds of death! Stay here, ring,

While sense can keep it on. And, sweetest, fairest, / As I my poor self did exchange for you, / To your so infinite loss, so in our trifles / I still win of you. For my sake wear this; / It is a manacle of love; I'll place it / Upon this fairest prisoner. [Puts a bracelet on her arm]

as long as I'm alive to wear you. And, sweetest and fairest, just as I swapped my poor self for you, to your enormous loss, I go on winning in our little exchanges too. Wear this for my sake: it's a handcuff of love, and I'll put it on this lovely prisoner. (He puts a bracelet on her arm.)
O the gods! / When shall we see again?
Oh, gods! When will we see each other again?
Thou basest thing, avoid; hence from my sight / If after this command thou fraught the court / With thy unworthiness, thou diest. Away! / Thou'rt poison to my blood.
You lowest of creatures, get out of my sight! If after this order you burden the court with your worthless presence, you die. Go! You're poison in my blood.
The gods protect you, / And bless the good remainders of the court! / I am gone.
May the gods protect you and bless the good people left at court! I'm going.
There cannot be a pinch in death / More sharp than this is.
Death can't hold a sharper pain than this.
O disloyal thing, / That shouldst repair my youth, thou heap'st / A year's age on me!
You disloyal thing, who should have made me young again, you're piling years of age on me!
I beseech you, sir, / Harm not yourself with your vexation. / I am senseless of your wrath; a touch more rare / Subdues all pangs, all fears.
I beg you, sir, don't harm yourself with this anger. I can't feel your rage; a rarer pain overpowers every pain and every fear.
Past hope, and in despair; that way past grace.
Beyond hope, and in despair. In that sense, beyond grace.
That mightst have had the sole son of my queen!
When you could have had my queen's only son!
O blessed that I might not! I chose an eagle, / And did avoid a puttock.
Blessed am I that I didn't! I chose an eagle and avoided a buzzard.
Thou took'st a beggar, wouldst have made my throne / A seat for baseness.
You took a beggar, and would have made my throne a seat for low birth.
No; I rather added / A lustre to it.
No, I added a shine to it.
Sir, / It is your fault that I have lov'd Posthumus. / You bred him as my playfellow, and he is / A man worth any woman; overbuys me / Almost the sum he pays.
Sir, it's your fault that I've loved Posthumus. You brought him up as my playmate, and he is a man worth any woman. He's worth far more than I am; he overpays for me.
Almost, sir. Heaven restore me! Would I were / A neat-herd's daughter, and my Leonatus / Our neighbour shepherd's son!
Nearly, sir. Heaven heal me! I wish I were a cowherd's daughter and my Leonatus our neighbour shepherd's son!
Thou foolish thing! / [To the Queen] They were again together. You have done / Not after our command. Away with her, / And pen her up.
You foolish girl! (To the Queen) They've been together again. You didn't do as I ordered. Take her away and lock her up.
Beseech your patience.—Peace, / Dear lady daughter, peace!—Sweet sovereign, / Leave us to ourselves, and make yourself some comfort / Out of your best advice.
Please be patient. (To Imogen) Quiet, dear daughter, quiet! (To Cymbeline) Sweet king, leave us alone and find some comfort in your own best judgment.
Nay, let her languish / A drop of blood a day and, being aged, / Die of this folly.
No, let her waste away a drop of blood a day, and die of this folly when she's old.
Fie! you must give way. / Here is your servant. How now, sir! What news?
Come, you must give in. Here's your servant. Well, sir, what news?
My lord your son drew on my master.
My lord your son drew his sword on my master.
Ha! / No harm, I trust, is done?
What! No harm done, I hope?
There might have been, / But that my master rather play'd than fought, / And had no help of anger; they were parted / By gentlemen at hand.
There could have been, except my master was playing rather than fighting, and wasn't driven by anger. Some gentlemen nearby separated them.

Your son's my father's friend; he takes his part / To draw upon an exile! O brave sir! / I would they were in Afric both together; / Myself by with a needle, that I might prick / The goer-back. Why came you from your master?

Your son is my father's friend; he takes his side by drawing on an exile! What a hero! I wish they were both in Africa together, with me standing by with a needle to stab whichever one ran away. Why did you leave your master?
On his command. He would not suffer me / To bring him to the haven; left these notes / Of what commands I should be subject to, / When't pleas'd you to employ me.
He ordered me to. He wouldn't let me go with him to the harbour, and he left these written instructions for how I should serve you whenever you need me.
This hath been / Your faithful servant. I dare lay mine honour / He will remain so.
He has been a loyal servant to you. I'd stake my honour that he'll stay one.
Please walk with me a while.
About some half-hour hence, / Pray you speak with me. You shall at least / Go see my lord aboard. For this time leave me.
In about half an hour, please come and talk to me. At least you can go and see my lord aboard ship. For now, leave me.
Sir, I would advise you to shift a shirt; the violence / of action hath made you reek as a sacrifice. Where air comes out, / air comes in; there's none abroad so wholesome as that you vent.
Sir, I'd advise you to change your shirt. All that action has made you steam like a burnt sacrifice. When air goes out, air comes in, and no air outside is as healthy as what you breathe out.
If my shirt were bloody, then to shift it. Have I hurt him?
If my shirt were bloody, then I'd change it. Did I hurt him?
[Aside] No, faith; not so much as his patience.
Hurt him! His body's a passable carcass if he be not / hurt. It is a throughfare for steel if it be not hurt.
Hurt him! If he isn't hurt, his body is a fine-looking corpse. It's a highway for swords if he isn't hurt.
[Aside] His steel was in debt; it went o' th' back / side the town.
(Aside) His sword was in debt; it slunk out the back way of town to avoid paying.
The villain would not stand me.
The villain wouldn't stand and face me.
[Aside] No; but he fled forward still, toward your / face.
(Aside) No, but he kept advancing toward your face.
Stand you? You have land enough of your own; but he / added to your having, gave you some ground.
Stand and face you? You've got plenty of land of your own, but he added to it: he gave you some ground.
[Aside] As many inches as you have oceans. / Puppies!
(Aside) About as many inches as you have oceans. Puppies!
I would they had not come between us.
I wish they hadn't come between us.
[Aside] So would I, till you had measur'd how long a / fool you were upon the ground.
(Aside) So do I, until you'd measured on the ground how long a fool you are.
And that she should love this fellow, and refuse me!
And to think she loves this fellow and refuses me!
[Aside] If it be a sin to make a true election, she is / damn'd.
(Aside) If it's a sin to make the right choice, she's damned.
Sir, as I told you always, her beauty and her brain go / not together; she's a good sign, but I have seen small reflection / of her wit.
Sir, as I've always told you, her beauty and her brain don't go together. She's a fine-looking sign, but I've seen little reflection of wit in her.
[Aside] She shines not upon fools, lest the reflection / should hurt her.
(Aside) She doesn't shine on fools, in case the reflection hurts her.
Come, I'll to my chamber. Would there had been some hurt / done!
Come, I'm going to my room. I wish some real harm had been done!
[Aside] I wish not so; unless it had been the fall of / an ass, which is no great hurt.
(Aside) I don't, unless it was the fall of an ass, which is no great harm.
No, come on, let's go together.

I would thou grew'st unto the shores o' th' haven, / And questioned'st every sail; if he should write, / And I not have it, 'twere a paper lost, / As offer'd mercy is. What was the last / That he spake to thee?

I wish you'd grown roots on the shore of the harbour and questioned every ship. If he writes and I don't get it, it's as much a loss as a pardon that never arrives. What was the last thing he said to you?
It was: his queen, his queen!
Senseless linen, happier therein than I! / And that was all?
Senseless linen, luckier than I am! And was that all?

No, madam; for so long / As he could make me with his eye, or care / Distinguish him from others, he did keep / The deck, with glove, or hat, or handkerchief, / Still waving, as the fits and stirs of's mind / Could best express how slow his soul sail'd on, / How swift his ship.

No, madam. For as long as he could make me out with his eye, or I could pick him out from the others, he stayed on deck, waving his glove or hat or handkerchief, as the rush of his feelings could best show how slowly his soul sailed and how fast his ship.
Thou shouldst have made him / As little as a crow, or less, ere left / To after-eye him.
You should have watched him until he was as small as a crow, or smaller, before you stopped looking.

I would have broke mine eyestrings, crack'd them but / To look upon him, till the diminution / Of space had pointed him sharp as my needle; / Nay, followed him till he had melted from / The smallness of a gnat to air, and then / Have turn'd mine eye and wept. But, good Pisanio, / When shall we hear from him?

I would have broken my eye muscles, cracked them, just to look at him until the distance made him as thin as my needle point. No, I'd have followed him with my eyes until he melted from a gnat into air, and then turned away and wept. But, good Pisanio, when will we hear from him?
Be assur'd, madam, / With his next vantage.
Be sure, madam, at his first chance.

I did not take my leave of him, but had / Most pretty things to say. Ere I could tell him / How I would think on him at certain hours / Such thoughts and such; or I could make him swear / The shes of Italy should not betray / Mine interest and his honour; or have charg'd him, / At the sixth hour of morn, at noon, at midnight, / T' encounter me with orisons, for then / I am in heaven for him; or ere I could / Give him that parting kiss which I had set / Betwixt two charming words, comes in my father, / And like the tyrannous breathing of the north / Shakes all our buds from growing.

I didn't say goodbye to him properly, and I had such pretty things to say. Before I could tell him how I'd think of him at certain hours, with such and such thoughts; or make him swear the women of Italy wouldn't betray my rights and his honour; or tell him to meet me in prayer at six in the morning, at noon and at midnight, because then I'm in heaven for him; or before I could give him the parting kiss I had placed between two magic words, in comes my father and, like the cruel north wind, shakes all our buds before they can grow.
The Queen, madam, / Desires your Highness' company.
Madam, the Queen would like your Highness's company.
Those things I bid you do, get them dispatch'd. / I will attend the Queen.
Get those things I asked you to do done. I'll go to the Queen.

Believe it, sir, I have seen him in Britain. He was then / of a crescent note, expected to prove so worthy as since he hath / been allowed the name of. But I could then have look'd on him / without the help of admiration, though the catalogue of his / endowments had been tabled by his side, and I to peruse him by / items.

Believe me, sir, I saw him in Britain. His reputation was growing then, and people expected him to become as worthy as he's since been said to be. But I could have looked at him then without any special admiration, even with a list of his qualities posted beside him for me to check off item by item.
You speak of him when he was less furnish'd than now he / is with that which makes him both without and within.
You're speaking of him when he had less of what makes him what he is, inside and out, than he has now.
I have seen him in France; we had very many there could / behold the sun with as firm eyes as he.
I've seen him in France. We had plenty of men there who could look at the sun as steadily as he does.
This matter of marrying his king's daughter, wherein he / must be weighed rather by her value than his own, words him, I / doubt not, a great deal from the matter.
This business of marrying his king's daughter, where he's being measured by her worth more than his own, inflates his reputation well beyond the truth, I'm sure.

Ay, and the approbation of those that weep this lamentable / divorce under her colours are wonderfully to extend him, be it / but to fortify her judgment, which else an easy battery might lay / flat, for taking a beggar, without less quality. But how comes it / he is to sojourn with you? How creeps acquaintance?

Yes, and the people who mourn this sad separation on her side praise him to the skies, if only to defend her judgment, which could otherwise be easily attacked for taking a beggar with no qualities. But how does he come to be staying with you? How did you get to know him?
His father and I were soldiers together, to whom I have / been often bound for no less than my life.
His father and I were soldiers together, and I often owed him my life.

Here comes the Briton. Let him be so entertained amongst you as / suits with gentlemen of your knowing to a stranger of his / quality. I beseech you all be better known to this gentleman, / whom I commend to you as a noble friend of mine. How worthy he is / I will leave to appear hereafter, rather than story him in his / own hearing.

Here comes the Briton. Gentlemen, welcome him as men of your breeding should welcome a stranger of his rank. Please get to know this gentleman, whom I recommend to you as a noble friend. I'll let his worth show itself later rather than describe it in his hearing.
Sir, we have known together in Orleans.
Sir, we knew each other in Orleans.
Since when I have been debtor to you for courtesies, / which I will be ever to pay and yet pay still.
And I've owed you for your kindnesses ever since; I'll keep paying that debt and still owe it.

Sir, you o'errate my poor kindness. I was glad I did / atone my countryman and you; it had been pity you should have / been put together with so mortal a purpose as then each bore, / upon importance of so slight and trivial a nature.

Sir, you overvalue my small kindness. I was glad to reconcile you and my countryman. It would have been a pity for you to fight with such deadly intent, as you both meant to then, over something so slight and trivial.

By your pardon, sir. I was then a young traveller; / rather shunn'd to go even with what I heard than in my every / action to be guided by others' experiences; but upon my mended / judgment—if I offend not to say it is mended—my quarrel was not / altogether slight.

Forgive me, sir. I was a young traveller then and preferred to act on my own judgment rather than be guided by other people's experience. But now that my judgment has improved (if it's not boastful to say so), I still think my quarrel wasn't so slight.
Faith, yes, to be put to the arbitrement of swords, and / by such two that would by all likelihood have confounded one the / other or have fall'n both.
Indeed it was, to be settled by swords, and between two men who would most likely have destroyed each other or both been killed.
Can we, with manners, ask what was the difference?
May we politely ask what the quarrel was?

Safely, I think. 'Twas a contention in public, which / may, without contradiction, suffer the report. It was much like / an argument that fell out last night, where each of us fell in / praise of our country mistresses; this gentleman at that time / vouching—and upon warrant of bloody affirmation—his to be more / fair, virtuous, wise, chaste, constant, qualified, and less / attemptable, than any the rarest of our ladies in France.

Safely, I think. It was a public argument, so it can be reported. It was much like the argument last night, when each of us praised the women of our own countries. This gentleman insisted then, and offered to prove it in blood, that his lady was more beautiful, virtuous, wise, chaste, faithful, accomplished and harder to seduce than the finest ladies of France.
That lady is not now living, or this gentleman's opinion, / by this, worn out.
Either that lady is dead by now, or this gentleman's opinion has worn out.
She holds her virtue still, and I my mind.
She still keeps her virtue, and I my opinion.
You must not so far prefer her fore ours of Italy.
You can't rank her so far above our Italian ladies.
Being so far provok'd as I was in France, I would abate / her nothing, though I profess myself her adorer, not her friend.
If I were provoked as I was in France, I wouldn't lower her one bit, though I'm her worshipper, not merely her lover.

As fair and as good—a kind of hand-in-hand comparison— / had been something too fair and too good for any lady in Britain. / If she went before others I have seen as that diamond of yours / outlustres many I have beheld, I could not but believe she / excelled many; but I have not seen the most precious diamond that / is, nor you the lady.

To call her as beautiful and as good as ours, side by side, would already be too much praise for any lady in Britain. If she outshone the women I've seen the way your diamond outshines many I've seen, I'd have to believe she excelled many. But I haven't seen the most precious diamond in the world, and you haven't seen the most precious lady.
I prais'd her as I rated her. So do I my stone.
I praised her at the value I put on her. I do the same with my stone.
What do you esteem it at?
What do you value it at?
More than the whole world owns.
Either your unparagon'd mistress is dead, or she's / outpriz'd by a trifle.
Then either your matchless lady is dead, or she's worth less than a trinket.
You are mistaken: the one may be sold or given, if there / were wealth enough for the purchase or merit for the gift; the / other is not a thing for sale, and only the gift of the gods.
You're wrong. The ring can be sold or given, if anyone were rich enough to buy it or worthy enough to receive it. The lady is not for sale; she can only be a gift from the gods.
Which the gods have given you?
And the gods have given her to you?
Which by their graces I will keep.
And by their grace I'll keep her.

You may wear her in title yours; but you know strange fowl / light upon neighbouring ponds. Your ring may be stol'n too. So / your brace of unprizable estimations, the one is but frail and / the other casual; a cunning thief, or a that-way-accomplish'd / courtier, would hazard the winning both of first and last.

She may be yours in name, but you know strange birds land on neighbouring ponds. Your ring may be stolen too. Of your two priceless treasures, one is frail and the other can be lost by chance. A clever thief, or a courtier skilled in that line, would risk trying to win both.

Your Italy contains none so accomplish'd a courtier to / convince the honour of my mistress, if in the holding or loss of / that you term her frail. I do nothing doubt you have store of / thieves; notwithstanding, I fear not my ring.

Your Italy has no courtier skilled enough to overcome my lady's honour, if it's in keeping or losing that you call her frail. I don't doubt you have plenty of thieves; still, I'm not worried about my ring.
Sir, with all my heart. This worthy signior, I thank / him, makes no stranger of me; we are familiar at first.
Sir, with all my heart. This worthy gentleman, I thank him, doesn't treat me as a stranger; we're on familiar terms already.
With five times so much conversation I should get ground / of your fair mistress; make her go back even to the yielding, had / I admittance and opportunity to friend.
With five times as much talk I'd gain ground on your lovely lady, and make her retreat all the way to giving in, if I had access and opportunity on my side.

I dare thereupon pawn the moiety of my estate to your / ring, which, in my opinion, o'ervalues it something. But I make / my wager rather against your confidence than her reputation; and, / to bar your offence herein too, I durst attempt it against any / lady in the world.

I'd dare to bet half my fortune against your ring on it, which in my opinion is worth rather less. But I'm betting against your confidence, not her reputation. And to spare you offence, I'd dare to try it against any lady in the world.
You are a great deal abus'd in too bold a persuasion, / and I doubt not you sustain what y'are worthy of by your attempt.
You're badly mistaken in being so sure of yourself, and I'm sure your attempt would get you what you deserve.
A repulse; though your attempt, as you call it, deserve / more—a punishment too.
A rejection. Though your attempt, as you call it, deserves more: a punishment too.
Gentlemen, enough of this. It came in too suddenly; let / it die as it was born, and I pray you be better acquainted.
Gentlemen, enough of this. It came up too suddenly; let it die as quickly as it was born, and please get to know each other better.
Would I had put my estate and my neighbour's on th' / approbation of what I have spoke!
I wish I'd bet my estate and my neighbour's on the truth of what I said!
What lady would you choose to assail?
Which lady would you choose to attack?

Yours, whom in constancy you think stands so safe. I will / lay you ten thousand ducats to your ring that, commend me to the / court where your lady is, with no more advantage than the / opportunity of a second conference, and I will bring from thence / that honour of hers which you imagine so reserv'd.

Yours, whom you think so safe in her faithfulness. I'll bet you ten thousand ducats against your ring that, if you give me an introduction to the court where your lady is, with no more advantage than the chance of a second meeting, I'll bring back from there that honour of hers which you think so well guarded.
I will wage against your gold, gold to it. My ring I / hold dear as my finger; 'tis part of it.
I'll bet gold against your gold. My ring I hold as dear as my finger; it's part of it.
You are a friend, and therein the wiser. If you buy / ladies' flesh at a million a dram, you cannot preserve it from / tainting. But I see you have some religion in you, that you fear.

You're her lover, and so you're the wiser not to risk it. If you bought ladies' flesh at a million a gram, you still couldn't keep it from going bad. But I see you have some religious scruple: you're afraid.
This is but a custom in your tongue; you bear a graver / purpose, I hope.
That's just a habit of your tongue. You have a more serious purpose, I hope.
I am the master of my speeches, and would undergo what's / spoken, I swear.
I'm the master of what I say, and I'll undertake what I've said, I swear.

Will you? I Shall but lend my diamond till your return. / Let there be covenants drawn between's. My mistress exceeds in / goodness the hugeness of your unworthy thinking. I dare you to / this match: here's my ring.

Will you? Then I'll only be lending you my diamond till you come back. Let's have an agreement drawn up between us. My lady's goodness is greater than the size of your unworthy thoughts. I dare you to this bet: here's my ring.
I will have it no lay.
I won't allow it as a bet.

By the gods, it is one. If I bring you no sufficient / testimony that I have enjoy'd the dearest bodily part of your / mistress, my ten thousand ducats are yours; so is your diamond / too. If I come off, and leave her in such honour as you have / trust in, she your jewel, this your jewel, and my gold are yours— / provided I have your commendation for my more free entertainment.

By the gods, it is one. If I don't bring you enough proof that I've enjoyed the dearest part of your lady's body, my ten thousand ducats are yours, and so is your diamond. If I fail, and leave her as honourable as you trust she is, then she your jewel, this your jewel, and my gold are all yours, provided you give me a letter of introduction to get me a warmer welcome.

I embrace these conditions; let us have articles betwixt / us. Only, thus far you shall answer: if you make your voyage upon / her, and give me directly to understand you have prevail'd, I am / no further your enemy—she is not worth our debate; if she remain / unseduc'd, you not making it appear otherwise, for your ill / opinion and th' assault you have made to her chastity you shall / answer me with your sword.

I accept these terms; let's have a contract between us. But on one point you'll answer to me: if you succeed with her and tell me plainly that you've won, I'm no longer your enemy, because she isn't worth our quarrel. If she stays unseduced and you can't show otherwise, then for your low opinion and your attack on her chastity you'll answer to me with your sword.

Your hand—a covenant! We will have these things set down / by lawful counsel, and straight away for Britain, lest the / bargain should catch cold and starve. I will fetch my gold and / have our two wagers recorded.

Your hand: it's a deal! We'll have it all written down by a lawyer, and I'll set off for Britain right away, before the bargain catches cold and dies. I'll fetch my gold and have both our stakes recorded.
Do you think this will go ahead?
Signior Iachimo will not from it. Pray let us follow 'em.
Signor Iachimo won't back out of it. Let's follow them.
Whiles yet the dew's on ground, gather those flowers; / Make haste; who has the note of them?
While the dew is still on the ground, gather those flowers. Hurry. Who has the list?
Now, Master Doctor, have you brought those drugs?
Now, Master Doctor, have you brought those drugs?
Pleaseth your Highness, ay. Here they are, madam.
Yes, if it please your Highness. Here they are, madam.

But I beseech your Grace, without offence— / My conscience bids me ask—wherefore you have / Commanded of me these most poisonous compounds / Which are the movers of a languishing death, / But, though slow, deadly?
But I beg your Grace, without offence (my conscience tells me to ask), why have you ordered these very poisonous mixtures from me, which cause a slow, wasting death, slow but deadly?

I wonder, Doctor, / Thou ask'st me such a question. Have I not been / Thy pupil long? Hast thou not learn'd me how / To make perfumes? distil? preserve? yea, so / That our great king himself doth woo me oft / For my confections? Having thus far proceeded— / Unless thou think'st me devilish—is't not meet / That I did amplify my judgment in / Other conclusions? I will try the forces / Of these thy compounds on such creatures as / We count not worth the hanging—but none human— / To try the vigour of them, and apply / Allayments to their act, and by them gather / Their several virtues and effects.

I'm surprised you ask me that, Doctor. Haven't I been your pupil for a long time? Haven't you taught me to make perfumes, to distil, to preserve, so well that the great King himself often begs me for my concoctions? Having come this far (unless you think I'm a devil), isn't it right that I should widen my knowledge into other experiments? I'll test the strength of your mixtures on creatures we don't think worth hanging, but no humans, to see how powerful they are, try out remedies against them, and so learn their various properties and effects.
Your Highness / Shall from this practice but make hard your heart; / Besides, the seeing these effects will be / Both noisome and infectious.
Your Highness will only harden your heart by this practice. Besides, watching these effects will be both disgusting and unhealthy.
[Aside] Here comes a flattering rascal; upon him / Will I first work. He's for his master, / An enemy to my son.—How now, Pisanio! / Doctor, your service for this time is ended; / Take your own way.
(Aside) Here comes a flattering rascal. I'll work on him first. He's on his master's side, and an enemy to my son. (Aloud) Hello, Pisanio! Doctor, I don't need you any more for now. Off you go.
[Aside] I do suspect you, madam; / But you shall do no harm.
(Aside) I suspect you, madam, but you won't do any harm.
(To Pisanio) Listen, a word with you.

[Aside] I do not like her. She doth think she has / Strange ling'ring poisons. I do know her spirit, / And will not trust one of her malice with / A drug of such damn'd nature. Those she has / Will stupefy and dull the sense awhile, / Which first perchance she'll prove on cats and dogs, / Then afterward up higher; but there is / No danger in what show of death it makes, / More than the locking up the spirits a time, / To be more fresh, reviving. She is fool'd / With a most false effect; and I the truer / So to be false with her.

(Aside) I don't like her. She thinks she has strange slow poisons. I know her nature and won't trust anyone so spiteful with a drug that deadly. What I've given her will stun and deaden the senses for a while. She'll probably test it first on cats and dogs, then on higher creatures. But there's no danger in the appearance of death it causes, beyond shutting down the vital spirits for a time, so they revive all the fresher. She's fooled by a completely false effect, and I'm all the more honest for being false to her.
No further service, Doctor, / Until I send for thee.
I don't need you any more, Doctor, until I send for you.

Weeps she still, say'st thou? Dost thou think in time / She will not quench, and let instructions enter / Where folly now possesses? Do thou work. / When thou shalt bring me word she loves my son, / I'll tell thee on the instant thou art then / As great as is thy master; greater, for / His fortunes all lie speechless, and his name / Is at last gasp. Return he cannot, nor / Continue where he is. To shift his being / Is to exchange one misery with another, / And every day that comes comes comes to / A day's work in him. What shalt thou expect / To be depender on a thing that leans, / Who cannot be new built, nor has no friends / So much as but to prop him?

Is she still crying, you say? Don't you think that in time she'll cool off and let good advice in where foolishness rules now? Work on her. When you bring me word that she loves my son, I'll tell you on the spot that you're as great as your master; greater, because his fortunes are struck dumb and his name is at its last gasp. He can't come back, and he can't stay where he is. To move would be to swap one misery for another, and every new day only undoes another day's work in him. What can you hope for by depending on a falling thing that can't be rebuilt and hasn't a friend to prop it up?

Thou tak'st up / Thou know'st not what; but take it for thy labour. / It is a thing I made, which hath the King / Five times redeem'd from death. I do not know / What is more cordial. Nay, I prithee take it; / It is an earnest of a further good / That I mean to thee. Tell thy mistress how / The case stands with her; do't as from thyself. / Think what a chance thou changest on; but think / Thou hast thy mistress still; to boot, my son, / Who shall take notice of thee. I'll move the King / To any shape of thy preferment, such / As thou'lt desire; and then myself, I chiefly, / That set thee on to this desert, am bound / To load thy merit richly. Call my women. / Think on my words.

You're picking up you don't know what, but keep it for your trouble. It's something I made that has saved the King from death five times. I don't know a better restorative. No, please take it. It's a down payment on more good things I mean to do for you. Tell your mistress how things stand for her; say it as if it came from you. Think what a chance you're getting to change sides; and think that you'll still have your mistress, and my son into the bargain, who'll take notice of you. I'll persuade the King to promote you any way you like, and I myself, who set you on to earn it, will be bound to reward you richly. Call my women. Think about what I've said.

A sly and constant knave, / Not to be shak'd; the agent for his master, / And the remembrancer of her to hold / The hand-fast to her lord. I have given him that / Which, if he take, shall quite unpeople her / Of leigers for her sweet; and which she after, / Except she bend her humour, shall be assur'd / To taste of too.

A sly, loyal rogue who can't be shaken: his master's agent, and the one who reminds her to keep her vow to her husband. I've given him something which, if he takes it, will rid her of all her sweetheart's messengers; and which she'll be sure to taste too afterwards, unless she changes her mind.
So, so. Well done, well done. / The violets, cowslips, and the primroses, / Bear to my closet. Fare thee well, Pisanio; / Think on my words.
Good, good. Well done. Take the violets, cowslips and primroses to my room. Goodbye, Pisanio. Think about what I've said.
And shall do. / But when to my good lord I prove untrue / I'll choke myself—there's all I'll do for you.
And I will. But when I prove untrue to my good lord, I'll strangle myself. That's all I'll do for you.

A father cruel and a step-dame false; / A foolish suitor to a wedded lady / That hath her husband banish'd. O, that husband! / My supreme crown of grief! and those repeated / Vexations of it! Had I been thief-stol'n, / As my two brothers, happy! but most miserable / Is the desire that's glorious. Blessed be those, / How mean soe'er, that have their honest wills, / Which seasons comfort. Who may this be? Fie!

A cruel father and a false stepmother; a foolish suitor chasing a married lady whose husband has been banished. Oh, that husband, the supreme crown of my grief, and all its repeated torments! If I'd been stolen by thieves like my two brothers, I'd be happy. But a desire set on a high, glorious thing is the most miserable. Blessed are those, however humble, who can have their honest wishes; that makes comfort sweet. Who could this be? Oh, no!
Madam, a noble gentleman of Rome / Comes from my lord with letters.
Madam, a noble gentleman from Rome has come with letters from my lord.
Change you, madam? / The worthy Leonatus is in safety, / And greets your Highness dearly. [Presents a letter]
You change colour, madam? The worthy Leonatus is safe and sends your Highness loving greetings. (He gives her a letter.)
Thanks, good sir. / You're kindly welcome.
Thank you, good sir. You're very welcome.

[Aside] All of her that is out of door most rich! / If she be furnish'd with a mind so rare, / She is alone th' Arabian bird, and I / Have lost the wager. Boldness be my friend! / Arm me, audacity, from head to foot! / Or, like the Parthian, I shall flying fight; / Rather, directly fly.

(Aside) Everything on the outside of her is splendid! If she has a mind as rare as that, she's the one and only phoenix, and I've lost the bet. Boldness, be my friend! Daring, arm me from head to foot! Or I'll have to fight while retreating, like the Parthians; or rather, simply run.

[Reads] 'He is one of the noblest note, to whose / kindnesses I am most infinitely tied. Reflect upon him / accordingly, as you value your trust. Leonatus.' / So far I read aloud; / But even the very middle of my heart / Is warm'd by th' rest and takes it thankfully. / You are as welcome, worthy sir, as I / Have words to bid you; and shall find it so / In all that I can do.

(Reading) "He is a man of the highest reputation, to whose kindness I am bound beyond measure. Treat him accordingly, as you value your loyalty to me. Leonatus." That much I read aloud, but the rest warms the very centre of my heart, and it accepts it gratefully. You are as welcome, worthy sir, as I have words to say, and you'll find it so in everything I can do.

Thanks, fairest lady. / What, are men mad? Hath nature given them eyes / To see this vaulted arch and the rich crop / Of sea and land, which can distinguish 'twixt / The fiery orbs above and the twinn'd stones / Upon the number'd beach, and can we not / Partition make with spectacles so precious / 'Twixt fair and foul?

Thank you, fairest lady. (As if to himself) Are men mad? Has nature given them eyes to see the arch of the sky and the rich harvest of sea and land, eyes that can tell the blazing stars above from the identical pebbles on the beach, and can't we, with such precious instruments, tell fair from foul?
What are you so amazed at?

It cannot be i' th' eye, for apes and monkeys, / 'Twixt two such shes, would chatter this way and / Contemn with mows the other; nor i' th' judgment, / For idiots in this case of favour would / Be wisely definite; nor i' th' appetite; / Sluttery, to such neat excellence oppos'd, / Should make desire vomit emptiness, / Not so allur'd to feed.

The fault can't be in the eye, because apes and monkeys, between two such women, would chatter in favour of this one and pull faces at the other. Nor in the judgment, because even idiots would decide wisely on this question of beauty. Nor in the appetite: filth, set against such pure excellence, would make desire throw up on an empty stomach, not tempt it to feed.
The cloyed will— / That satiate yet unsatisfied desire, that tub / Both fill'd and running—ravening first the lamb, / Longs after for the garbage.
The overfed appetite, that desire which is stuffed but never satisfied, like a tub that's both full and leaking, first devours the lamb and then craves the garbage.
What, dear sir, / Thus raps you? Are you well?
What, dear sir, has carried you away like this? Are you well?
Thanks, madam; well.—Beseech you, sir, / Desire my man's abode where I did leave him. / He's strange and peevish.
Thank you, madam, I'm well. (To Pisanio) Please, sir, go to my servant where I left him. He's a stranger here and easily upset.
I was going, sir, / To give him welcome.
I was just going, sir, to welcome him.
Continues well my lord? His health beseech you?
Is my lord still well? How is his health, please?
Is he dispos'd to mirth? I hope he is.
Is he in good spirits? I hope he is.
Exceeding pleasant; none a stranger there / So merry and so gamesome. He is call'd / The Britain reveller.
Extremely cheerful. No foreigner there is so merry and playful. They call him the British party-goer.
When he was here / He did incline to sadness, and oft-times / Not knowing why.
When he was here he tended to be sad, and often without knowing why.

I never saw him sad. / There is a Frenchman his companion, one / An eminent monsieur that, it seems, much loves / A Gallian girl at home. He furnaces / The thick sighs from him; whiles the jolly Briton— / Your lord, I mean—laughs from's free lungs, cries 'O, / Can my sides hold, to think that man—who knows / By history, report, or his own proof, / What woman is, yea, what she cannot choose / But must be—will's free hours languish for / Assured bondage?'

I never saw him sad. He has a companion there, a Frenchman, a distinguished gentleman who apparently loves a French girl back home very much. He pumps out heavy sighs like a furnace, while the jolly Briton (your lord, I mean) laughs from the bottom of his lungs and cries, "Oh, my sides will split, to think that a man who knows from history, gossip or his own experience what woman is, yes, what she can't help being, would waste his free hours pining for certain slavery!"
Ay, madam, with his eyes in flood with laughter. / It is a recreation to be by / And hear him mock the Frenchman. But heavens know / Some men are much to blame.
Yes, madam, with his eyes streaming with laughter. It's a treat to be there and hear him mock the Frenchman. But heaven knows some men are much to blame.

Not he; but yet heaven's bounty towards him might / Be us'd more thankfully. In himself, 'tis much; / In you, which I account his, beyond all talents. / Whilst I am bound to wonder, I am bound / To pity too.

Not he; but still, he could be more grateful for heaven's generosity to him. What he has in himself is a lot; what he has in you, which I count as his, is beyond all wealth. While I have to wonder at it, I also have to pity.
Two people, with all my heart.
Am I one, sir? / You look on me: what wreck discern you in me / Deserves your pity?
Am I one of them, sir? You're looking at me. What ruin do you see in me that deserves your pity?
Lamentable! What, / To hide me from the radiant sun and solace / I' th' dungeon by a snuff?
How sad! What, to hide from the radiant sun and take comfort in a dungeon by a candle stub?
I pray you, sir, / Deliver with more openness your answers / To my demands. Why do you pity me?
Please, sir, answer my questions more openly. Why do you pity me?
That others do, / I was about to say, enjoy your—But / It is an office of the gods to venge it, / Not mine to speak on't.
That others, I was about to say, enjoy your... But it's for the gods to take revenge for it, not for me to speak of it.

You do seem to know / Something of me, or what concerns me; pray you— / Since doubting things go ill often hurts more / Than to be sure they do; for certainties / Either are past remedies, or, timely knowing, / The remedy then born—discover to me / What both you spur and stop.

You seem to know something about me, or something that concerns me. Please, since suspecting that things are wrong often hurts more than knowing they are (because certainties are either past cure or, if known in time, bring their cure with them), tell me what you keep starting to say and then stopping.

Had I this cheek / To bathe my lips upon; this hand, whose touch, / Whose every touch, would force the feeler's soul / To th' oath of loyalty; this object, which / Takes prisoner the wild motion of mine eye, / Fixing it only here; should I, damn'd then, / Slaver with lips as common as the stairs / That mount the Capitol; join gripes with hands / Made hard with hourly falsehood—falsehood as / With labour; then by-peeping in an eye / Base and illustrious as the smoky light / That's fed with stinking tallow—it were fit / That all the plagues of hell should at one time / Encounter such revolt.

If I had this cheek to bathe my lips on, this hand whose every touch would force the toucher's soul to swear loyalty, this face that captures my wandering eye and fixes it here alone, would I then, damned for it, slobber on lips as common as the steps up to the Capitol, clasp hands made hard by hourly lying (lying as if it were hard work), then peep sideways into an eye as low and as bright as a smoky candle fed on stinking fat? It would be right for all the plagues of hell to strike such betrayal at once.
My lord, I fear, / Has forgot Britain.
My lord, I'm afraid, has forgotten Britain.
And himself. Not I / Inclin'd to this intelligence pronounce / The beggary of his change; but 'tis your graces / That from my mutest conscience to my tongue / Charms this report out.
And himself. I'm not eager to spread this news of how low he's sunk, but your graces charm this report from my silent conscience onto my tongue.

O dearest soul, your cause doth strike my heart / With pity that doth make me sick! A lady / So fair, and fasten'd to an empery, / Would make the great'st king double, to be partner'd / With tomboys hir'd with that self exhibition / Which your own coffers yield! with diseas'd ventures / That play with all infirmities for gold / Which rottenness can lend nature! such boil'd stuff / As well might poison poison! Be reveng'd; / Or she that bore you was no queen, and you / Recoil from your great stock.

Oh dearest soul, your situation strikes my heart with a pity that makes me sick! A lady so beautiful, and heir to an empire that would double the greatest king, to be put on a level with whores hired with the very allowance your own treasury pays him! With diseased prostitutes who gamble for gold with every sickness rottenness can give a body! Such stewed filth that it could poison poison! Get revenge, or the woman who gave birth to you was no queen, and you fall short of your great family.
Reveng'd? / How should I be reveng'd? If this be true— / As I have such a heart that both mine ears / Must not in haste abuse—if it be true, / How should I be reveng'd?
Revenge? How should I get revenge? If this is true (and my heart is such that I mustn't let my ears deceive it in a hurry), if it's true, how should I get revenge?

Should he make me / Live like Diana's priest betwixt cold sheets, / Whiles he is vaulting variable ramps, / In your despite, upon your purse? Revenge it. / I dedicate myself to your sweet pleasure, / More noble than that runagate to your bed, / And will continue fast to your affection, / Still close as sure.

Should he make me live like a priestess of Diana between cold sheets, while he leaps on changing whores, to spite you, and with your money? Get revenge for it. I offer myself to your sweet pleasure, nobler than that runaway from your bed, and I'll stay faithful to your love, as secret as I am loyal.
Let me my service tender on your lips.
Let me offer my service on your lips.

Away! I do condemn mine ears that have / So long attended thee. If thou wert honourable, / Thou wouldst have told this tale for virtue, not / For such an end thou seek'st, as base as strange. / Thou wrong'st a gentleman who is as far / From thy report as thou from honour; and / Solicits here a lady that disdains / Thee and the devil alike.—What ho, Pisanio!— / The King my father shall be made acquainted / Of thy assault. If he shall think it fit / A saucy stranger in his court to mart / As in a Romish stew, and to expound / His beastly mind to us, he hath a court / He little cares for, and a daughter who / He not respects at all.—What ho, Pisanio!

Get away! I blame my ears for listening to you so long. If you were honourable, you'd have told this story to serve virtue, not for the purpose you're after, as low as it is strange. You slander a gentleman who is as far from your report as you are from honour, and you try to seduce a lady who despises you and the devil alike. Pisanio! The King my father will be told of your attack. If he thinks it right for an insolent stranger to bargain in his court as if it were a Roman brothel, and to lay out his beastly mind to us, then he has a court he cares little for, and a daughter he doesn't respect at all. Pisanio!

O happy Leonatus! I may say / The credit that thy lady hath of thee / Deserves thy trust, and thy most perfect goodness / Her assur'd credit. Blessed live you long, / A lady to the worthiest sir that ever / Country call'd his! and you his mistress, only / For the most worthiest fit! Give me your pardon. / I have spoke this to know if your affiance / Were deeply rooted, and shall make your lord / That which he is new o'er; and he is one / The truest manner'd, such a holy witch / That he enchants societies into him, / Half all men's hearts are his.

Oh, lucky Leonatus! I can say your lady's faith in you deserves your trust, and your perfect goodness deserves her certain faith. Long may you both live happily, a lady married to the worthiest gentleman any country ever called its own, and you his lady, fit only for the worthiest! Forgive me. I said all that to find out whether your faith was deeply rooted, and I'll make your lord what he already is all over again. He's the most truly well-bred of men, such a holy enchanter that he charms company to him; half of every man's heart is his.

He sits 'mongst men like a descended god: / He hath a kind of honour sets him of / More than a mortal seeming. Be not angry, / Most mighty Princess, that I have adventur'd / To try your taking of a false report, which hath / Honour'd with confirmation your great judgment / In the election of a sir so rare, / Which you know cannot err. The love I bear him / Made me to fan you thus; but the gods made you, / Unlike all others, chaffless. Pray your pardon.

He sits among men like a god come down to earth. He has a kind of honour that makes him look more than mortal. Don't be angry, most mighty Princess, that I dared to test how you'd take a false report, which has proved again your great judgment in choosing so rare a gentleman, a judgment you know can't go wrong. My love for him made me winnow you like this, but the gods made you, unlike everyone else, without chaff. Please forgive me.
All's well, sir; take my pow'r i' th' court for yours.
All's well, sir. Use my power at court as if it were your own.

My humble thanks. I had almost forgot / T' entreat your Grace but in a small request, / And yet of moment too, for it concerns / Your lord; myself and other noble friends / Are partners in the business.
My humble thanks. I almost forgot to ask your Grace a small favour, though an important one, since it concerns your lord. I and some other noble friends are partners in the business.

Some dozen Romans of us, and your lord— / The best feather of our wing—have mingled sums / To buy a present for the Emperor; / Which I, the factor for the rest, have done / In France. 'Tis plate of rare device, and jewels / Of rich and exquisite form, their values great; / And I am something curious, being strange, / To have them in safe stowage. May it please you / To take them in protection?

About a dozen of us Romans, and your lord (the best feather in our wing), have pooled money to buy a present for the Emperor. I bought it in France as agent for the others. It's silver plate of rare design and jewels of rich and exquisite form, of great value, and being a stranger here I'm rather anxious to have them stored safely. Would you be willing to keep them?
Willingly; / And pawn mine honour for their safety. Since / My lord hath interest in them, I will keep them / In my bedchamber.
Gladly, and I'll stake my honour on their safety. Since my lord has a share in them, I'll keep them in my bedroom.
They are in a trunk, / Attended by my men. I will make bold / To send them to you only for this night; / I must aboard to-morrow.
They're in a trunk, guarded by my men. I'll be bold enough to send it to you just for tonight. I must go aboard ship tomorrow.
Yes, I beseech; or I shall short my word / By length'ning my return. From Gallia / I cross'd the seas on purpose and on promise / To see your Grace.
Yes, I'm afraid so, or I'll break my word by delaying my return. I crossed the sea from France on purpose, and as I'd promised, to see your Grace.
I thank you for your pains. / But not away to-morrow!
Thank you for your trouble. But don't leave tomorrow!
O, I must, madam. / Therefore I shall beseech you, if you please / To greet your lord with writing, do't to-night. / I have outstood my time, which is material / 'To th' tender of our present.
Oh, I must, madam. So, if you'd like to send your lord a letter, please write it tonight. I've already overstayed my time, which matters for the delivery of our present.
I will write. / Send your trunk to me; it shall safe be kept / And truly yielded you. You're very welcome.
I'll write. Send your trunk to me. It will be kept safe and faithfully returned to you. You're very welcome.

Was there ever man had such luck! When I kiss'd the jack, / upon an up-cast to be hit away! I had a hundred pound on't; and / then a whoreson jackanapes must take me up for swearing, as if I / borrowed mine oaths of him, and might not spend them at my / pleasure.

Was there ever a man with such luck! When I'd kissed the jack, to have my bowl knocked away at the last throw! I had a hundred pounds on it. And then some son-of-a-whore of a monkey has to tell me off for swearing, as if I'd borrowed my oaths from him and couldn't spend them as I like.
What got he by that? You have broke his pate with your / bowl.
What did he get for it? You broke his head with your bowl.
[Aside] If his wit had been like him that broke it, it / would have run all out.
(Aside) If his brains had been like the man who broke it, they'd all have run out.
When a gentleman is dispos'd to swear, it is not for any / standers-by to curtail his oaths. Ha?
When a gentleman feels like swearing, it's not for bystanders to cut his oaths short. Right?
No, my lord; [Aside] nor crop the ears of them.
No, my lord. (Aside) Nor to crop their ears either.
Whoreson dog! I give him satisfaction? Would he had been / one of my rank!
Son-of-a-whore dog! Me give him satisfaction in a duel? I wish he'd been of my rank!
[Aside] To have smell'd like a fool.
(Aside) So he'd smell like a fool too.

I am not vex'd more at anything in th' earth. A pox on't! I / had rather not be so noble as I am; they dare not fight with me, / because of the Queen my mother. Every jackslave hath his bellyful / of fighting, and I must go up and down like a cock that nobody / can match.

Nothing on earth annoys me more. Damn it! I'd rather not be as noble as I am. They don't dare fight me because of my mother the Queen. Every low servant gets his fill of fighting, and I have to strut about like a fighting cock nobody can match.
[Aside] You are cock and capon too; and you crow, / cock, with your comb on.
(Aside) You're a cock and a capon too, and you crow like a cock with your coxcomb on.
It is not fit your lordship should undertake every / companion that you give offence to.
It's not right for your lordship to take on every fellow you offend.
No, I know that; but it is fit I should commit offence to / my inferiors.
No, I know that. But it's right for me to offend my inferiors.
Ay, it is fit for your lordship only.
Yes, that's right for your lordship alone.
Did you hear of a stranger that's come to court / to-night?
Did you hear about a stranger who came to court tonight?
A stranger, and I not known on't?
A stranger, and I wasn't told?
[Aside] He's a strange fellow himself, and knows it / not.
(Aside) He's a strange fellow himself and doesn't know it.
There's an Italian come, and, 'tis thought, one of / Leonatus' friends.
An Italian has arrived, thought to be one of Leonatus's friends.
Leonatus? A banish'd rascal; and he's another, whatsoever / he be. Who told you of this stranger?
Leonatus? A banished scoundrel; and this one's another, whoever he is. Who told you about this stranger?
Is it fit I went to look upon him? Is there no derogation / in't?
Would it be suitable for me to go and look at him? Would it lower my dignity?
You can't be lowered, my lord.
[Aside] You are a fool granted; therefore your issues, / being foolish, do not derogate.
(Aside) You're an acknowledged fool, so your actions, being foolish, can't lower you.
Come, I'll go see this Italian. What I have lost to-day at / bowls I'll win to-night of him. Come, go.
Come on, I'll go and see this Italian. What I've lost at bowls today I'll win off him tonight. Come on.

That such a crafty devil as is his mother / Should yield the world this ass! A woman that / Bears all down with her brain; and this her son / Cannot take two from twenty, for his heart, / And leave eighteen. Alas, poor princess, / Thou divine Imogen, what thou endur'st, / Betwixt a father by thy step-dame govern'd, / A mother hourly coining plots, a wooer / More hateful than the foul expulsion is / Of thy dear husband, than that horrid act / Of the divorce he'd make! The heavens hold firm / The walls of thy dear honour, keep unshak'd / That temple, thy fair mind, that thou mayst stand / T' enjoy thy banish'd lord and this great land!

That such a crafty devil as his mother should give the world this ass! A woman who overpowers everything with her brain, and this son of hers can't take two from twenty and leave eighteen to save his life. Alas, poor princess, divine Imogen, what you endure: between a father ruled by your stepmother, a stepmother hatching plots every hour, and a suitor more hateful than the cruel banishment of your dear husband or the horrible divorce he'd make! May the heavens keep the walls of your honour strong and that temple, your pure mind, unshaken, so that you may live to enjoy your banished lord and this great country!

I have read three hours then. Mine eyes are weak; / Fold down the leaf where I have left. To bed. / Take not away the taper, leave it burning; / And if thou canst awake by four o' th' clock, / I prithee call me. Sleep hath seiz'd me wholly.

Then I've been reading for three hours. My eyes are tired. Fold down the page where I stopped. Go to bed. Don't take the candle away; leave it burning. And if you can wake at four o'clock, please call me. Sleep has taken hold of me completely.
To your protection I commend me, gods. / From fairies and the tempters of the night / Guard me, beseech ye!
I put myself in your protection, gods. Guard me from fairies and the tempters of the night, I beg you!

The crickets sing, and man's o'er-labour'd sense / Repairs itself by rest. Our Tarquin thus / Did softly press the rushes ere he waken'd / The chastity he wounded. Cytherea, / How bravely thou becom'st thy bed! fresh lily, / And whiter than the sheets! That I might touch! / But kiss; one kiss! Rubies unparagon'd, / How dearly they do't! 'Tis her breathing that / Perfumes the chamber thus. The flame o' th' taper / Bows toward her and would under-peep her lids / To see th' enclosed lights, now canopied / Under these windows white and azure, lac'd / With blue of heaven's own tinct. But my design / To note the chamber. I will write all down: / Such and such pictures; there the window; such / Th' adornment of her bed; the arras, figures— / Why, such and such; and the contents o' th' story. / Ah, but some natural notes about her body / Above ten thousand meaner movables / Would testify, t' enrich mine inventory. / O sleep, thou ape of death, lie dull upon her! / And be her sense but as a monument, / Thus in a chapel lying! Come off, come off;

The crickets are singing, and man's overworked senses are restoring themselves by rest. This is how our Tarquin stepped softly on the rushes before he woke the chastity he wounded. Venus, how beautifully you suit your bed! Fresh lily, whiter than the sheets! If only I could touch! Just kiss; one kiss! Matchless rubies, how sweetly they press together! It's her breath that perfumes the room like this. The candle flame bends toward her and wants to peep under her eyelids to see the lights shut in there, now curtained under these white and blue lids, laced with veins the colour of the sky. But my plan is to note the room. I'll write it all down: such and such pictures; the window there; her bed decorated like this; the tapestry, its figures, so and so, and what story it tells. Ah, but some natural marks on her body would be better evidence than ten thousand lesser furnishings, and would enrich my list. Oh sleep, you imitation of death, lie heavy on her, and let her senses be like a stone effigy lying in a chapel! Come off, come off;

As slippery as the Gordian knot was hard! / 'Tis mine; and this will witness outwardly, / As strongly as the conscience does within, / To th' madding of her lord. On her left breast / A mole cinque-spotted, like the crimson drops / I' th' bottom of a cowslip. Here's a voucher / Stronger than ever law could make; this secret / Will force him think I have pick'd the lock and ta'en / The treasure of her honour. No more. To what end? / Why should I write this down that's riveted, / Screw'd to my memory? She hath been reading late / The tale of Tereus; here the leaf's turn'd down / Where Philomel gave up. I have enough. / To th' trunk again, and shut the spring of it. / Swift, swift, you dragons of the night, that dawning / May bare the raven's eye! I lodge in fear; / Though this a heavenly angel, hell is here. [Clock strikes] / One, two, three. Time, time!

as slippery as the Gordian knot was tight! It's mine, and this will be outward proof, as strong as his conscience is within, to drive her lord mad. On her left breast there's a mole with five spots, like the red drops at the bottom of a cowslip. Here's proof stronger than any law could produce. This secret will force him to think I've picked the lock and taken the treasure of her honour. No more. What for? Why write down what's riveted and screwed into my memory? She's been reading late: the story of Tereus. Here's the page turned down where Philomel gave in. I have enough. Back into the trunk, and shut its spring. Hurry, hurry, you dragons that pull the night, so that dawn may open the raven's eye! I'm lodged in fear. Though this is a heavenly angel, hell is here. (A clock strikes.) One, two, three. Time, time!
Your lordship is the most patient man in loss, the most / coldest that ever turn'd up ace.
Your lordship is the most patient man when losing, the coolest who ever threw a one.
It would make any man cold to lose.
Losing would make any man cool.
But not every man patient after the noble temper of / your lordship. You are most hot and furious when you win.
But not every man as patient as your lordship's noble temper. You're hot and furious only when you win.
Winning will put any man into courage. If I could get this / foolish Imogen, I should have gold enough. It's almost morning, / is't not?
Winning puts courage into any man. If I could get this foolish Imogen, I'd have gold enough. It's almost morning, isn't it?
I would this music would come. I am advised to give her / music a mornings; they say it will penetrate.
I wish those musicians would come. I've been advised to play her music in the mornings; they say it will get through to her.

Come on, tune. If you can penetrate her with your fingering, so. / We'll try with tongue too. If none will do, let her remain; but / I'll never give o'er. First, a very excellent good-conceited / thing; after, a wonderful sweet air, with admirable rich words to / it—and then let her consider.

Come on, tune up. If you can get through to her with your fingering, good; we'll try with the voice too. If nothing works, let her be, but I'll never give up. First a very fine, cleverly made piece; then a wonderful sweet tune with admirable rich words to it, and then let her think it over.

Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings, / And Phoebus 'gins arise, / His steeds to water at those springs / On chalic'd flow'rs that lies; / And winking Mary-buds begin / To ope their golden eyes. / With everything that pretty bin, / My lady sweet, arise; / Arise, arise!

(Song) Listen, the lark is singing at heaven's gate, and the sun god is rising to water his horses at the springs that lie in the cup-shaped flowers. The marigold buds are opening their sleepy golden eyes. With every pretty thing there is, my sweet lady, get up; get up, get up!

So, get you gone. If this penetrate, I will consider your music / the better; if it do not, it is a vice in her ears which / horsehairs and calves' guts, nor the voice of unpaved eunuch to / boot, can never amend.
That'll do, off you go. If this gets through to her, I'll think the better of your music. If it doesn't, it's a defect in her ears that neither horsehair and catgut nor a eunuch's voice can ever fix.
I am glad I was up so late, for that's the reason I was up / so early. He cannot choose but take this service I have done / fatherly.—Good morrow to your Majesty and to my gracious mother.
I'm glad I stayed up so late, because that's why I was up so early. He can't help taking this effort of mine in a fatherly way. Good morning to your Majesty and to my gracious mother.
Attend you here the door of our stern daughter? / Will she not forth?
Are you waiting here at the door of our stubborn daughter? Won't she come out?
I have assail'd her with musics, but she vouchsafes no / notice.
I've attacked her with music, but she won't take any notice.
The exile of her minion is too new; / She hath not yet forgot him; some more time / Must wear the print of his remembrance out, / And then she's yours.
The banishment of her darling is too recent; she hasn't forgotten him yet. A little more time must wear away the imprint of his memory, and then she's yours.

You are most bound to th' King, / Who lets go by no vantages that may / Prefer you to his daughter. Frame yourself / To orderly soliciting, and be friended / With aptness of the season; make denials / Increase your services; so seem as if / You were inspir'd to do those duties which / You tender to her; that you in all obey her, / Save when command to your dismission tends, / And therein you are senseless.

You owe a great deal to the King, who lets no chance go by to recommend you to his daughter. Make yourself a proper suitor and choose your moments well. Let every refusal make you serve her more. Seem as if you were inspired to do the services you offer her; obey her in everything, except when she orders you to leave, and then act as if you hadn't heard.
So like you, sir, ambassadors from Rome; / The one is Caius Lucius.
If you please, sir, ambassadors from Rome. One of them is Caius Lucius.

A worthy fellow, / Albeit he comes on angry purpose now; / But that's no fault of his. We must receive him / According to the honour of his sender; / And towards himself, his goodness forespent on us, / We must extend our notice. Our dear son, / When you have given good morning to your mistress, / Attend the Queen and us; we shall have need / T' employ you towards this Roman. Come, our queen.

A worthy man, though he comes on an angry errand now; but that's not his fault. We must receive him as the honour of his master requires, and as for him personally, we must show him attention for his past kindness to us. Dear son, when you've said good morning to your lady, come to the Queen and me. We'll need you to deal with this Roman. Come, my queen.

If she be up, I'll speak with her; if not, / Let her lie still and dream. By your leave, ho! [Knocks] / I know her women are about her; what / If I do line one of their hands? 'Tis gold / Which buys admittance; oft it doth-yea, and makes / Diana's rangers false themselves, yield up / Their deer to th' stand o' th' stealer; and 'tis gold / Which makes the true man kill'd and saves the thief; / Nay, sometime hangs both thief and true man. What / Can it not do and undo? I will make / One of her women lawyer to me, for / I yet not understand the case myself. / By your leave. [Knocks]

If she's up, I'll speak to her; if not, let her lie and dream. Excuse me, hello! (He knocks.) I know her women are with her. What if I tip one of them? It's gold that buys entry; it often does, yes, and makes Diana's own gamekeepers betray her, and drive their deer to the poacher's stand. And it's gold that gets the honest man killed and saves the thief; no, sometimes hangs both thief and honest man. What can't it do and undo? I'll make one of her women my lawyer, because I don't understand the case myself yet. Excuse me. (He knocks.)
That's more / Than some whose tailors are as dear as yours / Can justly boast of. What's your lordship's pleasure?
That's more than some whose tailors cost as much as yours can truthfully claim. What does your lordship want?
Your lady's person; is she ready?
Your lady in person. Is she dressed?
Yes: to stay in her room.
There is gold for you; sell me your good report.
Here's some gold for you. Sell me your good word.
How? My good name? or to report of you / What I shall think is good? The Princess!
What? My good name? Or to say about you what I think good? The Princess!
Good morrow, fairest sister. Your sweet hand.
Good morning, fairest sister. Your sweet hand.
Good morrow, sir. You lay out too much pains / For purchasing but trouble. The thanks I give / Is telling you that I am poor of thanks, / And scarce can spare them.
Good morning, sir. You take too much trouble to buy nothing but trouble. My only thanks is to tell you I'm short of thanks and can hardly spare any.
Still I swear I love you.
Still, I swear I love you.
If you but said so, 'twere as deep with me. / If you swear still, your recompense is still / That I regard it not.
If you only said so, it would mean as much to me. If you keep swearing, your reward will always be that I don't care.

But that you shall not say I yield, being silent, / I would not speak. I pray you spare me. Faith, / I shall unfold equal discourtesy / To your best kindness; one of your great knowing / Should learn, being taught, forbearance.

I wouldn't speak at all, except that you'd say my silence meant I'd given in. Please leave me alone. Honestly, I'll show you as much rudeness as you show me kindness. A man of your great understanding should learn, once taught, to hold back.
To leave you in your madness 'twere my sin; / I will not.
It would be a sin to leave you in your madness. I won't.
Are you calling me a fool?

As I am mad, I do; / If you'll be patient, I'll no more be mad; / That cures us both. I am much sorry, sir, / You put me to forget a lady's manners / By being so verbal; and learn now, for all, / That I, which know my heart, do here pronounce, / By th' very truth of it, I care not for you, / And am so near the lack of charity / To accuse myself I hate you; which I had rather / You felt than make't my boast.

Since I'm mad, yes. If you'll be patient, I'll stop being mad; that cures us both. I'm very sorry, sir, that you make me forget a lady's manners by speaking so plainly, but learn once and for all that I, who know my own heart, declare here, by its very truth, that I don't care for you, and I'm so close to lacking charity that I'd accuse myself of hating you, which I'd rather you felt than heard me boast of.

You sin against / Obedience, which you owe your father.
