For / The contract you pretend with that base wretch, / One bred of alms and foster'd with cold dishes, / With scraps o' th' court—it is no contract, none. / And though it be allowed in meaner parties— / Yet who than he more mean?—to knit their souls— / On whom there is no more dependency / But brats and beggary—in self-figur'd knot, / Yet you are curb'd from that enlargement by / The consequence o' th' crown, and must not foil / The precious note of it with a base slave, / A hilding for a livery, a squire's cloth, / A pantler—not so eminent!

You sin against the obedience you owe your father. As for the marriage you claim with that low wretch, brought up on charity and fed on cold leftovers, scraps from the court: it's no marriage, none. And though lower people (but who's lower than he?) are allowed to tie the knot themselves, when all they have to depend on is brats and poverty, you are held back from that freedom by the importance of the crown, and mustn't stain its precious name with a low slave, a lackey fit for a servant's uniform, a squire's cast-off, a pantry boy, and not even that grand!

Profane fellow! / Wert thou the son of Jupiter, and no more / But what thou art besides, thou wert too base / To be his groom. Thou wert dignified enough, / Even to the point of envy, if 'twere made / Comparative for your virtues to be styl'd / The under-hangman of his kingdom, and hated / For being preferr'd so well.

Blasphemous man! If you were the son of Jupiter, and otherwise no more than you are, you'd be too low to be his groom. You'd be honoured enough, even to the point of being envied, if, judging by your merits, you were made under-hangman of his kingdom, and hated for being promoted so high.
May the foggy south wind rot him!

He never can meet more mischance than come / To be but nam'd of thee. His mean'st garment / That ever hath but clipp'd his body is dearer / In my respect than all the hairs above thee, / Were they all made such men. How now, Pisanio!

He can never meet worse luck than to be named by you. His humblest garment that ever touched his body is more precious to me than all the hairs on your head, even if every one were turned into a man like you. Hello, Pisanio!
To Dorothy my woman hie thee presently.
Go to Dorothy, my maid, at once.

I am sprited with a fool; / Frighted, and ang'red worse. Go bid my woman / Search for a jewel that too casually / Hath left mine arm. It was thy master's; shrew me, / If I would lose it for a revenue / Of any king's in Europe! I do think / I saw't this morning; confident I am / Last night 'twas on mine arm; I kiss'd it. / I hope it be not gone to tell my lord / That I kiss aught but he.

I'm haunted by a fool, frightened and worse, angered. Go and tell my maid to look for a jewel that has slipped off my arm by accident. It was your master's. Curse me if I'd lose it for the income of any king in Europe! I think I saw it this morning; I'm certain it was on my arm last night: I kissed it. I hope it hasn't gone to tell my lord that I kiss anything but him.
I hope so. Go and search.
I hope not. Go and search.
You have abus'd me. / 'His meanest garment'!
Ay, I said so, sir. / If you will make 't an action, call witness to 't.
Yes, I said so, sir. If you want to take me to court for it, call witnesses.
Your mother too. / She's my good lady and will conceive, I hope, / But the worst of me. So I leave you, sir, / To th' worst of discontent.
And your mother too. She's my good friend and will think only the worst of me, I expect. So I leave you, sir, to the worst of bad moods.
I'll be reveng'd. / 'His mean'st garment'! Well.
I'll get revenge. "His humblest garment"! Very well.
Fear it not, sir; I would I were so sure / To win the King as I am bold her honour / Will remain hers.
Don't worry, sir. I wish I were as sure of winning over the King as I am confident her honour will stay hers.
What means do you make to him?
What steps are you taking with him?

Not any; but abide the change of time, / Quake in the present winter's state, and wish / That warmer days would come. In these fear'd hopes / I barely gratify your love; they failing, / I must die much your debtor.

None; I just wait for times to change, shiver in this present winter, and wish warmer days would come. With these fearful hopes I can barely repay your kindness; if they fail, I'll die deeply in your debt.

Your very goodness and your company / O'erpays all I can do. By this your king / Hath heard of great Augustus. Caius Lucius / Will do's commission throughly; and I think / He'll grant the tribute, send th' arrearages, / Or look upon our Romans, whose remembrance / Is yet fresh in their grief.

Your goodness and your company more than repay anything I can do. By now your king will have heard from the great Augustus. Caius Lucius will carry out his orders thoroughly, and I think your king will agree to the tribute and send the back payments, or else face our Romans, whom the Britons still remember with pain.

I do believe / Statist though I am none, nor like to be, / That this will prove a war; and you shall hear / The legions now in Gallia sooner landed / In our not-fearing Britain than have tidings / Of any penny tribute paid. Our countrymen / Are men more order'd than when Julius Caesar / Smil'd at their lack of skill, but found their courage / Worthy his frowning at. Their discipline, / Now mingled with their courages, will make known / To their approvers they are people such / That mend upon the world.

I believe, though I'm no statesman and never will be, that this will turn into a war, and that you'll hear of the legions now in France landing in our unafraid Britain before you hear of a penny of tribute paid. Our countrymen are better organised than when Julius Caesar smiled at their lack of skill but found their courage worth frowning at. Their discipline, now joined to their courage, will show anyone who tests them that they're a people who improve with time.
The swiftest harts have posted you by land, / And winds of all the comers kiss'd your sails, / To make your vessel nimble.
The swiftest deer must have carried you over land, and the winds from every quarter kissed your sails to speed your ship.
I hope the briefness of your answer made / The speediness of your return.
I hope a short answer is what made your return so quick.
Your lady / Is one of the fairest that I have look'd upon.
Your lady is one of the most beautiful women I've ever seen.
And therewithal the best; or let her beauty / Look through a casement to allure false hearts, / And be false with them.
And the best as well; otherwise let her beauty lean out of a window to lure false hearts, and be false with them.
Good news in them, I trust.
Was Caius Lucius in the Britain court / When you were there?
Was Caius Lucius at the British court when you were there?
He was expected then, / But not approach'd.
He was expected, but hadn't arrived.
All is well yet. / Sparkles this stone as it was wont, or is't not / Too dull for your good wearing?
All's well so far. Does this stone sparkle as it used to, or is it too dull for you to wear?
If I have lost it, / I should have lost the worth of it in gold. / I'll make a journey twice as far t' enjoy / A second night of such sweet shortness which / Was mine in Britain; for the ring is won.
If I'd lost it, I'd have lost its value in gold. I'd travel twice as far to enjoy a second night as sweet and short as the one I had in Britain; because the ring is won.
The stone's too hard to come by.
The stone is too hard to get.
Not a whit, / Your lady being so easy.
Not at all, since your lady is so easy.
Make not, sir, / Your loss your sport. I hope you know that we / Must not continue friends.
Don't make a joke of your loss, sir. I hope you know we can't remain friends.

Good sir, we must, / If you keep covenant. Had I not brought / The knowledge of your mistress home, I grant / We were to question farther; but I now / Profess myself the winner of her honour, / Together with your ring; and not the wronger / Of her or you, having proceeded but / By both your wills.

Good sir, we must, if you keep our agreement. If I hadn't brought back knowledge of your lady, I grant we'd have to fight it out. But now I declare myself the winner of her honour, and of your ring, and I haven't wronged her or you, since I only acted with both your consent.

If you can make't apparent / That you have tasted her in bed, my hand / And ring is yours. If not, the foul opinion / You had of her pure honour gains or loses / Your sword or mine, or masterless leaves both / To who shall find them.

If you can prove you've had her in bed, my hand and ring are yours. If not, your foul opinion of her pure honour will win or lose your sword or mine, or leave both without owners for whoever finds them.

Sir, my circumstances, / Being so near the truth as I will make them, / Must first induce you to believe—whose strength / I will confirm with oath; which I doubt not / You'll give me leave to spare when you shall find / You need it not.
Sir, my details, which I'll make so close to the truth, must first make you believe. I'll back them with an oath, which I'm sure you'll let me skip when you see you don't need it.

First, her bedchamber, / Where I confess I slept not, but profess / Had that was well worth watching-it was hang'd / With tapestry of silk and silver; the story, / Proud Cleopatra when she met her Roman / And Cydnus swell'd above the banks, or for / The press of boats or pride. A piece of work / So bravely done, so rich, that it did strive / In workmanship and value; which I wonder'd / Could be so rarely and exactly wrought, / Since the true life on't was—

First, her bedroom (where, I admit, I didn't sleep, but I declare I had what was well worth staying awake for). It was hung with tapestry of silk and silver showing proud Cleopatra meeting her Roman, and the river Cydnus swelling over its banks, either from the crowd of boats or from pride. A piece of work so finely and richly done that its craftsmanship competed with its value. I wondered how it could be made so rarely and exactly, since the true life of it was...
This is true; / And this you might have heard of here, by me / Or by some other.
That's true. But you could have heard about it here, from me or someone else.
More particulars / Must justify my knowledge.
More details must prove what I know.
So they must, / Or do your honour injury.
They must, or you injure your honour.

The chimney / Is south the chamber, and the chimneypiece / Chaste Dian bathing. Never saw I figures / So likely to report themselves. The cutter / Was as another nature, dumb; outwent her, / Motion and breath left out.

The fireplace is on the south side of the room, and the carving over it shows chaste Diana bathing. I never saw figures so close to speaking for themselves. The sculptor was like a second nature, only silent; he outdid her, except that he left out movement and breath.
This is a thing / Which you might from relation likewise reap, / Being, as it is, much spoke of.
That's also something you could have picked up from hearsay, since it's much talked about.
The roof o' th' chamber / With golden cherubins is fretted; her andirons— / I had forgot them—were two winking Cupids / Of silver, each on one foot standing, nicely / Depending on their brands.
The ceiling of the room is decorated with golden cherubs. Her andirons (I'd forgotten them) were two silver Cupids with their eyes shut, each standing on one foot, neatly leaning on their torches.
This is her honour! / Let it be granted you have seen all this, and praise / Be given to your remembrance; the description / Of what is in her chamber nothing saves / The wager you have laid.
And this is her honour! Suppose you've seen all this, and well done for remembering it: describing what's in her room doesn't win the bet you made.
Then, if you can, [Shows the bracelet] / Be pale. I beg but leave to air this jewel. See! / And now 'tis up again. It must be married / To that your diamond; I'll keep them.
Then turn pale, if you can. (He shows the bracelet.) Just let me give this jewel some air. Look! And now it's put away again. It must be married to that diamond of yours; I'll keep them both.
Jove! / Once more let me behold it. Is it that / Which I left with her?
By Jupiter! Let me look at it once more. Is it the one I left with her?
Sir—I thank her—that. / She stripp'd it from her arm; I see her yet; / Her pretty action did outsell her gift, / And yet enrich'd it too. She gave it me, and said / She priz'd it once.

Yes, sir (and I thank her for it), that one. She slipped it off her arm; I can still see her. Her pretty way of doing it was worth more than the gift, and yet added to its value too. She gave it to me and said she had once treasured it.
May be she pluck'd it of / To send it me.
Maybe she took it off to send it to me.
She writes so to you, doth she?
She writes and tells you so, does she?
O, no, no, no! 'tis true. Here, take this too;
Oh, no, no, no! It's true. Here, take this too.

It is a basilisk unto mine eye, / Kills me to look on't. Let there be no honour / Where there is beauty; truth where semblance; love / Where there's another man. The vows of women / Of no more bondage be to where they are made / Than they are to their virtues, which is nothing. / O, above measure false!

It's a basilisk to my eye; it kills me to look at it. Let there be no honour where there's beauty, no truth where there's an appearance of it, no love where there's another man. Let women's vows be no more binding to those they're made to than women are to their own virtues, which is not at all. Oh, false beyond measure!
Have patience, sir, / And take your ring again; 'tis not yet won. / It may be probable she lost it, or / Who knows if one her women, being corrupted / Hath stol'n it from her?
Be patient, sir, and take your ring back. It isn't won yet. She may well have lost it; or who knows whether one of her women, bribed, stole it from her?
Very true; / And so I hope he came by't. Back my ring. / Render to me some corporal sign about her, / More evident than this; for this was stol'n.
Very true, and I hope that's how he got it. Give me back my ring. Give me some physical mark on her body, clearer than this, because this was stolen.
By Jupiter, I had it from her arm!
By Jupiter, I took it from her arm!

Hark you, he swears; by Jupiter he swears. / 'Tis true—nay, keep the ring, 'tis true. I am sure / She would not lose it. Her attendants are / All sworn and honourable—they induc'd to steal it! / And by a stranger! No, he hath enjoy'd her. / The cognizance of her incontinency / Is this: she hath bought the name of whore thus dearly. / There, take thy hire; and all the fiends of hell / Divide themselves between you!

Listen, he swears; by Jupiter he swears. It's true. No, keep the ring; it's true. I'm sure she wouldn't lose it. Her attendants are all under oath and honourable. Them, persuaded to steal it! And by a stranger! No, he's had her. This is the badge of her lust: she has bought the name of whore at this high price. There, take your fee, and may all the devils of hell share themselves between you!
Sir, be patient; / This is not strong enough to be believ'd / Of one persuaded well of.
Sir, be patient. This isn't strong enough to make you believe it of someone so well thought of.
Never talk on't; / She hath been colted by him.
Don't talk about it. He's ridden her like a colt.

If you seek / For further satisfying, under her breast— / Worthy the pressing—lies a mole, right proud / Of that most delicate lodging. By my life, / I kiss'd it; and it gave me present hunger / To feed again, though full. You do remember / This stain upon her?

If you want more proof: under her breast, which is worth pressing, there's a mole, very proud of its delicate lodging. On my life, I kissed it, and it made me hungry at once to feed again, though I was full. You remember this mark on her?
Ay, and it doth confirm / Another stain, as big as hell can hold, / Were there no more but it.
Yes, and it confirms another stain, as big as hell can hold, even if there were no other.
Spare your arithmetic; never count the turns. / Once, and a million!
Spare your arithmetic; don't count the times. Once, and a million!
No swearing. / If you will swear you have not done't, you lie; / And I will kill thee if thou dost deny / Thou'st made me cuckold.
No swearing. If you swear you haven't done it, you're lying, and I'll kill you if you deny you've made me a cuckold.
O that I had her here to tear her limb-meal! / I will go there and do't, i' th' court, before / Her father. I'll do something—
Oh, if I had her here, I'd tear her limb from limb! I'll go there and do it, at court, in front of her father. I'll do something...
Quite besides / The government of patience! You have won. / Let's follow him and pervert the present wrath / He hath against himself.
Completely beyond the control of patience! You've won. Let's follow him and turn aside the rage he has now against himself.

Is there no way for men to be, but women / Must be half-workers? We are all bastards, / And that most venerable man which I / Did call my father was I know not where / When I was stamp'd. Some coiner with his tools / Made me a counterfeit; yet my mother seem'd / The Dian of that time. So doth my wife / The nonpareil of this. O, vengeance, vengeance! / Me of my lawful pleasure she restrain'd, / And pray'd me oft forbearance; did it with / A pudency so rosy, the sweet view on't / Might well have warm'd old Saturn; that I thought her / As chaste as unsunn'd snow. O, all the devils! / This yellow Iachimo in an hour—was't not? / Or less!—at first? Perchance he spoke not, but, / Like a full-acorn'd boar, a German one, / Cried 'O!' and mounted; found no opposition / But what he look'd for should oppose and she / Should from encounter guard. Could I find out / The woman's part in me! For there's no motion / That tends to vice in man but I affirm / It is the woman's part. Be it lying, note it, / The woman's; flattering, hers; deceiving, hers; / Lust and rank thoughts, hers, hers; revenges, hers; / Ambitions, covetings, change of prides, disdain, / Nice longing, slanders, mutability, / All faults that man may name, nay, that hell knows, / Why, hers, in part or all; but rather all; / For even to vice / They are not constant, but are changing still / One vice but of a minute old for one / Not half so old as that. I'll write against them, / Detest them, curse them. Yet 'tis greater skill / In a true hate to pray they have their will: / The very devils cannot plague them better.

Is there no way for men to be born without women doing half the work? We're all bastards, and that most respected man I called my father was who knows where when I was minted. Some forger with his tools made me a fake coin; and yet my mother seemed the Diana of her day, as my wife seems the one and only of this one. Oh, revenge, revenge! She held me back from my lawful pleasure and often begged me to be patient, and did it with such rosy modesty that the sweet sight of it could have warmed old Saturn, so that I thought her as chaste as snow the sun has never touched. Oh, all the devils! This sallow Iachimo, in an hour, wasn't it? Or less, right from the start? Maybe he didn't even speak but, like a German boar stuffed with acorns, cried "Oh!" and mounted, and found no resistance except what he expected to meet, the part she should have guarded. If only I could find the woman's part in me! For there's no impulse toward vice in a man that isn't, I swear, the woman's part. If it's lying, mark it, it's the woman's; flattering, hers; deceiving, hers; lust and filthy thoughts, hers, hers; revenge, hers; ambition, greed, changing vanities, scorn, fussy cravings, slander, fickleness, every fault a man can name, no, that hell knows: hers, in part or all; but rather all. Because they aren't even constant in their vices, but keep swapping one that's a minute old for one not half as old. I'll write against them, hate them, curse them. And yet the cleverest true hatred is to pray they get what they want: the devils themselves couldn't punish them better.
Now say, what would Augustus Caesar with us?
Now tell me, what does Augustus Caesar want with us?

When Julius Caesar—whose remembrance yet / Lives in men's eyes, and will to ears and tongues / Be theme and hearing ever—was in this Britain, / And conquer'd it, Cassibelan, thine uncle, / Famous in Caesar's praises no whit less / Than in his feats deserving it, for him / And his succession granted Rome a tribute, / Yearly three thousand pounds, which by thee lately / Is left untender'd.

When Julius Caesar (whose memory still lives in men's eyes, and will always be a subject for tongues to tell and ears to hear) was here in Britain and conquered it, your uncle Cassibelan, as famous for Caesar's praise as for the deeds that earned it, granted Rome a yearly tribute for himself and his heirs of three thousand pounds, which you have recently failed to pay.
And, to kill the marvel, / Shall be so ever.
And, to end the surprise, never will again.
There be many Caesars / Ere such another Julius. Britain is / A world by itself, and we will nothing pay / For wearing our own noses.
There'll be many Caesars before another Julius. Britain is a world of its own, and we'll pay nothing for wearing our own noses.

That opportunity, / Which then they had to take from 's, to resume / We have again. Remember, sir, my liege, / The kings your ancestors, together with / The natural bravery of your isle, which stands / As Neptune's park, ribb'd and pal'd in / With rocks unscalable and roaring waters, / With sands that will not bear your enemies' boats / But suck them up to th' top-mast. A kind of conquest / Caesar made here; but made not here his brag / Of 'came, and saw, and overcame.' With shame— / The first that ever touch'd him—he was carried / From off our coast, twice beaten; and his shipping— / Poor ignorant baubles!—on our terrible seas, / Like egg-shells mov'd upon their surges, crack'd / As easily 'gainst our rocks; for joy whereof / The fam'd Cassibelan, who was once at point— / O, giglot fortune!—to master Caesar's sword, / Made Lud's Town with rejoicing fires bright / And Britons strut with courage.

That chance they had then to take it from us, we now have to take it back. Remember, sir, my king, the kings your ancestors, and the natural strength of your island, which stands like Neptune's park, ribbed and fenced with rocks that can't be climbed and roaring waters, with sands that won't hold up your enemies' boats but suck them down to the top of the mast. Caesar made a sort of conquest here, but he didn't make his boast of "I came, I saw, I conquered" here. With shame, the first he ever felt, he was carried off our coast, beaten twice; and his ships, poor ignorant toys, were tossed on our terrible seas like eggshells on the waves and cracked just as easily against our rocks. To celebrate, the famous Cassibelan, who was once on the point (oh, fickle fortune!) of mastering Caesar's sword, lit up London with bonfires and made Britons strut with courage.

Come, there's no more tribute to be paid. Our kingdom is / stronger than it was at that time; and, as I said, there is no / moe such Caesars. Other of them may have crook'd noses; but to / owe such straight arms, none.

Come on, there's no more tribute to pay. Our kingdom is stronger than it was then, and as I said, there are no more Caesars like that one. Others may have hooked noses, but none of them has such strong arms.

We have yet many among us can gripe as hard as Cassibelan. / I do not say I am one; but I have a hand. Why tribute? Why should / we pay tribute? If Caesar can hide the sun from us with a blanket, / or put the moon in his pocket, we will pay him tribute for light; / else, sir, no more tribute, pray you now.

We still have plenty of men who can grip as hard as Cassibelan. I don't say I'm one of them, but I have a hand. Why tribute? Why should we pay tribute? If Caesar can hide the sun from us with a blanket or put the moon in his pocket, we'll pay him tribute for light. Otherwise, sir, no more tribute, please.

You must know, / Till the injurious Romans did extort / This tribute from us, we were free. Caesar's ambition— / Which swell'd so much that it did almost stretch / The sides o' th' world—against all colour here / Did put the yoke upon's; which to shake of / Becomes a warlike people, whom we reckon / Ourselves to be.

You must know that until the unjust Romans extorted this tribute from us, we were free. Caesar's ambition, which swelled so much it nearly stretched the sides of the world, put the yoke on us here with no right to do it. Shaking it off is fitting for a warlike people, which we consider ourselves to be.

Say then to Caesar, / Our ancestor was that Mulmutius which / Ordain'd our laws—whose use the sword of Caesar / Hath too much mangled; whose repair and franchise / Shall, by the power we hold, be our good deed, / Though Rome be therefore angry. Mulmutius made our laws, / Who was the first of Britain which did put / His brows within a golden crown, and call'd / Himself a king.

Then tell Caesar this. Our ancestor was that Mulmutius who made our laws, laws Caesar's sword has badly mangled. Restoring them and their freedom, by the power we hold, will be our good deed, even if Rome is angry about it. Mulmutius made our laws, and he was the first in Britain to put a golden crown on his head and call himself king.

I am sorry, Cymbeline, / That I am to pronounce Augustus Caesar— / Caesar, that hath moe kings his servants than / Thyself domestic officers—thine enemy. / Receive it from me, then: war and confusion / In Caesar's name pronounce I 'gainst thee; look / For fury not to be resisted. Thus defied, / I thank thee for myself.

I'm sorry, Cymbeline, that I have to declare Augustus Caesar, who has more kings as servants than you have household officers, your enemy. Take it from me, then: in Caesar's name I declare war and destruction against you. Expect a fury that can't be resisted. Having defied you like this, I thank you for my own treatment.

Thou art welcome, Caius. / Thy Caesar knighted me; my youth I spent / Much under him; of him I gather'd honour, / Which he to seek of me again, perforce, / Behoves me keep at utterance. I am perfect / That the Pannonians and Dalmatians for / Their liberties are now in arms, a precedent / Which not to read would show the Britons cold; / So Caesar shall not find them.

You're welcome, Caius. Your Caesar knighted me; I spent much of my youth serving him. From him I gained honour, and since he's now trying to take it back from me by force, I'm bound to defend it to the death. I know for certain that the Pannonians and Dalmatians are now in arms for their freedom, an example the Britons would be cold not to follow. Caesar won't find them so.

His majesty bids you welcome. Make pastime with us a day or / two, or longer. If you seek us afterwards in other terms, you / shall find us in our salt-water girdle. If you beat us out of it, / it is yours; if you fall in the adventure, our crows shall fare / the better for you; and there's an end.

His majesty welcomes you. Enjoy yourself with us for a day or two, or longer. If you come looking for us later on other terms, you'll find us inside our belt of salt water. If you beat us out of it, it's yours. If you die trying, our crows will eat better because of you; and that's the end of it.
I know your master's pleasure, and he mine; / All the remain is, welcome.
I know your master's wishes, and he knows mine. All that's left is to say welcome.

How? of adultery? Wherefore write you not / What monsters her accuse? Leonatus! / O master, what a strange infection / Is fall'n into thy ear! What false Italian— / As poisonous-tongu'd as handed—hath prevail'd / On thy too ready hearing? Disloyal? No. / She's punish'd for her truth, and undergoes, / More goddess-like than wife-like, such assaults / As would take in some virtue. O my master! / Thy mind to her is now as low as were / Thy fortunes. How? that I should murder her? / Upon the love, and truth, and vows, which I / Have made to thy command? I, her? Her blood? / If it be so to do good service, never / Let me be counted serviceable. How look I / That I should seem to lack humanity / So much as this fact comes to? [Reads] 'Do't. The letter / That I have sent her, by her own command / Shall give thee opportunity.' O damn'd paper, / Black as the ink that's on thee! Senseless bauble, / Art thou a fedary for this act, and look'st / So virgin-like without? Lo, here she comes.

What? Adultery? Why don't you write what monsters accuse her? Leonatus! Oh, master, what strange infection has got into your ear! What false Italian, as poisonous of tongue as of hand, has worked on your too-willing hearing? Disloyal? No. She's punished for her faithfulness and endures, more like a goddess than a wife, attacks that would conquer most virtue. Oh, my master! Your opinion of her is now as low as your fortunes were. What? I should murder her? Because of the love and loyalty and vows I've given to serve you? I, kill her? Shed her blood? If that's good service, never call me a good servant. How do I look, that I should seem to lack humanity as much as this deed requires? (Reading) "Do it. The letter I've sent her will, by her own wish, give you the chance." Oh, damned paper, as black as the ink on you! Senseless thing, are you an accomplice in this act, and look so virgin-white outside? Look, here she comes.
I am ignorant in what I am commanded.
I'll pretend I don't know what I've been ordered to do.
Madam, here is a letter from my lord.
Madam, here's a letter from my lord.

Who? thy lord? That is my lord—Leonatus? / O, learn'd indeed were that astronomer / That knew the stars as I his characters— / He'd lay the future open. You good gods, / Let what is here contain'd relish of love, / Of my lord's health, of his content; yet not / That we two are asunder—let that grieve him! / Some griefs are med'cinable; that is one of them, / For it doth physic love—of his content, / All but in that. Good wax, thy leave. Blest be / You bees that make these locks of counsel! Lovers / And men in dangerous bonds pray not alike; / Though forfeiters you cast in prison, yet / You clasp young Cupid's tables. Good news, gods!

From whom? Your lord? That's my lord, Leonatus? Oh, that astronomer would be learned indeed who knew the stars as well as I know his handwriting: he'd lay the future open. Kind gods, let what's in here taste of love, of my lord's health, of his happiness; but not happiness that we're apart; let that grieve him! Some griefs are healing, and that's one, because it keeps love healthy. Of his happiness in everything but that. Good wax, excuse me. Blessed be you bees who make these seals for secrets! Lovers and men in dangerous debt don't pray alike: though you throw debtors in prison by sealing their bonds, you also seal young Cupid's love letters. Good news, gods!

'Justice and your father's wrath, should he take me in his / dominion, could not be so cruel to me as you, O the dearest of / creatures, would even renew me with your eyes. Take notice that I / am in Cambria, at Milford Haven. What your own love will out of / this advise you, follow. So he wishes you all happiness that / remains loyal to his vow, and your increasing in love / Leonatus Posthumus.' / O for a horse with wings! Hear'st thou, Pisanio? / He is at Milford Haven. Read, and tell me / How far 'tis thither. If one of mean affairs / May plod it in a week, why may not I / Glide thither in a day? Then, true Pisanio— / Who long'st like me to see thy lord, who long'st— / O, let me 'bate!—but not like me, yet long'st, / But in a fainter kind—O, not like me, / For mine's beyond beyond!-say, and speak thick— / Love's counsellor should fill the bores of hearing / To th' smothering of the sense—how far it is / To this same blessed Milford. And by th' way / Tell me how Wales was made so happy as / T' inherit such a haven. But first of all, / How we may steal from hence; and for the gap / That we shall make in time from our hence-going / And our return, to excuse. But first, how get hence. / Why should excuse be born or ere begot? / We'll talk of that hereafter. Prithee speak, / How many score of miles may we well ride / 'Twixt hour and hour?

(Reading) "Justice and your father's anger, if he caught me in his kingdom, could not be so cruel to me that you, dearest of creatures, could not restore me with your eyes. Know that I am in Wales, at Milford Haven. Follow whatever your own love advises you from this. So wishes you all happiness he who remains loyal to his vow, and grows in love for you, Leonatus Posthumus." Oh, for a horse with wings! Do you hear, Pisanio? He's at Milford Haven. Read it, and tell me how far it is there. If someone on ordinary business can plod it in a week, why can't I glide there in a day? So, faithful Pisanio, who longs like me to see your lord, who longs (oh, let me take that back) not like me, but still longs, in a fainter way (oh, not like me, because mine is beyond beyond!), tell me, and speak fast (love's adviser should cram the ears till they choke), how far it is to this blessed Milford. And while you're at it, tell me how Wales was lucky enough to own such a harbour. But first of all, how we can slip away from here, and how to excuse the gap our absence will leave between going and coming back. But first, how to get away. Why invent an excuse before there's anything to excuse? We'll talk about that later. Please tell me how many miles we can ride in an hour.
One score 'twixt sun and sun, / Madam, 's enough for you, and too much too.
Twenty miles between sunrise and sunset, madam, is enough for you, and too much.

Why, one that rode to's execution, man, / Could never go so slow. I have heard of riding wagers / Where horses have been nimbler than the sands / That run i' th' clock's behalf. But this is fool'ry. / Go bid my woman feign a sickness; say / She'll home to her father; and provide me presently / A riding suit, no costlier than would fit / A franklin's huswife.

Why, man, a man riding to his own execution couldn't go so slowly. I've heard of horse races where horses ran faster than the sand in an hourglass. But this is silly. Go and tell my maid to pretend to be ill and say she's going home to her father; and get me a riding outfit at once, no more expensive than a well-off farmer's wife would wear.
Madam, you'd better think about this.

I see before me, man. Nor here, nor here, / Nor what ensues, but have a fog in them / That I cannot look through. Away, I prithee; / Do as I bid thee. There's no more to say; / Accessible is none but Milford way.

I can see only what's in front of me, man. This way and that, and what comes after, are all in a fog I can't see through. Go, please; do as I tell you. There's nothing more to say: the only road open is the road to Milford.

A goodly day not to keep house with such / Whose roof's as low as ours! Stoop, boys; this gate / Instructs you how t' adore the heavens, and bows you / To a morning's holy office. The gates of monarchs / Are arch'd so high that giants may jet through / And keep their impious turbans on without / Good morrow to the sun. Hail, thou fair heaven! / We house i' th' rock, yet use thee not so hardly / As prouder livers do.

A fine day not to stay indoors, for people with a roof as low as ours! Bend down, boys: this doorway teaches you how to worship the heavens and bows you down for your morning prayers. The gates of kings are arched so high that giants can strut through with their wicked turbans on and never say good morning to the sun. Hail, lovely sky! We live in a rock, but we don't treat you as harshly as prouder people do.

Now for our mountain sport. Up to yond hill, / Your legs are young; I'll tread these flats. Consider, / When you above perceive me like a crow, / That it is place which lessens and sets off; / And you may then revolve what tales I have told you / Of courts, of princes, of the tricks in war. / This service is not service so being done, / But being so allow'd. To apprehend thus / Draws us a profit from all things we see, / And often to our comfort shall we find / The sharded beetle in a safer hold / Than is the full-wing'd eagle. O, this life / Is nobler than attending for a check, / Richer than doing nothing for a bribe, / Prouder than rustling in unpaid-for silk: / Such gain the cap of him that makes him fine, / Yet keeps his book uncross'd. No life to ours!

Now for our mountain hunting. Up that hill: your legs are young. I'll walk these flat lands. When you look down and see me as small as a crow, remember that it's position that makes things look small or great, and then you can think over the stories I've told you about courts, princes, and the tricks of war. Service isn't valued for being done, but for being recognised. Thinking like this, we can learn from everything we see, and we'll often find, to our comfort, that the beetle in its shell is safer than the eagle with its full wings. Oh, this life is nobler than waiting on a great man for a scolding, richer than doing nothing for a bribe, prouder than rustling in unpaid-for silk: such a man gets a bow from the tailor who dresses him, but never pays his bill. There's no life like ours!

Out of your proof you speak. We, poor unfledg'd, / Have never wing'd from view o' th' nest, nor know not / What air's from home. Haply this life is best, / If quiet life be best; sweeter to you / That have a sharper known; well corresponding / With your stiff age. But unto us it is / A cell of ignorance, travelling abed, / A prison for a debtor that not dares / To stride a limit.

You speak from experience. We poor fledglings have never flown out of sight of the nest and don't know what the air is like away from home. Maybe this life is best, if a quiet life is best; sweeter to you who've known a harsher one, and well suited to your stiff old age. But to us it's a cell of ignorance, travelling only in our beds, a prison for a debtor who doesn't dare step past its boundary.

What should we speak of / When we are old as you? When we shall hear / The rain and wind beat dark December, how, / In this our pinching cave, shall we discourse. / The freezing hours away? We have seen nothing; / We are beastly: subtle as the fox for prey, / Like warlike as the wolf for what we eat. / Our valour is to chase what flies; our cage / We make a choir, as doth the prison'd bird, / And sing our bondage freely.

What will we talk about when we're as old as you? When we hear rain and wind beating against dark December, how will we pass the freezing hours talking in this cramped cave? We've seen nothing. We're like animals: cunning as the fox for prey, fierce as the wolf for what we eat. Our courage is to chase what runs away. We make our cage a choir, like a caged bird, and sing freely about our captivity.

How you speak! / Did you but know the city's usuries, / And felt them knowingly—the art o' th' court, / As hard to leave as keep, whose top to climb / Is certain falling, or so slipp'ry that / The fear's as bad as falling; the toil o' th' war, / A pain that only seems to seek out danger / I' th'name of fame and honour, which dies i' th'search, / And hath as oft a sland'rous epitaph / As record of fair act; nay, many times, / Doth ill deserve by doing well; what's worse— / Must curtsy at the censure. O, boys, this story / The world may read in me; my body's mark'd / With Roman swords, and my report was once / first with the best of note. Cymbeline lov'd me; / And when a soldier was the theme, my name / Was not far off. Then was I as a tree / Whose boughs did bend with fruit; but in one night / A storm, or robbery, call it what you will, / Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves, / And left me bare to weather.

How you talk! If you only knew the city's money-lending and had felt it yourself; the skill of the court, as hard to leave as to keep, where climbing to the top means certain falling, or the top's so slippery that the fear is as bad as the fall; the hard work of war, a pain that seems only to look for danger in the name of fame and honour, which dies in the search and as often gets a slanderous epitaph as a record of good deeds; no, often gets punished for doing well; and what's worse, has to bow to the judgment. Oh, boys, the world can read this story in me. My body is marked by Roman swords, and my reputation was once among the very best. Cymbeline loved me, and whenever soldiers were talked of, my name wasn't far off. Then I was like a tree whose branches bent with fruit; but in one night a storm, or a robbery, call it what you like, shook down my ripe fruit, no, my leaves too, and left me bare to the weather.

My fault being nothing—as I have told you oft— / But that two villains, whose false oaths prevail'd / Before my perfect honour, swore to Cymbeline / I was confederate with the Romans. So / Follow'd my banishment, and this twenty years / This rock and these demesnes have been my world, / Where I have liv'd at honest freedom, paid / More pious debts to heaven than in all / The fore-end of my time. But up to th' mountains! / This is not hunters' language. He that strikes / The venison first shall be the lord o' th' feast; / To him the other two shall minister; / And we will fear no poison, which attends / In place of greater state. I'll meet you in the valleys.

My only fault, as I've often told you, was that two villains, whose lying oaths beat my perfect honour, swore to Cymbeline that I was in league with the Romans. So I was banished, and for twenty years this rock and these lands have been my world. Here I've lived in honest freedom and paid more devout debts to heaven than in all the earlier part of my life. But up to the mountains! This isn't hunters' talk. Whoever kills the deer first will be lord of the feast, and the other two will serve him. And we won't fear poison, which waits in places of greater state. I'll meet you in the valleys.

How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature! / These boys know little they are sons to th' King, / Nor Cymbeline dreams that they are alive. / They think they are mine; and though train'd up thus meanly / I' th' cave wherein they bow, their thoughts do hit / The roofs of palaces, and nature prompts them / In simple and low things to prince it much / Beyond the trick of others. This Polydore, / The heir of Cymbeline and Britain, who / The King his father call'd Guiderius—Jove! / When on my three-foot stool I sit and tell / The warlike feats I have done, his spirits fly out / Into my story; say 'Thus mine enemy fell, / And thus I set my foot on's neck'; even then / The princely blood flows in his cheek, he sweats, / Strains his young nerves, and puts himself in posture / That acts my words. The younger brother, Cadwal, / Once Arviragus, in as like a figure / Strikes life into my speech, and shows much more / His own conceiving. Hark, the game is rous'd! / O Cymbeline, heaven and my conscience knows / Thou didst unjustly banish me! Whereon, / At three and two years old, I stole these babes, / Thinking to bar thee of succession as / Thou refts me of my lands. Euriphile, / Thou wast their nurse; they took thee for their mother, / And every day do honour to her grave. / Myself, Belarius, that am Morgan call'd, / They take for natural father. The game is up.

How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature! These boys have no idea they're the King's sons, and Cymbeline doesn't dream they're alive. They think they're mine; and though they've been brought up so humbly in this cave where they have to stoop, their thoughts hit the roofs of palaces, and nature prompts them, even in simple, humble things, to act far more like princes than others do. This Polydore, the heir of Cymbeline and Britain, whom the King his father named Guiderius: by Jove! When I sit on my three-legged stool and tell of my brave deeds in war, his spirit flies into my story. When I say, "So my enemy fell, and so I put my foot on his neck," at once the royal blood flows into his cheek; he sweats, strains his young muscles, and takes up a stance that acts out my words. The younger brother, Cadwal, once Arviragus, brings my story to life in the same way, and shows even more of his own imagination. Listen, the game is up! Oh, Cymbeline, heaven and my conscience know you banished me unjustly! And so I stole these babies at three and two years old, meaning to rob you of heirs as you robbed me of my lands. Euriphile, you were their nurse; they thought you were their mother, and they honour her grave every day. Me, Belarius, now called Morgan, they think their real father. The game's up.

Thou told'st me, when we came from horse, the place / Was near at hand. Ne'er long'd my mother so / To see me first as I have now. Pisanio! Man! / Where is Posthumus? What is in thy mind / That makes thee stare thus? Wherefore breaks that sigh / From th' inward of thee? One but painted thus / Would be interpreted a thing perplex'd / Beyond self-explication. Put thyself / Into a haviour of less fear, ere wildness / Vanquish my staider senses. What's the matter? / Why tender'st thou that paper to me with / A look untender! If't be summer news, / Smile to't before; if winterly, thou need'st / But keep that count'nance still. My husband's hand? / That drug-damn'd Italy hath out-craftied him, / And he's at some hard point. Speak, man; thy tongue / May take off some extremity, which to read / Would be even mortal to me.

You told me, when we got off the horses, that the place was close by. My mother never longed to see me for the first time as much as I long now. Pisanio! Man! Where is Posthumus? What's on your mind that makes you stare like that? Why does that sigh break from deep inside you? Someone painted looking like that would be taken for a person confused beyond explaining himself. Look less frightened, before wild fear overcomes my calmer senses. What's the matter? Why do you hand me that paper with such an unkind look? If it's summer news, smile first; if it's wintry, you only need to keep that face. My husband's handwriting? That poison-cursed Italy has outwitted him, and he's in some terrible trouble. Speak, man. Your tongue may soften some disaster that would kill me to read.
Please you read, / And you shall find me, wretched man, a thing / The most disdain'd of fortune.
Please read it, and you'll find me, wretched man, the most scorned of fortune's creatures.

[Reads] 'Thy mistress, Pisanio, hath play'd the strumpet in / my bed, the testimonies whereof lie bleeding in me. I speak not / out of weak surmises, but from proof as strong as my grief and as / certain as I expect my revenge. That part thou, Pisanio, must act / for me, if thy faith be not tainted with the breach of hers. Let / thine own hands take away her life; I shall give thee opportunity / at Milford Haven; she hath my letter for the purpose; where, if / thou fear to strike, and to make me certain it is done, thou art / the pander to her dishonour, and equally to me disloyal.'

(Reading) "Your mistress, Pisanio, has played the whore in my bed. The proofs of it lie bleeding in my heart. I'm not speaking from weak suspicion but from proof as strong as my grief and as certain as I expect my revenge to be. You, Pisanio, must carry out that part for me, if your loyalty isn't tainted by her betrayal. Take her life with your own hands. I'll give you the chance at Milford Haven: she has my letter for the purpose. If you're afraid to strike, and to assure me it's done, you're the pimp of her dishonour, and just as disloyal to me."

What shall I need to draw my sword? The paper / Hath cut her throat already. No, 'tis slander, / Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue / Outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath / Rides on the posting winds and doth belie / All corners of the world. Kings, queens, and states, / Maids, matrons, nay, the secrets of the grave, / This viperous slander enters. What cheer, madam?

Why should I need to draw my sword? The paper has already cut her throat. No, it's slander, whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue is more poisonous than all the snakes of the Nile, whose breath rides on the speeding winds and spreads lies to every corner of the world. Kings, queens and states, virgins, wives, even the secrets of the grave: this viper slander gets into all of them. How are you, madam?

False to his bed? What is it to be false? / To lie in watch there, and to think on him? / To weep twixt clock and clock? If sleep charge nature, / To break it with a fearful dream of him, / And cry myself awake? That's false to's bed, / Is it?

False to his bed? What does it mean to be false? To lie awake there thinking of him? To cry from hour to hour? If sleep overpowers me, to break it with a frightening dream about him and wake myself up crying? Is that being false to his bed?

I false! Thy conscience witness! Iachimo, / Thou didst accuse him of incontinency; / Thou then look'dst like a villain; now, methinks, / Thy favour's good enough. Some jay of Italy, / Whose mother was her painting, hath betray'd him. / Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion, / And for I am richer than to hang by th' walls / I must be ripp'd. To pieces with me! O, / Men's vows are women's traitors! All good seeming, / By thy revolt, O husband, shall be thought / Put on for villainy; not born where't grows, / But worn a bait for ladies.

I, false? Your conscience is my witness! Iachimo, when you accused him of lust, you looked like a villain; now I think your face looks honest enough. Some flashy Italian bird, whose mother was her makeup, has seduced him. Poor me, I'm stale, a dress gone out of fashion, and since I'm too rich to hang on the wall, I must be ripped up. Tear me to pieces! Oh, men's vows betray women! Because of your betrayal, husband, every good appearance will be thought to be put on for wickedness; not natural, but worn as bait for ladies.

True honest men being heard, like false Aeneas, / Were, in his time, thought false; and Sinon's weeping / Did scandal many a holy tear, took pity / From most true wretchedness. So thou, Posthumus, / Wilt lay the leaven on all proper men: / Goodly and gallant shall be false and perjur'd / From thy great fail. Come, fellow, be thou honest; / Do thou thy master's bidding; when thou seest him, / A little witness my obedience. Look! / I draw the sword myself; take it, and hit / The innocent mansion of my love, my heart. / Fear not; 'tis empty of all things but grief; / Thy master is not there, who was indeed / The riches of it. Do his bidding; strike. / Thou mayst be valiant in a better cause, / But now thou seem'st a coward.

Truly honest men, because of what was said about false Aeneas, were thought false in his time, and Sinon's weeping brought shame on many holy tears and took pity away from real misery. So you, Posthumus, will taint all good men: the handsome and the gallant will be thought false and lying because of your great failure. Come on, fellow, be honest: do what your master orders. When you see him, testify a little to my obedience. Look, I'll draw the sword myself. Take it, and strike the innocent house of my love, my heart. Don't be afraid; it's empty of everything but grief. Your master isn't there, who used to be its whole treasure. Do as he says; strike. You may be brave in a better cause, but right now you look like a coward.
Hence, vile instrument! / Thou shalt not damn my hand.
Get away, vile weapon! You won't damn my hand.

Why, I must die; / And if I do not by thy hand, thou art / No servant of thy master's. Against self-slaughter / There is a prohibition so divine / That cravens my weak hand. Come, here's my heart— / Something's afore't. Soft, soft! we'll no defence!— / Obedient as the scabbard. What is here? / The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus / All turn'd to heresy? Away, away, / Corrupters of my faith! you shall no more / Be stomachers to my heart. Thus may poor fools / Believe false teachers; though those that are betray'd / Do feel the treason sharply, yet the traitor / Stands in worse case of woe. And thou, Posthumus, / That didst set up my disobedience 'gainst the King / My father, and make me put into contempt the suits / Of princely fellows, shalt hereafter find / It is no act of common passage but / A strain of rareness; and I grieve myself / To think, when thou shalt be disedg'd by her / That now thou tirest on, how thy memory / Will then be pang'd by me. Prithee dispatch. / The lamp entreats the butcher. Where's thy knife? / Thou art too slow to do thy master's bidding, / When I desire it too.

Why, I must die, and if it isn't by your hand, you're no servant of your master's. There's a law against suicide so holy that it makes my weak hand a coward. Come, here's my heart. Something's in front of it. Wait, wait! We'll have no protection, obedient as a scabbard. What's this? The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus, all turned to heresy? Away, away, corrupters of my faith! You'll be no armour for my heart any more. That's how poor fools believe false teachers; and though the betrayed feel the treason sharply, the traitor is in a worse state of misery. And you, Posthumus, who made me disobey the King my father and scorn the proposals of princes, will find later that it was no ordinary act but a rare one; and it grieves me to think how, when you've grown tired of the woman you now feed on, your memory will be tormented by me. Please, get it over with. The lamb begs the butcher. Where's your knife? You're too slow to do your master's bidding, when I want it too.
O gracious lady, / Since I receiv'd command to do this busines / I have not slept one wink.
Oh, gracious lady, since I got the order to do this, I haven't slept a wink.
Do it, and then go to bed.
I'll stay awake till my eyes fall out first.

Wherefore then / Didst undertake it? Why hast thou abus'd / So many miles with a pretence? This place? / Mine action and thine own? our horses' labour? / The time inviting thee? the perturb'd court, / For my being absent?—whereunto I never / Purpose return. Why hast thou gone so far / To be unbent when thou hast ta'en thy stand, / Th' elected deer before thee?

Then why did you take it on? Why have you wasted so many miles with a pretence? This place? What I've done and what you've done? Our horses' effort? The chance this time gives you? The court in turmoil over my absence, where I never mean to go back? Why have you come so far only to unstring your bow when you've taken your position and the chosen deer is in front of you?
But to win time / To lose so bad employment, in the which / I have consider'd of a course. Good lady, / Hear me with patience.
Only to win time to get out of such a wicked job, and meanwhile I've thought of a plan. Good lady, hear me patiently.
Talk thy tongue weary—speak. / I have heard I am a strumpet, and mine ear, / Therein false struck, can take no greater wound, / Nor tent to bottom that. But speak.
Talk till your tongue's tired. Speak. I've heard I'm a whore, and my ear, wrongly struck there, can't take a greater wound, nor any probe reach the bottom of that one. But speak.
Then, madam, / I thought you would not back again.
Then, madam, I thought you wouldn't go back.
Most like— / Bringing me here to kill me.
Very likely, since you brought me here to kill me.

Not so, neither; / But if I were as wise as honest, then / My purpose would prove well. It cannot be / But that my master is abus'd. Some villain, / Ay, and singular in his art, hath done you both / This cursed injury.

Not that either. But if I were as wise as I am honest, my plan would work. It must be that my master has been deceived. Some villain, and an exceptional one at his trade, has done you both this cursed wrong.
No, on my life! / I'll give but notice you are dead, and send him / Some bloody sign of it, for 'tis commanded / I should do so. You shall be miss'd at court, / And that will well confirm it.
No, on my life! I'll just send word that you're dead, and send him some bloody token of it, because I've been ordered to. You'll be missed at court, and that will confirm it nicely.
Why, good fellow, / What shall I do the while? where bide? how live? / Or in my life what comfort, when I am / Dead to my husband?
But, good fellow, what will I do meanwhile? Where will I stay? How will I live? What comfort will there be in my life when I'm dead to my husband?
If you'll back to th' court—
If you'll go back to court...
No court, no father, nor no more ado / With that harsh, noble, simple nothing— / That Cloten, whose love-suit hath been to me / As fearful as a siege.
No court, no father, and no more trouble with that harsh, noble, empty nothing, that Cloten, whose courting has been as terrifying to me as a siege.
If not at court, / Then not in Britain must you bide.
If not at court, then you mustn't stay in Britain.

Where then? / Hath Britain all the sun that shines? Day, night, / Are they not but in Britain? I' th' world's volume / Our Britain seems as of it, but not in't; / In a great pool a swan's nest. Prithee think / There's livers out of Britain.

Where then? Does Britain have all the sun that shines? Are day and night only in Britain? In the book of the world, our Britain seems part of it but not in it: a swan's nest in a great pool. Please believe there are people living outside Britain.

I am most glad / You think of other place. Th' ambassador, / Lucius the Roman, comes to Milford Haven / To-morrow. Now, if you could wear a mind / Dark as your fortune is, and but disguise / That which t' appear itself must not yet be / But by self-danger, you should tread a course / Pretty and full of view; yea, happily, near / The residence of Posthumus; so nigh, at least, / That though his actions were not visible, yet / Report should render him hourly to your ear / As truly as he moves.

I'm very glad you're thinking of somewhere else. The ambassador, Lucius the Roman, comes to Milford Haven tomorrow. Now, if you could make your mind as dark as your fortune, and disguise what you are, which can't show itself yet without danger to you, you could take a path that's promising and full of prospects; yes, perhaps near where Posthumus is living; so close, at least, that even if you couldn't see what he does, news would bring him to your ear every hour as truly as he moves.
O! for such means, / Though peril to my modesty, not death on't, / I would adventure.
Oh, for a way like that I'd take the risk, even if it endangered my modesty, though not my life.

Well then, here's the point: / You must forget to be a woman; change / Command into obedience; fear and niceness— / The handmaids of all women, or, more truly, / Woman it pretty self—into a waggish courage; / Ready in gibes, quick-answer'd, saucy, and / As quarrelous as the weasel. Nay, you must / Forget that rarest treasure of your cheek, / Exposing it—but, O, the harder heart! / Alack, no remedy!—to the greedy touch / Of common-kissing Titan, and forget / Your laboursome and dainty trims wherein / You made great Juno angry.

Well then, here's the point. You must forget you're a woman: change commanding into obeying, and fear and delicacy, the servants of all women, or more truly, woman's own pretty self, into a cheeky courage; quick with jokes, quick with answers, saucy, and as quarrelsome as a weasel. No, you must forget that rarest treasure, your complexion, and expose it (oh, how hard-hearted! but there's no help for it) to the greedy touch of the sun, who kisses everyone, and forget the elaborate, dainty clothes that made great Juno jealous.
Nay, be brief; / I see into thy end, and am almost / A man already.
No, be quick. I can see where you're going, and I'm almost a man already.

First, make yourself but like one. / Fore-thinking this, I have already fit— / 'Tis in my cloak-bag—doublet, hat, hose, all / That answer to them. Would you, in their serving, / And with what imitation you can borrow / From youth of such a season, fore noble Lucius / Present yourself, desire his service, tell him / Wherein you're happy—which will make him know / If that his head have ear in music; doubtless / With joy he will embrace you; for he's honourable, / And, doubling that, most holy. Your means abroad— / You have me, rich; and I will never fail / Beginning nor supplyment.

First, just make yourself look like one. Foreseeing this, I've already got ready (it's in my cloak-bag) a doublet, hat, breeches, everything that goes with them. If you'd dress in them and, with whatever imitation you can borrow from a boy of that age, present yourself to noble Lucius, ask to serve him, tell him what you're good at (and he'll find that out if he has any ear for music), he'll surely take you on gladly, because he's honourable and, more than that, very religious. As for your money while abroad, you have me, who has plenty, and I'll never fail to provide what you need now and later.

Thou art all the comfort / The gods will diet me with. Prithee away! / There's more to be consider'd; but we'll even / All that good time will give us. This attempt / I am soldier to, and will abide it with / A prince's courage. Away, I prithee.

You're all the comfort the gods will feed me with. Please go! There's more to think about, but we'll fit ourselves to whatever good time brings us. I'm a soldier in this attempt and I'll see it through with a prince's courage. Go, please.

Well, madam, we must take a short farewell, / Lest, being miss'd, I be suspected of / Your carriage from the court. My noble mistress, / Here is a box; I had it from the Queen. / What's in't is precious. If you are sick at sea / Or stomach-qualm'd at land, a dram of this / Will drive away distemper. To some shade, / And fit you to your manhood. May the gods / Direct you to the best!

Well, madam, we must say a quick goodbye, in case I'm missed and suspected of taking you from court. My noble mistress, here's a box. I got it from the Queen. What's in it is precious. If you're seasick, or queasy on land, a sip of this will cure the sickness. Find somewhere shady and dress yourself as a man. May the gods guide you to the best!
This far, then; and so goodbye.
Thanks, royal sir. / My emperor hath wrote; I must from hence, / And am right sorry that I must report ye / My master's enemy.
Thank you, royal sir. My emperor has written; I must leave, and I'm truly sorry I must report you as my master's enemy.
Our subjects, sir, / Will not endure his yoke; and for ourself / To show less sovereignty than they, must needs / Appear unkinglike.
Our subjects, sir, won't bear his yoke, and if I showed less independence than they do, I'd look unkingly.
So, sir. I desire of you / A conduct overland to Milford Haven. / Madam, all joy befall your Grace, and you!
Very well, sir. I ask you for an escort overland to Milford Haven. Madam, may all joy come to your Grace, and to you!
My lords, you are appointed for that office; / The due of honour in no point omit. / So farewell, noble Lucius.
My lords, you are appointed to that duty. Leave out no part of the honour due to him. Goodbye, noble Lucius.
Receive it friendly; but from this time forth / I wear it as your enemy.
Take it as a friend; but from now on I wear it as your enemy.
Sir, the event / Is yet to name the winner. Fare you well.
Sir, the outcome has yet to name the winner. Farewell.
Leave not the worthy Lucius, good my lords, / Till he have cross'd the Severn. Happiness!
Don't leave the worthy Lucius, my good lords, until he's crossed the Severn. Good luck!
He goes hence frowning; but it honours us / That we have given him cause.
He leaves frowning, but it's to our honour that we've given him reason to.
'Tis all the better; / Your valiant Britons have their wishes in it.
All the better: your brave Britons get their wish.

Lucius hath wrote already to the Emperor / How it goes here. It fits us therefore ripely / Our chariots and our horsemen be in readiness. / The pow'rs that he already hath in Gallia / Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves / His war for Britain.

Lucius has already written to the Emperor about how things stand here. So it's high time our chariots and cavalry were ready. The forces he already has in France will soon be gathered, and from there he'll launch his war on Britain.
'Tis not sleepy business, / But must be look'd to speedily and strongly.
This is no business to sleep on. It must be dealt with quickly and strongly.

Our expectation that it would be thus / Hath made us forward. But, my gentle queen, / Where is our daughter? She hath not appear'd / Before the Roman, nor to us hath tender'd / The duty of the day. She looks us like / A thing more made of malice than of duty; / We have noted it. Call her before us, for / We have been too slight in sufferance.

We expected this, so we're prepared. But, my gentle queen, where is our daughter? She hasn't appeared before the Roman or paid us her daily respects. She seems to us more full of spite than duty; we've noticed it. Call her to us; we've been too lenient.

Royal sir, / Since the exile of Posthumus, most retir'd / Hath her life been; the cure whereof, my lord, / 'Tis time must do. Beseech your Majesty, / Forbear sharp speeches to her; she's a lady / So tender of rebukes that words are strokes, / And strokes death to her.

Royal sir, since Posthumus was exiled she has lived very much alone. Time must cure that, my lord. I beg your Majesty, don't speak sharply to her. She's so sensitive to scolding that words are blows to her, and blows are death.
Where is she, sir? How / Can her contempt be answer'd?
Where is she, sir? How can her contempt be explained?
Please you, sir, / Her chambers are all lock'd, and there's no answer / That will be given to th' loud of noise we make.
If you please, sir, her rooms are all locked, and there's no answer, however loudly we knock.

My lord, when last I went to visit her, / She pray'd me to excuse her keeping close; / Whereto constrain'd by her infirmity / She should that duty leave unpaid to you / Which daily she was bound to proffer. This / She wish'd me to make known; but our great court / Made me to blame in memory.

My lord, when I last visited her, she asked me to excuse her keeping to her rooms. Her illness forced her to leave unpaid the respects she owed you daily. She asked me to tell you, but the business of our great court made me forget.
Her doors lock'd? / Not seen of late? Grant, heavens, that which I fear / Prove false!
Her doors locked? Not seen lately? Heavens, let what I fear be false!
Son, I say, follow the King.
Son, I tell you, follow the King.
That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant, / I have not seen these two days.
That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant, I haven't seen for two days.

Pisanio, thou that stand'st so for Posthumus! / He hath a drug of mine. I pray his absence / Proceed by swallowing that; for he believes / It is a thing most precious. But for her, / Where is she gone? Haply despair hath seiz'd her; / Or, wing'd with fervour of her love, she's flown / To her desir'd Posthumus. Gone she is / To death or to dishonour, and my end / Can make good use of either. She being down, / I have the placing of the British crown.

Pisanio, you who stand up so for Posthumus! He has a drug of mine. I pray his absence is because he swallowed it, since he thinks it's very precious. But as for her, where has she gone? Maybe despair has taken hold of her, or, carried on the wings of her passionate love, she's flown to her beloved Posthumus. She's gone to death or to dishonour, and my purposes can make good use of either. With her out of the way, the British crown is mine to place.
'Tis certain she is fled. / Go in and cheer the King. He rages; none / Dare come about him.
It's certain she's run away. Go in and calm the King. He's raging; nobody dares go near him.
All the better. May / This night forestall him of the coming day!
All the better. I hope this night robs him of the coming day!

I love and hate her; for she's fair and royal, / And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite / Than lady, ladies, woman. From every one / The best she hath, and she, of all compounded, / Outsells them all. I love her therefore; but / Disdaining me and throwing favours on / The low Posthumus slanders so her judgment / That what's else rare is chok'd; and in that point / I will conclude to hate her, nay, indeed, / To be reveng'd upon her. For when fools / Shall—

I love her and hate her. I love her because she's beautiful and royal, and has every courtly grace more exquisitely than any lady, all ladies, or womankind. She has the best of each of them and, made up of them all, outshines them all. That's why I love her. But scorning me and throwing her favours on that low Posthumus so disgraces her judgment that her other rare qualities are choked. On that point I've decided to hate her; no, in fact, to get revenge on her. For when fools shall...
Who is here? What, are you packing, sirrah? / Come hither. Ah, you precious pander! Villain, / Where is thy lady? In a word, or else / Thou art straightway with the fiends.
Who's this? What, are you sneaking off, sirrah? Come here. Ah, you precious pimp! Villain, where's your lady? In a word, or you go straight to the devils.

Where is thy lady? or, by Jupiter— / I will not ask again. Close villain, / I'll have this secret from thy heart, or rip / Thy heart to find it. Is she with Posthumus? / From whose so many weights of baseness cannot / A dram of worth be drawn.

Where's your lady? Or, by Jupiter... I won't ask again. Secretive villain, I'll have this secret out of your heart, or rip your heart out to find it. Is she with Posthumus, from whose great weight of lowness not one gram of worth can be squeezed?
Alas, my lord, / How can she be with him? When was she miss'd? / He is in Rome.
Alas, my lord, how can she be with him? When was she missed? He's in Rome.
Where is she, sir? Come nearer. / No farther halting! Satisfy me home / What is become of her.
Where is she, sir? Come closer. No more stalling! Tell me fully what's become of her.
All-worthy villain! / Discover where thy mistress is at once, / At the next word. No more of 'worthy lord'! / Speak, or thy silence on the instant is / Thy condemnation and thy death.
Most worthy villain! Tell me where your mistress is at once, with your next word. No more "worthy lord"! Speak, or your silence is your sentence and your death on the spot.
Then, sir, / This paper is the history of my knowledge / Touching her flight. [Presenting a letter]
Then, sir, this paper is everything I know about her escape. (He hands over a letter.)
Let's see't. I will pursue her / Even to Augustus' throne.
Let me see it. I'll chase her even to Augustus's throne.
[Aside] Or this or perish. / She's far enough; and what he learns by this / May prove his travel, not her danger.
(Aside) It was this or die. She's far enough away, and what he learns from this may only cost him a journey, not put her in danger.
[Aside] I'll write to my lord she's dead. O Imogen, / Safe mayst thou wander, safe return again!
(Aside) I'll write to my lord that she's dead. Oh, Imogen, may you wander safely and come safely back!

It is Posthumus' hand; I know't. Sirrah, if thou wouldst / not be a villain, but do me true service, undergo those / employments wherein I should have cause to use thee with a / serious industry—that is, what villainy soe'er I bid thee do, to / perform it directly and truly—I would think thee an honest man; / thou shouldst neither want my means for thy relief nor my voice / for thy preferment.

It's Posthumus's handwriting; I know it. Sirrah, if you'd stop being a villain and serve me faithfully, and carry out seriously whatever jobs I have for you (that is, whatever villainy I order you to do, do it directly and properly), I'd think you an honest man. You wouldn't lack my money to help you or my word to promote you.

Wilt thou serve me? For since patiently and constantly thou / hast stuck to the bare fortune of that beggar Posthumus, thou / canst not, in the course of gratitude, but be a diligent follower / of mine. Wilt thou serve me?

Will you serve me? Since you've stuck so patiently and loyally to the miserable fortune of that beggar Posthumus, you can't help, out of gratitude, being a hard-working follower of mine. Will you serve me?
Give me thy hand; here's my purse. Hast any of thy late / master's garments in thy possession?
Give me your hand. Here's my purse. Do you have any of your old master's clothes?
I have, my lord, at my lodging, the same suit he wore when / he took leave of my lady and mistress.
I have, my lord, in my lodging: the same suit he wore when he said goodbye to my lady and mistress.
The first service thou dost me, fetch that suit hither. Let / it be thy first service; go.
The first thing you do for me: bring that suit here. Let that be your first service. Go.

Meet thee at Milford Haven! I forgot to ask him one thing; / I'll remember't anon. Even there, thou villain Posthumus, will I / kill thee. I would these garments were come. She said upon a / time—the bitterness of it I now belch from my heart—that she / held the very garment of Posthumus in more respect than my noble / and natural person, together with the adornment of my qualities. / With that suit upon my back will I ravish her; first kill him, / and in her eyes. There shall she see my valour, which will then / be a torment to her contempt. He on the ground, my speech of / insultment ended on his dead body, and when my lust hath dined— / which, as I say, to vex her I will execute in the clothes that / she so prais'd—to the court I'll knock her back, foot her home / again. She hath despis'd me rejoicingly, and I'll be merry in my / revenge.

Meet him at Milford Haven! I forgot to ask him one thing; I'll remember it in a moment. Right there, you villain Posthumus, I'll kill you. I wish those clothes would come. She once said (I belch the bitterness of it up from my heart now) that she valued Posthumus's mere clothes more than my noble person and all my fine qualities. With that suit on my back I'll rape her: but first kill him, in front of her. There she'll see my courage, which will then torment her scorn. With him on the ground and my insults spoken over his dead body, and when my lust has dined (which, as I say, I'll do in the clothes she praised so much, to spite her), I'll beat her back to court and kick her home. She's taken pleasure in scorning me, and I'll be merry in my revenge.
How long is't since she went to Milford Haven?
How long is it since she left for Milford Haven?
She can scarce be there yet.
She can hardly be there yet.

Bring this apparel to my chamber; that is the second thing / that I have commanded thee. The third is that thou wilt be a / voluntary mute to my design. Be but duteous and true, preferment / shall tender itself to thee. My revenge is now at Milford, would / I had wings to follow it! Come, and be true.

Take these clothes to my room; that's the second thing I've ordered you. The third is that you keep quiet about my plan of your own accord. Just be obedient and loyal, and promotion will come to you. My revenge is now at Milford; I wish I had wings to follow it! Come, and be loyal.

Thou bid'st me to my loss; for true to thee / Were to prove false, which I will never be, / To him that is most true. To Milford go, / And find not her whom thou pursuest. Flow, flow, / You heavenly blessings, on her! This fool's speed / Be cross'd with slowness! Labour be his meed!

You order me to my ruin: to be loyal to you would be to prove false to him who is most loyal, which I never will be. Go to Milford, and don't find the one you're chasing. Flow, flow, heavenly blessings, on her! May this fool's speed be blocked with slowness, and may his only reward be wasted effort!

I see a man's life is a tedious one. / I have tir'd myself, and for two nights together / Have made the ground my bed. I should be sick / But that my resolution helps me. Milford, / When from the mountain-top Pisanio show'd thee, / Thou wast within a ken. O Jove! I think / Foundations fly the wretched; such, I mean, / Where they should be reliev'd. Two beggars told me / I could not miss my way. Will poor folks lie, / That have afflictions on them, knowing 'tis / A punishment or trial? Yes; no wonder, / When rich ones scarce tell true. To lapse in fulness / Is sorer than to lie for need; and falsehood / Is worse in kings than beggars. My dear lord! / Thou art one o' th' false ones. Now I think on thee / My hunger's gone; but even before, I was / At point to sink for food. But what is this? / Here is a path to't; 'tis some savage hold. / I were best not call; I dare not call. Yet famine, / Ere clean it o'erthrow nature, makes it valiant. / Plenty and peace breeds cowards; hardness ever / Of hardiness is mother. Ho! who's here? / If anything that's civil, speak; if savage, / Take or lend. Ho! No answer? Then I'll enter. / Best draw my sword; and if mine enemy / But fear the sword, like me, he'll scarcely look on't. / Such a foe, good heavens!

I can see a man's life is a hard one. I've tired myself out, and for two nights running I've slept on the ground. I'd be ill, except my determination keeps me going. Milford, when Pisanio showed you to me from the mountain top, you were in sight. Oh, Jove! I think places of refuge run away from the wretched; I mean the places where they should get help. Two beggars told me I couldn't miss my way. Would poor people lie, when they're suffering and know it's a punishment or a test? Yes; no wonder, when rich people hardly tell the truth. To sin when you have plenty is worse than lying out of need, and lying is worse in kings than in beggars. My dear lord! You're one of the false ones. Now that I think of you my hunger's gone, though just before I was about to collapse for lack of food. But what's this? Here's a path to it; it's some wild man's den. I'd better not call; I don't dare call. But hunger, before it overthrows nature completely, makes it brave. Plenty and peace breed cowards; hardship is always the mother of hardiness. Hello! Who's here? If you're anything civilised, speak; if you're savage, take from me or lend to me. Hello! No answer? Then I'll go in. I'd better draw my sword; and if my enemy fears a sword as much as I do, he'll hardly dare look at it. Give me such an enemy, good heavens!

You, Polydore, have prov'd best woodman and / Are master of the feast. Cadwal and I / Will play the cook and servant; 'tis our match. / The sweat of industry would dry and die / But for the end it works to. Come, our stomachs / Will make what's homely savoury; weariness / Can snore upon the flint, when resty sloth / Finds the down pillow hard. Now, peace be here, / Poor house, that keep'st thyself!

You, Polydore, have proved the best hunter and are master of the feast. Cadwal and I will be cook and servant: that was our bargain. The sweat of hard work would dry up and die, if not for the purpose it serves. Come, our appetites will make plain food tasty. Tiredness can snore on a stone, while lazy idleness finds a feather pillow hard. Now, peace be with you, poor house that looks after yourself!
I am weak with toil, yet strong in appetite.
I'm weak from work but strong in appetite.
There is cold meat i' th' cave; we'll browse on that / Whilst what we have kill'd be cook'd.
There's cold meat in the cave. We'll nibble on that while what we've killed is cooked.
