[Looking into the cave] Stay, come not in. / But that it eats our victuals, I should think / Here were a fairy.
(Looking into the cave) Wait, don't go in. If it weren't eating our food, I'd think there was a fairy here.
By Jupiter, an angel! or, if not, / An earthly paragon! Behold divineness / No elder than a boy!
By Jupiter, an angel! Or if not, an earthly perfection! Look: divinity no older than a boy!

Good masters, harm me not. / Before I enter'd here I call'd, and thought / To have begg'd or bought what I have took. Good troth, / I have stol'n nought; nor would not though I had found / Gold strew'd i' th' floor. Here's money for my meat. / I would have left it on the board, so soon / As I had made my meal, and parted / With pray'rs for the provider.

Good sirs, don't hurt me. Before I came in I called out, and I meant to beg or buy what I've taken. Honestly, I've stolen nothing, and I wouldn't even if I'd found gold scattered on the floor. Here's money for my food. I'd have left it on the table as soon as I'd eaten and gone away with prayers for the person who provided it.
All gold and silver rather turn to dirt, / As 'tis no better reckon'd but of those / Who worship dirty gods.
Let all gold and silver turn to dirt instead, since it's valued no higher than dirt except by those who worship dirty gods.
I see you're angry. / Know, if you kill me for my fault, I should / Have died had I not made it.
I see you're angry. Know that if you kill me for my offence, I'd have died if I hadn't committed it.
Fidele, sir. I have a kinsman who / Is bound for Italy; he embark'd at Milford; / To whom being going, almost spent with hunger, / I am fall'n in this offence.
Fidele, sir. I have a relative who's bound for Italy; he sailed from Milford. On my way to him, almost dead with hunger, I fell into this offence.

Prithee, fair youth, / Think us no churls, nor measure our good minds / By this rude place we live in. Well encounter'd! / 'Tis almost night; you shall have better cheer / Ere you depart, and thanks to stay and eat it. / Boys, bid him welcome.

Please, fair youth, don't think we're rough peasants, and don't judge our good hearts by this rough place we live in. Well met! It's almost night. You'll have better food before you leave, and thanks for staying to eat it. Boys, welcome him.
Were you a woman, youth, / I should woo hard but be your groom. In honesty / I bid for you as I'd buy.
If you were a woman, young man, I'd court you hard to be your husband. Honestly, I'd bid for you as I'd want to buy.

I'll make't my comfort / He is a man. I'll love him as my brother; / And such a welcome as I'd give to him / After long absence, such is yours. Most welcome! / Be sprightly, for you fall 'mongst friends.
It'll be my comfort that he's a man. I'll love him as my brother, and the welcome I'd give my brother after a long absence is yours. Most welcome! Cheer up, you've fallen among friends.
'Mongst friends, / If brothers. [Aside] Would it had been so that they / Had been my father's sons! Then had my prize / Been less, and so more equal ballasting / To thee, Posthumus.
Among friends, if brothers. (Aside) I wish they had been my father's sons! Then my value as heir would have been less, and I'd have been a more equal weight to balance you, Posthumus.
I wish I could free him from it!
Or I, whate'er it be, / What pain it cost, what danger! Gods!
Or I, whatever it is, whatever pain or danger it cost! Gods!

[Aside] Great men, / That had a court no bigger than this cave, / That did attend themselves, and had the virtue / Which their own conscience seal'd them, laying by / That nothing-gift of differing multitudes, / Could not out-peer these twain. Pardon me, gods! / I'd change my sex to be companion with them, / Since Leonatus' false.

(Aside) Great men with a court no bigger than this cave, who served themselves and had only the virtue their own consciences gave them, setting aside the worthless flattery of fickle crowds, couldn't outshine these two. Forgive me, gods! I'd change my sex to be their companion, since Leonatus is false.
It shall be so. / Boys, we'll go dress our hunt. Fair youth, come in. / Discourse is heavy, fasting; when we have supp'd, / We'll mannerly demand thee of thy story, / So far as thou wilt speak it.

That's settled. Boys, let's go and prepare our game. Fair youth, come in. Talking is hard work on an empty stomach. When we've eaten, we'll politely ask you for your story, as much as you want to tell.
The night to th' owl and morn to th' lark less welcome.
Night is less welcome to the owl and morning to the lark than you are to us.

This is the tenour of the Emperor's writ: / That since the common men are now in action / 'Gainst the Pannonians and Dalmatians, / And that the legions now in Gallia are / Full weak to undertake our wars against / The fall'n-off Britons, that we do incite / The gentry to this business. He creates / Lucius proconsul; and to you, the tribunes, / For this immediate levy, he commands / His absolute commission. Long live Caesar!

This is the gist of the Emperor's order: since the common soldiers are now fighting the Pannonians and Dalmatians, and the legions now in France are too weak to take on our war against the rebel Britons, we are to call on the gentlemen to take up this business. He makes Lucius proconsul, and to you tribunes he gives full authority for this immediate call-up. Long live Caesar!
Is Lucius general of the forces?
Is Lucius general of the forces?
With those legions / Which I have spoke of, whereunto your levy / Must be supplyant. The words of your commission / Will tie you to the numbers and the time / Of their dispatch.
With the legions I mentioned, which your recruits must reinforce. The words of your orders will fix the numbers and the time to send them.

I am near to th' place where they should meet, if Pisanio / have mapp'd it truly. How fit his garments serve me! Why should / his mistress, who was made by him that made the tailor, not be / fit too? The rather—saving reverence of the word—for 'tis said / a woman's fitness comes by fits. Therein I must play the workman. / I dare speak it to myself, for it is not vain-glory for a man and / his glass to confer in his own chamber—I mean, the lines of my / body are as well drawn as his; no less young, more strong, not / beneath him in fortunes, beyond him in the advantage of the time, / above him in birth, alike conversant in general services, and / more remarkable in single oppositions. Yet this imperceiverant / thing loves him in my despite. What mortality is! Posthumus, thy / head, which now is growing upon thy shoulders, shall within this / hour be off; thy mistress enforced; thy garments cut to pieces / before her face; and all this done, spurn her home to her father, / who may, haply, be a little angry for my so rough usage; but my / mother, having power of his testiness, shall turn all into my / commendations. My horse is tied up safe. Out, sword, and to a / sore purpose! Fortune, put them into my hand. This is the very / description of their meeting-place; and the fellow dares not / deceive me.

I'm near the place where they're supposed to meet, if Pisanio's map is accurate. How well his clothes fit me! Why shouldn't his lady, who was made by the same God who made the tailor, fit me too? All the more since (pardon the expression) they say a woman's fitness comes in fits. I'll have to work at that. I can say it to myself, because it isn't vanity for a man to consult his mirror in his own room: I mean, my body is as well drawn as his: no less young, stronger, not below him in fortune, ahead of him in present favour, above him in birth, just as experienced in battle, and more outstanding in single combat. And yet this undiscerning thing loves him to spite me. What a thing human life is! Posthumus, your head, which is now growing on your shoulders, will be off within the hour; your lady raped; your clothes cut to pieces in front of her; and when all that's done, I'll kick her home to her father, who may be a little angry at my rough treatment; but my mother, who can control his temper, will turn it all into praise of me. My horse is tied up safely. Out, sword, to a cruel purpose! Fortune, put them into my hands. This is exactly the place described for their meeting, and the fellow wouldn't dare deceive me.
[To Imogen] You are not well. Remain here in the cave; / We'll come to you after hunting.
(To Imogen) You're not well. Stay here in the cave. We'll come back to you after hunting.
[To Imogen] Brother, stay here. / Are we not brothers?
(To Imogen) Brother, stay here. Aren't we brothers?
So man and man should be; / But clay and clay differs in dignity, / Whose dust is both alike. I am very sick.
That's how man and man should be; but clay and clay differ in rank, though their dust is just the same. I'm very ill.
Go you to hunting; I'll abide with him.
You go hunting. I'll stay with him.

So sick I am not, yet I am not well; / But not so citizen a wanton as / To seem to die ere sick. So please you, leave me; / Stick to your journal course. The breach of custom / Is breach of all. I am ill, but your being by me / Cannot amend me; society is no comfort / To one not sociable. I am not very sick, / Since I can reason of it. Pray you trust me here. / I'll rob none but myself; and let me die, / Stealing so poorly.

I'm not so very ill, yet I'm not well; but I'm not such a spoilt city boy as to act as if I'm dying before I'm sick. Please, leave me; keep to your daily routine. Breaking a habit breaks everything. I'm ill, but your being with me can't cure me. Company is no comfort to someone not in the mood for it. I'm not very ill, since I can reason about it. Please trust me here. I'll rob no one but myself, and let me die if I steal that poorly.
I love thee; I have spoke it. / How much the quantity, the weight as much / As I do love my father.
I love you; I've said it. As much in quantity and weight as I love my father.

If it be sin to say so, sir, I yoke me / In my good brother's fault. I know not why / I love this youth, and I have heard you say / Love's reason's without reason. The bier at door, / And a demand who is't shall die, I'd say / 'My father, not this youth.'

If it's a sin to say so, sir, I share my good brother's fault. I don't know why I love this boy, and I've heard you say love has no reason. If the coffin were at the door and someone asked who should die, I'd say, "My father, not this boy."

[Aside] O noble strain! / O worthiness of nature! breed of greatness! / Cowards father cowards and base things sire base. / Nature hath meal and bran, contempt and grace. / I'm not their father; yet who this should be / Doth miracle itself, lov'd before me.— / 'Tis the ninth hour o' th' morn.

(Aside) Oh, noble blood! Oh, natural worth! The breeding of greatness! Cowards father cowards, and low things beget low things. Nature has fine flour and bran, the despised and the graceful. I'm not their father; and yet who this boy is, that they love him more than me, is a miracle. (Aloud) It's nine in the morning.
Your health. [To Belarius] So please you, sir.
Get well. (To Belarius) Ready when you are, sir.

[Aside] These are kind creatures. Gods, what lies I have / heard! / Our courtiers say all's savage but at court. / Experience, O, thou disprov'st report! / Th' imperious seas breed monsters; for the dish, / Poor tributary rivers as sweet fish. / I am sick still; heart-sick. Pisanio, / I'll now taste of thy drug. [Swallows some]

(Aside) These are kind creatures. Gods, what lies I've heard! Our courtiers say everything is savage except the court. Experience, how you disprove gossip! The mighty seas breed monsters, while poor little rivers that flow into them give fish just as sweet for eating. I'm still sick, heart-sick. Pisanio, I'll try your drug now. (She swallows some.)
I could not stir him. / He said he was gentle, but unfortunate; / Dishonestly afflicted, but yet honest.
I couldn't get anything out of him. He said he was well born but unlucky; dishonourably wronged, but still honourable.
Thus did he answer me; yet said hereafter / I might know more.
That's what he told me too; but he said I might know more later.
To th' field, to th' field! / We'll leave you for this time. Go in and rest.
To the fields, to the fields! We'll leave you for now. Go in and rest.
Pray be not sick, / For you must be our huswife.
Please don't be ill, because you have to be our housekeeper.
Well, or ill, / I am bound to you.
Well or ill, I'm in your debt.
This youth, howe'er distress'd, appears he hath had / Good ancestors.
This boy, however troubled he is, seems to come of good ancestors.
How like an angel he sings!
But his neat cookery! He cut our roots in characters, / And sauc'd our broths as Juno had been sick, / And he her dieter.
And his neat cooking! He cut our root vegetables into letters and seasoned our broths as if Juno were sick and he were her dietician.

Nobly he yokes / A smiling with a sigh, as if the sigh / Was that it was for not being such a smile; / The smile mocking the sigh that it would fly / From so divine a temple to commix / With winds that sailors rail at.
He joins a smile and a sigh so nobly, as if the sigh were sorry it wasn't such a smile, and the smile mocked the sigh for wanting to fly from such a divine temple to mix with the winds sailors curse.
I do note / That grief and patience, rooted in him both, / Mingle their spurs together.
I notice that grief and patience, both rooted in him, tangle their roots together.
Grow patience! / And let the stinking elder, grief, untwine / His perishing root with the increasing vine!
Grow, patience! And let that stinking elder tree, grief, untwine its dying root from the growing vine!
It is great morning. Come, away! Who's there?
It's broad daylight. Come on, let's go! Who's there?
I cannot find those runagates; that villain / Hath mock'd me. I am faint.
I can't find those runaways. That villain has fooled me. I'm worn out.

Those runagates? / Means he not us? I partly know him; 'tis / Cloten, the son o' th' Queen. I fear some ambush. / I saw him not these many years, and yet / I know 'tis he. We are held as outlaws. Hence!

"Those runaways"? Doesn't he mean us? I half know him: it's Cloten, the Queen's son. I'm afraid of an ambush. I haven't seen him for many years, but I know it's him. We're considered outlaws. Let's go!
He is but one; you and my brother search / What companies are near. Pray you away; / Let me alone with him.
He's only one man. You and my brother search for any troops nearby. Please go. Leave me alone with him.
Soft! What are you / That fly me thus? Some villain mountaineers? / I have heard of such. What slave art thou?
Wait! Who are you, running away from me like that? Some villainous mountain men? I've heard of such people. What sort of slave are you?
A thing / More slavish did I ne'er than answering / 'A slave' without a knock.
I never did anything more slavish than to answer to "slave" without hitting back.
Thou art a robber, / A law-breaker, a villain. Yield thee, thief.
You're a robber, a lawbreaker, a villain. Surrender, thief.

To who? To thee? What art thou? Have not I / An arm as big as thine, a heart as big? / Thy words, I grant, are bigger, for I wear not / My dagger in my mouth. Say what thou art; / Why I should yield to thee.

To whom? To you? Who are you? Haven't I got an arm as strong as yours, and a heart as brave? Your words, I'll grant, are bigger, because I don't carry my dagger in my mouth. Tell me who you are and why I should surrender to you.
Thou villain base, / Know'st me not by my clothes?
You low villain, don't you know me by my clothes?
No, nor thy tailor, rascal, / Who is thy grandfather; he made those clothes, / Which, as it seems, make thee.
No, rascal, nor your tailor, who's your grandfather. He made those clothes, which seem to be what made you.
Thou precious varlet, / My tailor made them not.
You precious rogue, my tailor didn't make them.
Hence, then, and thank / The man that gave them thee. Thou art some fool; / I am loath to beat thee.
Then go away and thank the man who gave them to you. You're some sort of fool. I don't want to beat you.
Thou injurious thief, / Hear but my name, and tremble.
You insolent thief, just hear my name and tremble.
Cloten, thou double villain, be thy name, / I cannot tremble at it. Were it toad, or adder, spider, / 'Twould move me sooner.
Cloten, you double villain, let that be your name: I can't tremble at it. If it were Toad, or Adder, or Spider, it would move me sooner.
To thy further fear, / Nay, to thy mere confusion, thou shalt know / I am son to th' Queen.
To frighten you more, no, to destroy you completely, know that I'm the Queen's son.
I'm sorry for't; not seeming / So worthy as thy birth.
I'm sorry about that; you don't seem as worthy as your birth.
Those that I reverence, those I fear—the wise: / At fools I laugh, not fear them.
I fear those I respect: the wise. Fools I laugh at, I don't fear them.
Die the death. / When I have slain thee with my proper hand, / I'll follow those that even now fled hence, / And on the gates of Lud's Town set your heads. / Yield, rustic mountaineer.
Then die. When I've killed you with my own hand, I'll go after those who just ran off, and set your heads on the gates of London. Surrender, you country bumpkin.
None in the world; you did mistake him, sure.
None at all. You must have mistaken him.

I cannot tell; long is it since I saw him, / But time hath nothing blurr'd those lines of favour / Which then he wore; the snatches in his voice, / And burst of speaking, were as his. I am absolute / 'Twas very Cloten.
I can't be sure. It's a long time since I saw him, but time hasn't blurred the features he had then. The jerks in his voice and the bursts of speech were his. I'm certain it was Cloten himself.
In this place we left them. / I wish my brother make good time with him, / You say he is so fell.
This is where we left them. I hope my brother deals with him well, since you say he's so fierce.
Being scarce made up, / I mean to man, he had not apprehension / Or roaring terrors; for defect of judgment / Is oft the cease of fear.
Being hardly grown into a man, I mean, he had no sense of fear's roaring terrors; lack of judgment often means lack of fear.
This Cloten was a fool, an empty purse; / There was no money in't. Not Hercules / Could have knock'd out his brains, for he had none; / Yet I not doing this, the fool had borne / My head as I do his.

This Cloten was a fool, an empty purse with no money in it. Not even Hercules could have knocked out his brains, because he had none. Still, if I hadn't done this, the fool would be carrying my head as I'm carrying his.

I am perfect what: cut off one Cloten's head, / Son to the Queen, after his own report; / Who call'd me traitor, mountaineer, and swore / With his own single hand he'd take us in, / Displace our heads where—thank the gods!—they grow, / And set them on Lud's Town.

I know exactly what: cut off the head of one Cloten, the Queen's son, by his own account, who called me traitor and mountain man and swore he'd capture us single-handed, take our heads off where (thank the gods!) they grow, and set them up on the gates of London.

Why, worthy father, what have we to lose / But that he swore to take, our lives? The law / Protects not us; then why should we be tender / To let an arrogant piece of flesh threat us, / Play judge and executioner all himself, / For we do fear the law? What company / Discover you abroad?

Why, worthy father, what have we to lose except what he swore to take, our lives? The law doesn't protect us, so why should we be so soft as to let an arrogant lump of flesh threaten us and play judge and executioner all by himself, just because we're afraid of the law? Did you find any troops about?

No single soul / Can we set eye on, but in an safe reason / He must have some attendants. Though his humour / Was nothing but mutation—ay, and that / From one bad thing to worse—not frenzy, not / Absolute madness could so far have rav'd, / To bring him here alone. Although perhaps / It may be heard at court that such as we / Cave here, hunt here, are outlaws, and in time / May make some stronger head—the which he hearing, / As it is like him, might break out and swear / He'd fetch us in; yet is't not probable / To come alone, either he so undertaking / Or they so suffering. Then on good ground we fear, / If we do fear this body hath a tail / More perilous than the head.

We can't see a single soul. But common sense says he must have some attendants. Though his mood was nothing but changes, and those from one bad thing to worse, not even frenzy or total madness could have driven him to come here alone. Perhaps it's been heard at court that people like us live in caves here, hunt here, are outlaws, and might one day gather a stronger force; and hearing that, he might, as is just like him, burst out swearing he'd bring us in. But it's not likely he'd come alone, either that he'd undertake it or that they'd allow it. So we have good reason to fear that this body has a tail more dangerous than its head.
Let ordinance / Come as the gods foresay it. Howsoe'er, / My brother hath done well.
Let what's fated come as the gods decree. However it turns out, my brother did well.
I had no mind / To hunt this day; the boy Fidele's sickness / Did make my way long forth.
I didn't feel like hunting today. The boy Fidele's sickness made the way feel long.

With his own sword, / Which he did wave against my throat, I have ta'en / His head from him. I'll throw't into the creek / Behind our rock, and let it to the sea / And tell the fishes he's the Queen's son, Cloten. / That's all I reck.

With his own sword, which he waved at my throat, I've cut off his head. I'll throw it into the creek behind our rock and send it out to sea to tell the fishes he's the Queen's son, Cloten. That's all I care.
I fear'twill be reveng'd. / Would, Polydore, thou hadst not done't! though valour / Becomes thee well enough.
I'm afraid it will be avenged. I wish you hadn't done it, Polydore, though bravery suits you well enough.

Would I had done't, / So the revenge alone pursu'd me! Polydore, / I love thee brotherly, but envy much / Thou hast robb'd me of this deed. I would revenges, / That possible strength might meet, would seek us through, / And put us to our answer.

I wish I'd done it, so that the revenge would come after me alone! Polydore, I love you like a brother, but I'm very jealous that you've robbed me of this deed. I wish any revenge that human strength could meet would come looking for us and make us answer for it.

Well, 'tis done. / We'll hunt no more to-day, nor seek for danger / Where there's no profit. I prithee to our rock. / You and Fidele play the cooks; I'll stay / Till hasty Polydore return, and bring him / To dinner presently.

Well, it's done. We'll hunt no more today, and not look for danger where there's nothing to gain. Please go back to our rock. You and Fidele do the cooking. I'll wait for hasty Polydore to come back, and bring him to dinner at once.
Poor sick Fidele! / I'll willingly to him; to gain his colour / I'd let a parish of such Cloten's blood, / And praise myself for charity.
Poor sick Fidele! I'll go to him gladly. To bring back his colour I'd shed the blood of a whole parish of Clotens and call it charity.

O thou goddess, / Thou divine Nature, thou thyself thou blazon'st / In these two princely boys! They are as gentle / As zephyrs blowing below the violet, / Not wagging his sweet head; and yet as rough, / Their royal blood enchaf'd, as the rud'st wind / That by the top doth take the mountain pine / And make him stoop to th' vale. 'Tis wonder / That an invisible instinct should frame them / To royalty unlearn'd, honour untaught, / Civility not seen from other, valour / That wildly grows in them, but yields a crop / As if it had been sow'd. Yet still it's strange / What Cloten's being here to us portends, / Or what his death will bring us.

Oh, goddess, divine Nature, how you display yourself in these two princely boys! They're as gentle as the breeze blowing under the violet without even stirring its sweet head; and yet, when their royal blood is heated, as rough as the wildest wind that seizes the mountain pine by its top and bends it to the valley. It's a wonder that an invisible instinct should shape them to royalty without learning it, honour without teaching, courtesy they've never seen in others, and courage that grows wild in them but yields a crop as if it had been sown. Still, it's strange what Cloten's coming here means for us, or what his death will bring us.
Where's my brother? / I have sent Cloten's clotpoll down the stream, / In embassy to his mother; his body's hostage / For his return. [Solemn music]
Where's my brother? I've sent Cloten's blockhead down the stream as an ambassador to his mother; his body stays as hostage for its return. (Solemn music.)
My ingenious instrument! / Hark, Polydore, it sounds. But what occasion / Hath Cadwal now to give it motion? Hark!
My ingenious instrument! Listen, Polydore, it's playing. But what reason does Cadwal have to play it now? Listen!

What does he mean? Since death of my dear'st mother / It did not speak before. All solemn things / Should answer solemn accidents. The matter? / Triumphs for nothing and lamenting toys / Is jollity for apes and grief for boys. / Is Cadwal mad?

What does he mean by it? It hasn't sounded since my dear mother died. Solemn things should answer solemn events. What's the matter? Celebrating nothing and mourning trifles is merriment for apes and grief for boys. Is Cadwal mad?
Look, here he comes, / And brings the dire occasion in his arms / Of what we blame him for!
Look, here he comes, carrying in his arms the terrible reason for what we were blaming him for!
The bird is dead / That we have made so much on. I had rather / Have skipp'd from sixteen years of age to sixty, / To have turn'd my leaping time into a crutch, / Than have seen this.
The bird we loved so much is dead. I'd rather have jumped from sixteen to sixty and turned my leaping days into a crutch than have seen this.
O sweetest, fairest lily! / My brother wears thee not the one half so well / As when thou grew'st thyself.
Oh, sweetest, fairest lily! My brother doesn't wear you half as well as when you grew by yourself.

O melancholy! / Who ever yet could sound thy bottom? find / The ooze to show what coast thy sluggish crare / Might'st easiliest harbour in? Thou blessed thing! / Jove knows what man thou mightst have made; but I, / Thou diedst, a most rare boy, of melancholy. / How found you him?

Oh, melancholy! Who has ever sounded your depths, or found the seabed to show on what coast your sluggish boat could most easily harbour? You blessed thing! Jove knows what a man you might have made; but I know that you died, a most rare boy, of melancholy. How did you find him?
Stark, as you see; / Thus smiling, as some fly had tickled slumber, / Not as death's dart, being laugh'd at; his right cheek / Reposing on a cushion.
Stiff, as you see; smiling like this, as if a fly had tickled him in his sleep, not as if he'd laughed at death's arrow; his right cheek resting on a cushion.
O' th' floor; / His arms thus leagu'd. I thought he slept, and put / My clouted brogues from off my feet, whose rudeness / Answer'd my steps too loud.
On the floor, his arms folded like this. I thought he was asleep and took off my hobnailed shoes, because their roughness made my steps too loud.
Why, he but sleeps. / If he be gone he'll make his grave a bed; / With female fairies will his tomb be haunted, / And worms will not come to thee.
Why, he's only asleep. If he's gone, he'll make his grave a bed. His tomb will be visited by female fairies, and worms won't come near you.

With fairest flowers, / Whilst summer lasts and I live here, Fidele, / I'll sweeten thy sad grave. Thou shalt not lack / The flower that's like thy face, pale primrose; nor / The azur'd hare-bell, like thy veins; no, nor / The leaf of eglantine, whom not to slander, / Out-sweet'ned not thy breath. The ruddock would, / With charitable bill—O bill, sore shaming / Those rich-left heirs that let their fathers lie / Without a monument!—bring thee all this; / Yea, and furr'd moss besides, when flow'rs are none, / To winter-ground thy corse—

With the loveliest flowers, while summer lasts and I live here, Fidele, I'll sweeten your sad grave. You won't lack the flower that's like your face, the pale primrose, nor the blue harebell, like your veins; no, nor the sweet-briar leaf, which, to be fair to it, was no sweeter than your breath. The robin, with its charitable beak (oh, a beak that shames those rich heirs who leave their fathers without a monument!), would bring you all this; yes, and furry moss as well, when there are no flowers, to cover your body against the winter...
Prithee have done, / And do not play in wench-like words with that / Which is so serious. Let us bury him, / And not protract with admiration what / Is now due debt. To th' grave.
Please stop, and don't play with girlish words about something so serious. Let's bury him and not delay, with our admiring, what is now a debt we owe. To the grave.
Tell me, where shall we lay him?
Be't so; / And let us, Polydore, though now our voices / Have got the mannish crack, sing him to th' ground, / As once to our mother; use like note and words, / Save that Euriphile must be Fidele.
So be it. And, Polydore, though our voices have broken now like men's, let's sing him into the ground as we once did our mother, with the same tune and words, except that Euriphile must be Fidele.
Cadwal, / I cannot sing. I'll weep, and word it with thee; / For notes of sorrow out of tune are worse / Than priests and fanes that lie.
Cadwal, I can't sing. I'll weep and say the words with you, because songs of sorrow sung out of tune are worse than lying priests and temples.

Great griefs, I see, med'cine the less, for Cloten / Is quite forgot. He was a queen's son, boys; / And though he came our enemy, remember / He was paid for that. Though mean and mighty rotting / Together have one dust, yet reverence— / That angel of the world—doth make distinction / Of place 'tween high and low. Our foe was princely; / And though you took his life, as being our foe, / Yet bury him as a prince.

Great griefs, I see, cure smaller ones, because Cloten is quite forgotten. He was a queen's son, boys, and though he came as our enemy, remember he's paid for that. Though the low and the mighty rot into the same dust, respect, that angel of the world, still distinguishes between high and low rank. Our enemy was a prince, and though you took his life because he was our enemy, bury him as a prince.
Pray you fetch him hither. / Thersites' body is as good as Ajax', / When neither are alive.
Please bring him here. Thersites' body is as good as Ajax's when neither is alive.
If you'll go fetch him, / We'll say our song the whilst. Brother, begin.
If you'll go and fetch him, we'll say our song meanwhile. Brother, begin.
Nay, Cadwal, we must lay his head to th' East; / My father hath a reason for't.
No, Cadwal, we must lay his head to the east. Our father has a reason for it.
Come on, then, and remove him.
Come on, then, and move him.

Fear no more the heat o' th' sun / Nor the furious winter's rages; / Thou thy worldly task hast done, / Home art gone, and ta'en thy wages. / Golden lads and girls all must, / As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.

(Song) Don't fear the heat of the sun any more, or the raging of fierce winter. You've done your work in the world, gone home and been paid your wages. Golden boys and girls, like chimney-sweeps, must all come to dust.

Fear no more the frown o' th' great; / Thou art past the tyrant's stroke. / Care no more to clothe and eat; / To thee the reed is as the oak. / The sceptre, learning, physic, must / All follow this and come to dust.

Don't fear the frown of the great any more; you're beyond the tyrant's blow. Don't worry any more about clothes and food; to you the reed is the same as the oak. Kings, scholars and doctors must all follow this way and come to dust.
Fear no more the lightning flash,
Don't fear the lightning flash any more,
Don't fear slander or hasty blame.
Thou hast finish'd joy and moan.
You've finished with joy and grief.
All lovers young, all lovers must / Consign to thee and come to dust.
All young lovers, all lovers must go the way you've gone and come to dust.
May no one raising spirits disturb you!
May no restless ghost trouble you!
May nothing evil come near you!
Quiet consummation have, / And renowned be thy grave!
Have a quiet end, and may your grave be honoured!
We have done our obsequies. Come, lay him down.
We've done our funeral rites. Come, lay him down.

Here's a few flowers; but 'bout midnight, more. / The herbs that have on them cold dew o' th' night / Are strewings fit'st for graves. Upon their faces. / You were as flow'rs, now wither'd. Even so / These herblets shall which we upon you strew. / Come on, away. Apart upon our knees. / The ground that gave them first has them again. / Their pleasures here are past, so is their pain.

Here are a few flowers, but I'll bring more around midnight. Herbs with the cold night dew on them are the best things to scatter on graves. (To the bodies) Upon your faces. You were like flowers, now withered; so will these little herbs we scatter on you. Come on, let's go. We'll kneel apart. The earth that gave them life has them back again. Their pleasures here are over, and so is their pain.

[Awaking] Yes, sir, to Milford Haven. Which is the way? / I thank you. By yond bush? Pray, how far thither? / 'Ods pittikins! can it be six mile yet? / I have gone all night. Faith, I'll lie down and sleep. / But, soft! no bedfellow. O gods and goddesses!

(Waking) Yes, sir, to Milford Haven. Which way is it? Thank you. By that bush? Please, how far is it? Goodness, can it still be six miles? I've walked all night. Honestly, I'll lie down and sleep. But wait, no bedfellow! Oh, gods and goddesses!

These flow'rs are like the pleasures of the world; / This bloody man, the care on't. I hope I dream; / For so I thought I was a cave-keeper, / And cook to honest creatures. But 'tis not so; / 'Twas but a bolt of nothing, shot at nothing, / Which the brain makes of fumes. Our very eyes / Are sometimes, like our judgments, blind. Good faith, / I tremble still with fear; but if there be / Yet left in heaven as small a drop of pity / As a wren's eye, fear'd gods, a part of it! / The dream's here still. Even when I wake it is / Without me, as within me; not imagin'd, felt. / A headless man? The garments of Posthumus? / I know the shape of's leg; this is his hand, / His foot Mercurial, his Martial thigh, / The brawns of Hercules; but his Jovial face— / Murder in heaven! How! 'Tis gone. Pisanio, / All curses madded Hecuba gave the Greeks, / And mine to boot, be darted on thee! Thou, / Conspir'd with that irregulous devil, Cloten, / Hath here cut off my lord. To write and read / Be henceforth treacherous! Damn'd Pisanio / Hath with his forged letters—damn'd Pisanio— / From this most bravest vessel of the world / Struck the main-top. O Posthumus! alas, / Where is thy head? Where's that? Ay me! where's that? / Pisanio might have kill'd thee at the heart, / And left this head on. How should this be? Pisanio? / 'Tis he and Cloten; malice and lucre in them / Have laid this woe here. O, 'tis pregnant, pregnant! / The drug he gave me, which he said was precious / And cordial to me, have I not found it / Murd'rous to th' senses? That confirms it home. / This is Pisanio's deed, and Cloten. O! / Give colour to my pale cheek with thy blood, / That we the horrider may seem to those / Which chance to find us. O, my lord, my lord!

These flowers are like the pleasures of the world; this bloody man is like its troubles. I hope I'm dreaming, because I thought I was a cave-keeper and cook to honest people. But it's not so; it was just an arrow of nothing shot at nothing, the kind of thing the brain makes out of vapours. Our very eyes are sometimes blind, like our judgment. Truly, I'm still trembling with fear; but if there's still a drop of pity left in heaven, as small as a wren's eye, you feared gods, give me some of it! The dream is still here. Even now that I'm awake it's outside me as well as inside: not imagined, but felt. A headless man? Posthumus's clothes? I know the shape of his leg. This is his hand, his foot as swift as Mercury's, his thigh strong as Mars's, his Herculean muscles; but his face, like Jove's... Murder in heaven? What? It's gone! Pisanio, may all the curses mad Hecuba threw at the Greeks, and mine as well, strike you! You, conspiring with that lawless devil Cloten, have killed my lord here. From now on let writing and reading be treacherous! Damned Pisanio, with his forged letters (damned Pisanio!), has knocked the mainmast off the bravest ship in the world. Oh, Posthumus! Alas, where's your head? Where is it? Oh, where is it? Pisanio could have stabbed you in the heart and left this head on. How could this happen? Pisanio? It's him and Cloten: malice and greed in them have caused this sorrow here. Oh, it's clear, clear! The drug he gave me, which he said was precious and restoring, didn't I find it deadening to the senses? That proves it completely. This is Pisanio's work, and Cloten's. Oh! Let me colour my pale cheek with your blood, so we'll look the more horrible to whoever finds us. Oh, my lord, my lord!
To them the legions garrison'd in Gallia, / After your will, have cross'd the sea, attending / You here at Milford Haven; with your ships, / They are in readiness.
In addition to them, the legions stationed in France have crossed the sea as you ordered, and are waiting for you here at Milford Haven with your ships. They're ready.
The Senate hath stirr'd up the confiners / And gentlemen of Italy, most willing spirits, / That promise noble service; and they come / Under the conduct of bold Iachimo, / Sienna's brother.
The Senate has roused the frontier people and gentlemen of Italy, very willing men who promise noble service. They're coming under the command of brave Iachimo, the Duke of Siena's brother.
With the next benefit o' th' wind.
This forwardness / Makes our hopes fair. Command our present numbers / Be muster'd; bid the captains look to't. Now, sir, / What have you dream'd of late of this war's purpose?
This readiness makes our hopes look good. Order the troops we have now to be assembled; tell the captains to see to it. Now, sir, what have you dreamed lately about the outcome of this war?

Last night the very gods show'd me a vision— / I fast and pray'd for their intelligence—thus: / I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, wing'd / From the spongy south to this part of the west, / There vanish'd in the sunbeams; which portends, / Unless my sins abuse my divination, / Success to th' Roman host.

Last night the gods themselves showed me a vision (I fasted and prayed for their knowledge). I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, fly from the damp south to this part of the west, and vanish there in the sunbeams. That means, unless my sins have spoiled my prophecy, success for the Roman army.

Dream often so, / And never false. Soft, ho! what trunk is here / Without his top? The ruin speaks that sometime / It was a worthy building. How? a page? / Or dead or sleeping on him? But dead, rather; / For nature doth abhor to make his bed / With the defunct, or sleep upon the dead. / Let's see the boy's face.

Dream like that often, and never falsely. Wait, what's this trunk without a top? The ruin shows it was once a fine building. What? A page? Dead, or asleep on him? Dead, more likely, because nature hates to make its bed with the dead or sleep on a corpse. Let's see the boy's face.

He'll then instruct us of this body. Young one, / Inform us of thy fortunes; for it seems / They crave to be demanded. Who is this / Thou mak'st thy bloody pillow? Or who was he / That, otherwise than noble nature did, / Hath alter'd that good picture? What's thy interest / In this sad wreck? How came't? Who is't? What art thou?

Then he'll tell us about this body. Young one, tell us your story, for it seems to be begging to be asked. Who is this you're using as a bloody pillow? Or who was it that has spoiled this fine picture that noble nature made? What's your connection to this sad wreck? How did it happen? Who is it? Who are you?

I am nothing; or if not, / Nothing to be were better. This was my master, / A very valiant Briton and a good, / That here by mountaineers lies slain. Alas! / There is no more such masters. I may wander / From east to occident; cry out for service; / Try many, all good; serve truly; never / Find such another master.

I'm nothing; or if I am something, it would be better to be nothing. This was my master, a very brave and good Briton, killed here by mountain men. Alas, there are no more masters like him. I may wander from east to west, beg for work, try many masters, all good, serve them faithfully, and never find another like him.
'Lack, good youth! / Thou mov'st no less with thy complaining than / Thy master in bleeding. Say his name, good friend.
Alas, good boy! You move me as much with your lament as your master does by bleeding. Tell me his name, good friend.
Richard du Champ. [Aside] If I do lie, and do / No harm by it, though the gods hear, I hope / They'll pardon it.—Say you, sir?
Richard du Champ. (Aside) If I lie and do no harm by it, I hope the gods will pardon it, though they hear me. (Aloud) What did you say, sir?

Thou dost approve thyself the very same; / Thy name well fits thy faith, thy faith thy name. / Wilt take thy chance with me? I will not say / Thou shalt be so well master'd; but, be sure, / No less belov'd. The Roman Emperor's letters, / Sent by a consul to me, should not sooner / Than thine own worth prefer thee. Go with me.

You prove yourself exactly that: your name fits your faithfulness, and your faithfulness your name. Will you take your chances with me? I won't say you'll have as good a master, but you can be sure you'll be just as loved. Letters from the Roman Emperor, sent to me by a consul, wouldn't recommend you sooner than your own worth does. Come with me.

I'll follow, sir. But first, an't please the gods, / I'll hide my master from the flies, as deep / As these poor pickaxes can dig; and when / With wild wood-leaves and weeds I ha' strew'd his grave, / And on it said a century of prayers, / Such as I can, twice o'er, I'll weep and sigh; / And leaving so his service, follow you, / So please you entertain me.

I'll follow, sir. But first, if the gods allow, I'll hide my master from the flies, as deep as these poor fingers can dig; and when I've covered his grave with wild leaves and weeds and said a hundred prayers over it, such as I can, twice over, I'll weep and sigh; and leaving his service like that, I'll follow you, if you'll take me on.

Ay, good youth; / And rather father thee than master thee. / My friends, / The boy hath taught us manly duties; let us / Find out the prettiest daisied plot we can, / And make him with our pikes and partisans / A grave. Come, arm him. Boy, he is preferr'd / By thee to us; and he shall be interr'd / As soldiers can. Be cheerful; wipe thine eyes. / Some falls are means the happier to arise.

Yes, good boy, and I'll be more your father than your master. My friends, the boy has taught us our duty as men. Let's find the prettiest daisy-covered patch we can and dig him a grave with our pikes and spears. Come, pick him up. Boy, your loyalty has recommended him to us, and he'll be buried as well as soldiers can manage. Cheer up; wipe your eyes. Some falls are the way to rise more happily.
Again! and bring me word how 'tis with her.
Again! And bring me word how she is.

A fever with the absence of her son; / A madness, of which her life's in danger. Heavens, / How deeply you at once do touch me! Imogen, / The great part of my comfort, gone; my queen / Upon a desperate bed, and in a time / When fearful wars point at me; her son gone, / So needful for this present. It strikes me past / The hope of comfort. But for thee, fellow, / Who needs must know of her departure and / Dost seem so ignorant, we'll enforce it from thee / By a sharp torture.

A fever from the absence of her son; a madness that endangers her life. Heavens, how deeply you strike me all at once! Imogen, the greater part of my comfort, gone; my queen on her deathbed, and at a time when terrible wars are aimed at me; her son gone, who's so needed right now. It strikes me beyond all hope of comfort. But you, fellow, who must know about her leaving and seem so ignorant: we'll force it out of you with sharp torture.

Sir, my life is yours; / I humbly set it at your will; but for my mistress, / I nothing know where she remains, why gone, / Nor when she purposes return. Beseech your Highness, / Hold me your loyal servant.

Sir, my life is yours. I humbly put it at your disposal. But as for my mistress, I know nothing about where she is, why she went, or when she means to come back. I beg your Highness, think of me as your loyal servant.

Good my liege, / The day that she was missing he was here. / I dare be bound he's true and shall perform / All parts of his subjection loyally. For Cloten, / There wants no diligence in seeking him, / And will no doubt be found.

My good king, the day she went missing he was here. I'd stake my word that he's loyal and will do every part of his duty faithfully. As for Cloten, no effort is being spared in searching for him, and he'll surely be found.
The time is troublesome. / [To Pisanio] We'll slip you for a season; but our jealousy / Does yet depend.
These are troubled times. (To Pisanio) We'll let you go for now, but our suspicion still hangs over you.
So please your Majesty, / The Roman legions, all from Gallia drawn, / Are landed on your coast, with a supply / Of Roman gentlemen by the Senate sent.
If it please your Majesty, the Roman legions, all brought over from France, have landed on your coast, with reinforcements of Roman gentlemen sent by the Senate.
Now for the counsel of my son and queen! / I am amaz'd with matter.
Now I need the advice of my son and queen! I'm overwhelmed with business.
Good my liege, / Your preparation can affront no less / Than what you hear of. Come more, for more you're ready. / The want is but to put those pow'rs in motion / That long to move.
My good king, your forces can face no less than what you hear of. If more come, you're ready for more. All that's needed is to set in motion the forces that are longing to move.
I thank you. Let's withdraw, / And meet the time as it seeks us. We fear not / What can from Italy annoy us; but / We grieve at chances here. Away!
Thank you. Let's withdraw and meet events as they come for us. We're not afraid of anything Italy can do to harm us; but we grieve at what's happening here. Let's go!

I heard no letter from my master since / I wrote him Imogen was slain. 'Tis strange. / Nor hear I from my mistress, who did promise / To yield me often tidings. Neither know / What is betid to Cloten, but remain / Perplex'd in all. The heavens still must work. / Wherein I am false I am honest; not true, to be true. / These present wars shall find I love my country, / Even to the note o' th' King, or I'll fall in them. / All other doubts, by time let them be clear'd: / Fortune brings in some boats that are not steer'd.

I've had no letter from my master since I wrote to him that Imogen was killed. It's strange. And I don't hear from my mistress either, who promised to send me news often. Nor do I know what's happened to Cloten. I'm puzzled by everything. The heavens must still be at work. Where I'm false I'm honest; I'm untrue in order to be true. These wars will find that I love my country, even so the King notices, or I'll die in them. All my other doubts, let time clear them up: fortune brings some boats into harbour that nobody steers.
The noise is round about us.
The noise is all around us.
What pleasure, sir, find we in life, to lock it / From action and adventure?
What pleasure do we get from life, sir, if we lock it away from action and adventure?
Nay, what hope / Have we in hiding us? This way the Romans / Must or for Britons slay us, or receive us / For barbarous and unnatural revolts / During their use, and slay us after.
No, what hope do we have by hiding? This way the Romans will either kill us as Britons, or take us on as savage, unnatural rebels while they need us, and kill us afterwards.

Sons, / We'll higher to the mountains; there secure us. / To the King's party there's no going. Newness / Of Cloten's death—we being not known, not muster'd / Among the bands-may drive us to a render / Where we have liv'd, and so extort from's that / Which we have done, whose answer would be death, / Drawn on with torture.

Sons, we'll go higher into the mountains and keep safe there. We can't go to the King's side. The news of Cloten's death, since we're not known or enlisted in the army, might force us to account for where we've lived, and so squeeze out of us what we've done, and the answer to that would be death, with torture first.
This is, sir, a doubt / In such a time nothing becoming you / Nor satisfying us.
That's a fear, sir, that doesn't suit you at all at a time like this, and doesn't convince us.

It is not likely / That when they hear the Roman horses neigh, / Behold their quarter'd fires, have both their eyes / And ears so cloy'd importantly as now, / That they will waste their time upon our note, / To know from whence we are.

It's not likely that when they hear the Roman horses neighing, see their campfires, and have their eyes and ears so fully taken up with important things, they'll waste their time noticing us and asking where we come from.

O, I am known / Of many in the army. Many years, / Though Cloten then but young, you see, not wore him / From my remembrance. And, besides, the King / Hath not deserv'd my service nor your loves, / Who find in my exile the want of breeding, / The certainty of this hard life; aye hopeless / To have the courtesy your cradle promis'd, / But to be still hot summer's tanlings and / The shrinking slaves of winter.

Oh, many people in the army know me. Many years, as you saw, didn't wear Cloten out of my memory, though he was only young then. And besides, the King hasn't deserved my service or your love, since my exile has left you without education and certain of this hard life, forever without hope of the courtly manners your birth promised, and always the sunburnt children of hot summer and the shivering slaves of winter.
Than be so, / Better to cease to be. Pray, sir, to th' army. / I and my brother are not known; yourself / So out of thought, and thereto so o'ergrown, / Cannot be questioned.
Better to stop living than live like that. Please, sir, let's go to the army. My brother and I aren't known; and you're so long forgotten and so overgrown with beard that nobody can question you.

By this sun that shines, / I'll thither. What thing is't that I never / Did see man die! scarce ever look'd on blood / But that of coward hares, hot goats, and venison! / Never bestrid a horse, save one that had / A rider like myself, who ne'er wore rowel / Nor iron on his heel! I am asham'd / To look upon the holy sun, to have / The benefit of his blest beams, remaining / So long a poor unknown.

By this shining sun, I'll go there. What kind of man am I, never to have seen a man die! I've hardly ever seen blood except from cowardly hares, lusty goats and deer! I've never ridden a horse, except one whose rider was like me and never wore spurs or iron on his heel! I'm ashamed to look at the holy sun and enjoy its blessed rays, while staying so long a poor nobody.
By heavens, I'll go! / If you will bless me, sir, and give me leave, / I'll take the better care; but if you will not, / The hazard therefore due fall on me by / The hands of Romans!
By heaven, I'll go! If you'll bless me, sir, and give me permission, I'll take better care of myself; but if you won't, let the danger that brings fall on me by Roman hands!

No reason I, since of your lives you set / So slight a valuation, should reserve / My crack'd one to more care. Have with you, boys! / If in your country wars you chance to die, / That is my bed too, lads, and there I'll lie. / Lead, lead. [Aside] The time seems long; their blood thinks scorn / Till it fly out and show them princes born.

Since you value your lives so cheaply, I've no reason to take more care of my cracked old one. I'm with you, boys! If you happen to die in your country's wars, that's my bed too, lads, and I'll lie there. Lead on, lead on. (Aside) Time seems slow to them. Their blood is impatient until it flies out and shows they were born princes.

Yea, bloody cloth, I'll keep thee; for I wish'd / Thou shouldst be colour'd thus. You married ones, / If each of you should take this course, how many / Must murder wives much better than themselves / For wrying but a little! O Pisanio! / Every good servant does not all commands; / No bond but to do just ones. Gods! if you / Should have ta'en vengeance on my faults, I never / Had liv'd to put on this; so had you saved / The noble Imogen to repent, and struck / Me, wretch more worth your vengeance. But alack, / You snatch some hence for little faults; that's love, / To have them fall no more. You some permit / To second ills with ills, each elder worse, / And make them dread it, to the doer's thrift. / But Imogen is your own. Do your best wills, / And make me blest to obey. I am brought hither / Among th' Italian gentry, and to fight / Against my lady's kingdom. 'Tis enough / That, Britain, I have kill'd thy mistress; peace! / I'll give no wound to thee. Therefore, good heavens, / Hear patiently my purpose. I'll disrobe me / Of these Italian weeds, and suit myself / As does a Britain peasant. So I'll fight / Against the part I come with; so I'll die / For thee, O Imogen, even for whom my life / Is every breath a death. And thus unknown, / Pitied nor hated, to the face of peril / Myself I'll dedicate. Let me make men know / More valour in me than my habits show. / Gods, put the strength o' th' Leonati in me! / To shame the guise o' th' world, I will begin / The fashion—less without and more within.

Yes, bloody cloth, I'll keep you, because I wished you to be coloured like this. You married men, if each of you followed my course, how many would murder wives much better than themselves for straying just a little! Oh, Pisanio! A good servant doesn't obey every order; he's only bound to obey just ones. Gods! If you'd taken vengeance on my faults, I'd never have lived to do this. You'd have saved the noble Imogen to repent, and struck me, the wretch who deserved your vengeance more. But alas, you take some people away for small faults; that's love, so they don't sin again. Others you allow to pile sin on sin, each worse than the last, and make them dread it, for their own good. But Imogen is yours now. Do what you will, and make me blessed by obeying. I've been brought here among the Italian gentlemen to fight against my lady's kingdom. It's enough, Britain, that I've killed your princess. Peace! I won't wound you. So, good heavens, listen patiently to my plan. I'll strip off these Italian clothes and dress myself like a British peasant. That way I'll fight against the side I came with; that way I'll die for you, Imogen, for whom every breath of my life is a death. And so, unknown, neither pitied nor hated, I'll throw myself in the face of danger. Let me show men more courage in me than my clothes suggest. Gods, give me the strength of the Leonati! To shame the fashion of the world, I'll start a new one: less on the outside and more within.

The heaviness and guilt within my bosom / Takes off my manhood. I have belied a lady, / The Princess of this country, and the air on't / Revengingly enfeebles me; or could this carl, / A very drudge of nature's, have subdu'd me / In my profession? Knighthoods and honours borne / As I wear mine are titles but of scorn. / If that thy gentry, Britain, go before / This lout as he exceeds our lords, the odds / Is that we scarce are men, and you are gods.

The weight of guilt in my heart takes away my manhood. I've slandered a lady, the princess of this country, and its very air weakens me in revenge. Otherwise, could this peasant, one of nature's drudges, have beaten me at my own profession? Knighthoods and honours worn as I wear mine are only titles of scorn. If your gentlemen, Britain, are as much better than this lout as he is better than our lords, then the difference is that we're hardly men and you are gods.
Stand, stand! We have th' advantage of the ground; / The lane is guarded; nothing routs us but / The villainy of our fears.
Stand, stand! We have the advantage of the ground. The lane is guarded. Nothing can rout us but our own cowardly fears.
Away, boy, from the troops, and save thyself; / For friends kill friends, and the disorder's such / As war were hoodwink'd.
Get away from the troops, boy, and save yourself. Friends are killing friends, and the chaos is such that war seems blindfolded.
It is a day turn'd strangely. Or betimes / Let's reinforce or fly.
It's a day that has turned strangely. We must quickly either reinforce or run.
Cam'st thou from where they made the stand?
Did you come from where they made their stand?
I did: / Though you, it seems, come from the fliers.
I did, though you, it seems, come from the ones who ran.

No blame be to you, sir, for all was lost, / But that the heavens fought. The King himself / Of his wings destitute, the army broken, / And but the backs of Britons seen, an flying, / Through a strait lane—the enemy, full-hearted, / Lolling the tongue with slaught'ring, having work / More plentiful than tools to do't, struck down / Some mortally, some slightly touch'd, some falling / Merely through fear, that the strait pass was damm'd / With dead men hurt behind, and cowards living / To die with length'ned shame.

No blame to you, sir, because all was lost if the heavens hadn't fought for us. The King himself was cut off from his wings, the army broken, and nothing to be seen but the backs of Britons, all fleeing through a narrow lane. The enemy, full of spirit, tongues hanging out from slaughter, with more work than tools to do it, struck some down fatally, some lightly wounded, some fell from pure fear, so that the narrow way was blocked with dead men wounded in the back and cowards who lived only to die in long shame.

Close by the battle, ditch'd, and wall'd with turf, / Which gave advantage to an ancient soldier— / An honest one, I warrant, who deserv'd / So long a breeding as his white beard came to, / In doing this for's country. Athwart the lane / He, with two striplings—lads more like to run / The country base than to commit such slaughter; / With faces fit for masks, or rather fairer / Than those for preservation cas'd or shame— / Made good the passage, cried to those that fled / 'Our Britain's harts die flying, not our men. / To darkness fleet souls that fly backwards! Stand; / Or we are Romans and will give you that, / Like beasts, which you shun beastly, and may save / But to look back in frown. Stand, stand!' These three, / Three thousand confident, in act as many— / For three performers are the file when all / The rest do nothing—with this word 'Stand, stand!' / Accommodated by the place, more charming / With their own nobleness, which could have turn'd / A distaff to a lance, gilded pale looks, / Part shame, part spirit renew'd; that some turn'd coward / But by example—O, a sin in war / Damn'd in the first beginners!—gan to look / The way that they did and to grin like lions / Upon the pikes o' th' hunters. Then began / A stop i' th' chaser, a retire; anon / A rout, confusion thick. Forthwith they fly, / Chickens, the way which they stoop'd eagles; slaves, / The strides they victors made; and now our cowards, / Like fragments in hard voyages, became / The life o' th' need. Having found the back-door open / Of the unguarded hearts, heavens, how they wound! / Some slain before, some dying, some their friends / O'erborne i' th' former wave. Ten chas'd by one / Are now each one the slaughterman of twenty. / Those that would die or ere resist are grown / The mortal bugs o' th' field.

Right by the battlefield, with a ditch and turf walls. It gave the advantage to an old soldier, an honest one, I'd swear, who deserved the long life his white beard showed by doing this for his country. Across the lane he, with two youngsters (lads who looked more fit to play country games than to do such slaughter, with faces fit for masks, or fairer than faces covered to keep them pale or hide shame), held the passage and shouted to those running away: "Our Britain's deer die running, not our men. Souls that run backwards fly to darkness! Stand, or we'll act like Romans and give you the death like beasts that you're running from like beasts, and which you can avoid only by turning round to face them. Stand, stand!" These three, with the confidence of three thousand, and as good as that many in action (because three who act are a whole army when all the rest do nothing), with this cry of "Stand, stand!", helped by the place, and even more inspiring by their own nobility, which could have turned a spinning stick into a lance, brought colour back to pale faces, partly from shame, partly from renewed spirit. Some who had become cowards only by example (oh, a sin in war, damnable in those who start it) began to look the way the three did and to snarl like lions at the hunters' spears. Then the pursuers paused, then retreated; soon there was a rout, thick confusion. At once they ran like chickens the way they had swooped like eagles; they ran back like slaves over the ground they'd crossed as victors. And now our cowards, like scraps of food saved on hard voyages, became the lifesavers in the crisis. Finding the back door of the unguarded hearts open, heavens, how they struck! Some at those already dead, some at the dying, some at their own friends knocked down in the first wave. Ten who'd been chased by one now each became the butcher of twenty. Those who'd have died rather than resist became the deadly terrors of the field.
This was strange chance: / A narrow lane, an old man, and two boys.
That was a strange event: a narrow lane, an old man, and two boys.

Nay, do not wonder at it; you are made / Rather to wonder at the things you hear / Than to work any. Will you rhyme upon't, / And vent it for a mock'ry? Here is one: / 'Two boys, an old man (twice a boy), a lane, / Preserv'd the Britons, was the Romans' bane.'

No, don't wonder at it. You're made to wonder at things you hear, not to do any. Will you make a rhyme about it and pass it round as a joke? Here's one: "Two boys, an old man (twice a boy), a lane, saved the Britons and were the Romans' bane."
'Lack, to what end? / Who dares not stand his foe I'll be his friend; / For if he'll do as he is made to do, / I know he'll quickly fly my friendship too. / You have put me into rhyme.
Alas, what for? If a man won't stand and face his enemy, I'll be his friend; because if he does what's natural to him, I know he'll quickly run from my friendship too. You've set me rhyming.

Still going? This is a lord! O noble misery, / To be i' th' field and ask 'What news?' of me! / To-day how many would have given their honours / To have sav'd their carcasses! took heel to do't, / And yet died too! I, in mine own woe charm'd, / Could not find death where I did hear him groan, / Nor feel him where he struck. Being an ugly monster, / 'Tis strange he hides him in fresh cups, soft beds, / Sweet words; or hath moe ministers than we / That draw his knives i' th' war. Well, I will find him; / For being now a favourer to the Briton, / No more a Briton, I have resum'd again / The part I came in. Fight I will no more, / But yield me to the veriest hind that shall / Once touch my shoulder. Great the slaughter is / Here made by th' Roman; great the answer be / Britons must take. For me, my ransom's death; / On either side I come to spend my breath, / Which neither here I'll keep nor bear again, / But end it by some means for Imogen.

Still running? That's a lord! Oh, noble wretch, to be on the battlefield and ask me "What's the news?" Today how many would have given their honour to save their skins, ran for it, and still died! I, protected by my own misery, couldn't find death where I heard him groaning, or feel him where he struck. Being such an ugly monster, it's strange he hides himself in fresh cups of wine, soft beds, sweet words, or has more servants there than we who draw his knives in war. Well, I'll find him. Since I've been fighting for the Britons, I'll be a Briton no more; I'll take up again the part I came in. I won't fight any more, but surrender to the lowest peasant who touches my shoulder. Great is the slaughter the Romans have made here; great must be the revenge the Britons take. For me, death will be my ransom. I came to spend my life on either side, and I won't keep it here or take it home again, but end it somehow for Imogen.
Great Jupiter be prais'd! Lucius is taken. / 'Tis thought the old man and his sons were angels.
Great Jupiter be praised! Lucius is captured. People think the old man and his sons were angels.
There was a fourth man, in a silly habit, / That gave th' affront with them.
There was a fourth man in shabby clothes who fought the enemy with them.
So 'tis reported; / But none of 'em can be found. Stand! who's there?
So it's said, but none of them can be found. Halt! Who's there?
A Roman, / Who had not now been drooping here if seconds / Had answer'd him.
A Roman, who wouldn't be hanging his head here now if his comrades had backed him up.
Lay hands on him; a dog! / A leg of Rome shall not return to tell / What crows have peck'd them here. He brags his service, / As if he were of note. Bring him to th' King.
Seize him, the dog! Not one Roman leg will go home to tell what crows have pecked them here. He boasts of his service as if he were someone important. Take him to the King.
You shall not now be stol'n, you have locks upon you; / So graze as you find pasture.
You won't be stolen now; you've got locks on you. So graze wherever you find pasture.

Most welcome, bondage! for thou art a way, / I think, to liberty. Yet am I better / Than one that's sick o' th' gout, since he had rather / Groan so in perpetuity than be cur'd / By th' sure physician death, who is the key / T' unbar these locks. My conscience, thou art fetter'd / More than my shanks and wrists; you good gods, give me / The penitent instrument to pick that bolt, / Then, free for ever! Is't enough I am sorry? / So children temporal fathers do appease; / Gods are more full of mercy. Must I repent, / I cannot do it better than in gyves, / Desir'd more than constrain'd. To satisfy, / If of my freedom 'tis the main part, take / No stricter render of me than my all. / I know you are more clement than vile men, / Who of their broken debtors take a third, / A sixth, a tenth, letting them thrive again / On their abatement; that's not my desire. / For Imogen's dear life take mine; and though / 'Tis not so dear, yet 'tis a life; you coin'd it. / 'Tween man and man they weigh not every stamp; / Though light, take pieces for the figure's sake; / You rather mine, being yours. And so, great pow'rs, / If you will take this audit, take this life, / And cancel these cold bonds. O Imogen! / I'll speak to thee in silence. [Sleeps]

Welcome, imprisonment! Because I think you're a way to freedom. Still, I'm better off than a man sick with gout, since he'd rather groan like that forever than be cured by the sure doctor, death, who holds the key to unlock these locks. My conscience, you're chained more tightly than my ankles and wrists. Good gods, give me the tool of penitence to pick that lock, and then I'm free for ever! Is it enough that I'm sorry? That's how children calm their earthly fathers; gods are more full of mercy. If I must repent, I can't do it better than in chains I want rather than chains forced on me. If making amends is the main part of my freedom, take nothing less from me than my all. I know you're more merciful than vile men, who take a third, a sixth, a tenth from their bankrupt debtors and let them recover on what's left. That's not what I want. For Imogen's precious life take mine; and though it's not as precious, still it's a life: you minted it. Between man and man they don't weigh every coin; even if they're light, they accept them for the image stamped on them. Take mine all the more because it's yours. And so, great powers, if you'll accept this account, take this life and cancel these cold chains. Oh, Imogen! I'll speak to you in silence. (He sleeps.)

No more, thou thunder-master, show / Thy spite on mortal flies. / With Mars fall out, with Juno chide, / That thy adulteries / Rates and revenges. / Hath my poor boy done aught but well, / Whose face I never saw? / I died whilst in the womb he stay'd / Attending nature's law; / Whose father then, as men report / Thou orphans' father art, / Thou shouldst have been, and shielded him / From this earth-vexing smart.

Thunder-master, stop showing your spite to mortal flies. Quarrel with Mars, argue with Juno, who scolds you for your affairs and pays you back for them. Has my poor boy, whose face I never saw, done anything but good? I died while he was still in the womb waiting to be born. You, who are said to be the father of orphans, should have been his father then and shielded him from this earthly pain.
Lucina lent not me her aid, / But took me in my throes, / That from me was Posthumus ripp'd, / Came crying 'mongst his foes, / A thing of pity.
The goddess of childbirth didn't help me, but took me in my labour pains, so that Posthumus was ripped from me and came crying into the world among his enemies, a thing to be pitied.
Great Nature like his ancestry / Moulded the stuff so fair / That he deserv'd the praise o' th' world / As great Sicilius' heir.
Great Nature, like his ancestors, moulded him so finely that he deserved the world's praise as great Sicilius's heir.
When once he was mature for man, / In Britain where was he / That could stand up his parallel, / Or fruitful object be / In eye of Imogen, that best / Could deem his dignity?
When he grew to manhood, where in Britain was there anyone who could stand up as his equal, or win Imogen's eye, who could best judge his worth?
With marriage wherefore was he mock'd, / To be exil'd and thrown / From Leonati seat and cast / From her his dearest one, / Sweet Imogen?
Why was he mocked with marriage, only to be exiled and thrown out of the Leonati's home, cast away from his dearest one, sweet Imogen?
Why did you suffer Iachimo, / Slight thing of Italy, / To taint his nobler heart and brain / With needless jealousy, / And to become the geck and scorn / O' th' other's villainy?
Why did you let Iachimo, a worthless Italian, poison his nobler heart and mind with groundless jealousy, and make him the dupe and laughing-stock of the other's villainy?
For this from stiller seats we came, / Our parents and us twain, / That, striking in our country's cause, / Fell bravely and were slain, / Our fealty and Tenantius' right / With honour to maintain.

For this we came from the quiet fields of the blessed, our parents and the two of us, who fought for our country and fell bravely and were killed, defending with honour our loyalty and Tenantius's right.
Like hardiment Posthumus hath / To Cymbeline perform'd. / Then, Jupiter, thou king of gods, / Why hast thou thus adjourn'd / The graces for his merits due, / Being all to dolours turn'd?
Posthumus has done just as bravely for Cymbeline. So, Jupiter, king of the gods, why have you held back the rewards his merits deserve and turned them all to sorrows?
Thy crystal window ope; look out; / No longer exercise / Upon a valiant race thy harsh / And potent injuries.
Open your crystal window and look out. Stop inflicting your harsh and mighty injuries on a brave family.
Since, Jupiter, our son is good, / Take off his miseries.
Since our son is good, Jupiter, take away his miseries.
Peep through thy marble mansion. Help! / Or we poor ghosts will cry / To th' shining synod of the rest / Against thy deity.
Look out of your marble palace. Help! Or we poor ghosts will appeal to the shining council of the other gods against your godhead.
Help, Jupiter! or we appeal, / And from thy justice fly.
Help, Jupiter, or we'll appeal and fly from your justice!

No more, you petty spirits of region low, / Offend our hearing; hush! How dare you ghosts / Accuse the Thunderer whose bolt, you know, / Sky-planted, batters all rebelling coasts? / Poor shadows of Elysium, hence and rest / Upon your never-withering banks of flow'rs. / Be not with mortal accidents opprest: / No care of yours it is; you know 'tis ours. / Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift, / The more delay'd, delighted. Be content; / Your low-laid son our godhead will uplift; / His comforts thrive, his trials well are spent. / Our Jovial star reign'd at his birth, and in / Our temple was he married. Rise and fade! / He shall be lord of Lady Imogen, / And happier much by his affliction made. / This tablet lay upon his breast, wherein / Our pleasure his full fortune doth confine; / And so, away; no farther with your din / Express impatience, lest you stir up mine. / Mount, eagle, to my palace crystalline. [Ascends]

No more, you petty spirits from the lower world; stop offending my ears. Quiet! How dare you ghosts accuse the Thunderer, whose bolt, as you know, hurled from the sky, smashes every rebellious coast? Poor shadows from Elysium, go back and rest on your banks of flowers that never fade. Don't trouble yourselves with mortal matters: they're not your concern; you know they're ours. I test those I love best, to make my gift more delightful for being delayed. Be content. My godhead will raise up your fallen son. His comforts will grow; his trials are nearly over. My star, Jupiter, ruled at his birth, and he was married in my temple. Rise and vanish! He'll be husband of Lady Imogen, and much happier for his suffering. Lay this tablet on his breast; in it I've set out his whole fortune. And so, go; don't show your impatience with any more noise, or you'll stir up mine. Rise, eagle, to my crystal palace. (He ascends.)

He came in thunder; his celestial breath / Was sulpherous to smell; the holy eagle / Stoop'd as to foot us. His ascension is / More sweet than our blest fields. His royal bird / Prunes the immortal wing, and cloys his beak, / As when his god is pleas'd.

He came in thunder; his heavenly breath smelled of sulphur. The holy eagle swooped as if to seize us. His going up is sweeter than our blessed fields. His royal bird preens its immortal wing and cleans its beak, as it does when its god is pleased.
The marble pavement closes, he is enter'd / His radiant roof. Away! and, to be blest, / Let us with care perform his great behest. [Ghosts vanish]
The marble floor of heaven closes; he's gone into his shining palace. Let's go, and to be blessed, let's carry out his great command with care. (The ghosts vanish.)

[Waking] Sleep, thou has been a grandsire and begot / A father to me; and thou hast created / A mother and two brothers. But, O scorn, / Gone! They went hence so soon as they were born. / And so I am awake. Poor wretches, that depend / On greatness' favour, dream as I have done; / Wake and find nothing. But, alas, I swerve; / Many dream not to find, neither deserve, / And yet are steep'd in favours; so am I, / That have this golden chance, and know not why. / What fairies haunt this ground? A book? O rare one! / Be not, as is our fangled world, a garment / Nobler than that it covers. Let thy effects / So follow to be most unlike our courtiers, / As good as promise. / [Reads] 'When as a lion's whelp shall, to himself unknown, / without seeking find, and be embrac'd by a piece of tender air; / and when from a stately cedar shall be lopp'd branches which, / being dead many years, shall after revive, be jointed to the old / stock, and freshly grow; then shall Posthumus end his miseries, / Britain be fortunate and flourish in peace and plenty.' / 'Tis still a dream, or else such stuff as madmen / Tongue, and brain not; either both or nothing, / Or senseless speaking, or a speaking such / As sense cannot untie. Be what it is, / The action of my life is like it, which / I'll keep, if but for sympathy.

(Waking) Sleep, you've been a grandfather and given me a father, and you've created a mother and two brothers. But oh, the mockery: gone! They went as soon as they were born. And so I'm awake. Poor wretches who depend on great men's favour dream as I have done, and wake to find nothing. But alas, I'm going wrong: many don't dream of finding it, or deserve it, and are still soaked in favours. So am I, who have this golden chance and don't know why. What fairies haunt this place? A book? Oh, a fine one! Don't be, like our showy world, a garment nobler than what it covers. Let what you do be as good as what you promise, quite unlike our courtiers. (Reading) "When a lion's cub, unknown to himself, shall find without searching, and be embraced by a piece of tender air; and when from a stately cedar branches are cut which, after being dead for many years, revive, are joined to the old trunk, and grow fresh again; then Posthumus will end his miseries, and Britain will be fortunate and flourish in peace and plenty." It's still a dream, or else the kind of thing madmen say without thinking; either both or nothing; either senseless talk or talk that sense can't untangle. Whatever it is, the course of my life is like it, so I'll keep it, if only because it matches me.
Come, sir, are you ready for death?
Come, sir, are you ready to die?
Over-cooked, rather; I've been ready a long time.
Hanging is the word, sir; if you be ready for that, you are / well cook'd.
Hanging's the word, sir. If you're ready for that, you're well cooked.
So, if I prove a good repast to the spectators, the dish / pays the shot.
Then if I make a good meal for the spectators, the dish pays the bill.

A heavy reckoning for you, sir. But the comfort is, you / shall be called to no more payments, fear no more tavern bills, / which are often the sadness of parting, as the procuring of mirth. / You come in faint for want of meat, depart reeling with too much / drink; sorry that you have paid too much, and sorry that you are / paid too much; purse and brain both empty; the brain the heavier / for being too light, the purse too light, being drawn of / heaviness. O, of this contradiction you shall now be quit. O, the / charity of a penny cord! It sums up thousands in a trice. You / have no true debitor and creditor but it; of what's past, is, and / to come, the discharge. Your neck, sir, is pen, book, and / counters; so the acquittance follows.

A heavy bill for you, sir. But the comfort is, you'll be asked to pay nothing more, and needn't fear any more tavern bills, which are often as sad at parting time as they were cheerful at the start. You come in faint with hunger and leave reeling with too much drink, sorry you've paid too much and sorry you've been paid out too much; purse and brain both empty, the brain heavier for being too light, the purse too light for being emptied of its weight.
