Oh, you'll be free of this contradiction now. Oh, the charity of a penny rope! It settles thousands in an instant. It's your only true accountant, settling everything past, present and to come. Your neck, sir, is pen, ledger and counters; so the receipt follows.
I am merrier to die than thou art to live.
I'm merrier to die than you are to live.

Indeed, sir, he that sleeps feels not the toothache. But a / man that were to sleep your sleep, and a hangman to help him to / bed, I think he would change places with his officer; for look / you, sir, you know not which way you shall go.

Indeed, sir, a man who's asleep doesn't feel toothache. But a man about to sleep your sleep, with a hangman to help him to bed, would gladly change places with his officer, I think; because, you see, sir, you don't know which way you're going.

Your death has eyes in's head, then; I have not seen him so / pictur'd. You must either be directed by some that take upon them / to know, or to take upon yourself that which I am sure you do not / know, or jump the after-inquiry on your own peril. And how you / shall speed in your journey's end, I think you'll never return to / tell one.

Then your death has eyes in his head; I've never seen him painted that way. You must either be guided by people who claim to know, or claim to know yourself what I'm sure you don't, or risk finding out afterwards on your own head. And how you'll fare at your journey's end, I don't think you'll ever come back to tell anyone.
I tell thee, fellow, there are none want eyes to direct / them the way I am going, but such as wink and will not use them.
I tell you, fellow, nobody lacks eyes to guide them the way I'm going, except those who shut them and won't use them.
What an infinite mock is this, that a man should have the / best use of eyes to see the way of blindness! I am sure hanging's / the way of winking.
What an endless joke this is, that a man should have the best use of his eyes to see the way to blindness! I'm sure hanging is the way to shut your eyes.
Knock off his manacles; bring your prisoner to the King.
Knock off his handcuffs and bring your prisoner to the King.
Thou bring'st good news: I am call'd to be made free.
You bring good news: I'm called to be set free.
Thou shalt be then freer than a gaoler; no bolts for the / dead.
Then you'll be freer than a jailer: the dead have no locks.

Unless a man would marry a gallows and beget young gibbets, / I never saw one so prone. Yet, on my conscience, there are verier / knaves desire to live, for all he be a Roman; and there be some / of them too that die against their wills; so should I, if I were / one. I would we were all of one mind, and one mind good. O, there / were desolation of gaolers and gallowses! I speak against my / present profit, but my wish hath a preferment in't.

Unless a man wanted to marry a gallows and father little gallows, I never saw anyone so eager. And yet, I swear, there are bigger rogues who want to live, even though he's a Roman; and some of them die against their will too; so would I, if I were one. I wish we were all of one mind, and a good mind. Oh, then there'd be an end of jailers and gallows! I'm speaking against my own present profit, but my wish has a promotion in it.

Stand by my side, you whom the gods have made / Preservers of my throne. Woe is my heart / That the poor soldier that so richly fought, / Whose rags sham'd gilded arms, whose naked breast / Stepp'd before targes of proof, cannot be found. / He shall be happy that can find him, if / Our grace can make him so.

Stand beside me, you whom the gods have made the saviours of my throne. My heart grieves that the poor soldier who fought so splendidly, whose rags shamed gilded armour, whose bare chest stepped in front of tested shields, can't be found. Whoever can find him will be made happy, if my favour can do it.
I never saw / Such noble fury in so poor a thing; / Such precious deeds in one that promis'd nought / But beggary and poor looks.
I never saw such noble fury in so poor a figure, such precious deeds from someone who looked like nothing but a beggar.
He hath been search'd among the dead and living, / But no trace of him.
He's been searched for among the dead and the living, but there's no trace of him.

To my grief, I am / The heir of his reward; [To Belarius, Guiderius, and Arviragus] / which I will add / To you, the liver, heart, and brain, of Britain, / By whom I grant she lives. 'Tis now the time / To ask of whence you are. Report it.

To my sorrow, I inherit his reward, (to Belarius, Guiderius and Arviragus) which I'll add to yours, the liver, heart and brain of Britain, by whom I admit she lives. Now it's time to ask where you come from. Tell me.
Sir, / In Cambria are we born, and gentlemen; / Further to boast were neither true nor modest, / Unless I add we are honest.
Sir, we were born in Wales, and we're gentlemen. To boast further would be neither true nor modest, unless I add that we're honest.
Bow your knees. / Arise my knights o' th' battle; I create you / Companions to our person, and will fit you / With dignities becoming your estates.
Kneel. Rise, my knights of the battle. I make you companions of my person, and I'll give you titles to match your new rank.
There's business in these faces. Why so sadly / Greet you our victory? You look like Romans, / And not o' th' court of Britain.
There's trouble in these faces. Why do you greet our victory so sadly? You look like Romans, not members of the British court.
Hail, great King! / To sour your happiness I must report / The Queen is dead.
Hail, great King! To sour your happiness I have to tell you the Queen is dead.
Who worse than a physician / Would this report become? But I consider / By med'cine'life may be prolong'd, yet death / Will seize the doctor too. How ended she?
Who'd be a worse bearer of this news than a doctor? But I remember that medicine may lengthen life, yet death will seize the doctor too. How did she die?

With horror, madly dying, like her life; / Which, being cruel to the world, concluded / Most cruel to herself. What she confess'd / I will report, so please you; these her women / Can trip me if I err, who with wet cheeks / Were present when she finish'd.

In horror, dying madly, as she lived. Her life, cruel to the world, ended most cruelly to herself. I'll report what she confessed, if you please. These women of hers, who were there in tears when she died, can correct me if I'm wrong.
First, she confess'd she never lov'd you; only / Affected greatness got by you, not you; / Married your royalty, was wife to your place; / Abhorr'd your person.
First, she confessed she never loved you. She only loved the greatness she got through you, not you. She married your royalty, was a wife to your position, and loathed your person.
She alone knew this; / And but she spoke it dying, I would not / Believe her lips in opening it. Proceed.
Only she knew this; and if she hadn't said it dying, I wouldn't believe her lips if they told me. Go on.
Your daughter, whom she bore in hand to love / With such integrity, she did confess / Was as a scorpion to her sight; whose life, / But that her flight prevented it, she had / Ta'en off by poison.
Your daughter, whom she pretended to love so sincerely, she confessed was like a scorpion to her eyes, and she would have killed her with poison if her running away hadn't prevented it.
O most delicate fiend! / Who is't can read a woman? Is there more?
Oh, most exquisite devil! Who can read a woman? Is there more?

More, sir, and worse. She did confess she had / For you a mortal mineral, which, being took, / Should by the minute feed on life, and ling'ring, / By inches waste you. In which time she purpos'd, / By watching, weeping, tendance, kissing, to / O'ercome you with her show; and in time, / When she had fitted you with her craft, to work / Her son into th' adoption of the crown; / But failing of her end by his strange absence, / Grew shameless-desperate, open'd, in despite / Of heaven and men, her purposes, repented / The evils she hatch'd were not effected; so, / Despairing, died.

More, sir, and worse. She confessed she had a deadly mineral poison for you which, once taken, would feed on your life minute by minute and waste you away by inches. Meanwhile she planned, by sitting up with you, weeping, nursing and kissing, to win you over with her show, and in time, when she'd worked on you with her cunning, to get her son named heir to the crown. But when her plan failed because of his strange absence, she grew shamelessly desperate, revealed her plans in defiance of heaven and men, regretted that the evils she'd hatched hadn't been carried out, and so died in despair.
Heard you all this, her women?
Did you hear all this, her women?
We did, so please your Highness.
We did, if it please your Highness.

Mine eyes / Were not in fault, for she was beautiful; / Mine ears, that heard her flattery; nor my heart / That thought her like her seeming. It had been vicious / To have mistrusted her; yet, O my daughter! / That it was folly in me thou mayst say, / And prove it in thy feeling. Heaven mend all!

My eyes weren't to blame, for she was beautiful; nor my ears, which heard her flattery; nor my heart, which thought she was what she seemed. It would have been wicked to mistrust her. And yet, oh, my daughter! You can say it was folly in me, and prove it by what you've suffered. Heaven put it all right!

Thou com'st not, Caius, now for tribute; that / The Britons have raz'd out, though with the loss / Of many a bold one, whose kinsmen have made suit / That their good souls may be appeas'd with slaughter / Of you their captives, which ourself have granted; / So think of your estate.

You don't come for tribute now, Caius. The Britons have wiped that out, though with the loss of many brave men, whose relatives have asked that their good souls be appeased by the slaughter of you, their prisoners, which I have granted. So think about your situation.

Consider, sir, the chance of war. The day / Was yours by accident; had it gone with us, / We should not, when the blood was cool, have threaten'd / Our prisoners with the sword. But since the gods / Will have it thus, that nothing but our lives / May be call'd ransom, let it come. Sufficeth / A Roman with a Roman's heart can suffer. / Augustus lives to think on't; and so much / For my peculiar care. This one thing only / I will entreat: my boy, a Briton born, / Let him be ransom'd. Never master had / A page so kind, so duteous, diligent, / So tender over his occasions, true, / So feat, so nurse-like; let his virtue join / With my request, which I'll make bold your Highness / Cannot deny; he hath done no Briton harm / Though he have serv'd a Roman. Save him, sir, / And spare no blood beside.

Consider, sir, the fortunes of war. The day was yours by chance. If it had gone our way, we wouldn't have threatened our prisoners with the sword once our blood had cooled. But since the gods want it this way, that nothing but our lives will pay our ransom, let it come. It's enough that a Roman can suffer with a Roman's heart. Augustus lives to think about it; and that's enough about my own concerns. There's just one thing I'll beg: my boy, a Briton by birth, let him be ransomed. No master ever had a page so kind, so dutiful, hard-working, so attentive to his needs, so loyal, so skilful, so like a nurse. Let his virtue join with my request, which I'm bold enough to think your Highness can't refuse. He's done no Briton any harm, though he's served a Roman. Save him, sir, and spare no other blood.

I have surely seen him; / His favour is familiar to me. Boy, / Thou hast look'd thyself into my grace, / And art mine own. I know not why, wherefore / To say 'Live, boy.' Ne'er thank thy master. Live; / And ask of Cymbeline what boon thou wilt, / Fitting my bounty and thy state, I'll give it; / Yea, though thou do demand a prisoner, / The noblest ta'en.

I've certainly seen him; his face is familiar to me. Boy, your looks have won my favour, and you're mine. I don't know why or for what reason I say, "Live, boy." Don't thank your master. Live, and ask Cymbeline for any favour you like that suits my generosity and your rank, and I'll grant it; yes, even if you ask for a prisoner, the noblest captured.
I do not bid thee beg my life, good lad, / And yet I know thou wilt.
I don't tell you to beg for my life, good lad, but I know you will.
No, no! Alack, / There's other work in hand. I see a thing / Bitter to me as death; your life, good master, / Must shuffle for itself.
No, no! Alas, there's other work to do. I see something as bitter to me as death. Your life, good master, will have to look after itself.
The boy disdains me, / He leaves me, scorns me. Briefly die their joys / That place them on the truth of girls and boys. / Why stands he so perplex'd?
The boy scorns me; he leaves me, despises me. Their joys die quickly who rest them on the loyalty of girls and boys. Why does he stand there so troubled?
What wouldst thou, boy? / I love thee more and more; think more and more / What's best to ask. Know'st him thou look'st on? Speak, / Wilt have him live? Is he thy kin? thy friend?
What do you want, boy? I love you more and more; think more and more about what's best to ask. Do you know the man you're looking at? Speak, do you want him to live? Is he your relative? Your friend?
He is a Roman, no more kin to me / Than I to your Highness; who, being born your vassal, / Am something nearer.
He's a Roman, no more related to me than I am to your Highness; and being born your subject, I'm rather closer.
Why do you stare at him like that?
I'll tell you, sir, in private, if you please / To give me hearing.
I'll tell you in private, sir, if you'll hear me.
Ay, with all my heart, / And lend my best attention. What's thy name?
Yes, with all my heart, and I'll give you my full attention. What's your name?
Thou'rt my good youth, my page; / I'll be thy master. Walk with me; speak freely.
You're my good boy, my page. I'll be your master. Walk with me; speak freely.
Is not this boy reviv'd from death?
Isn't this boy come back from the dead?
One sand another / Not more resembles—that sweet rosy lad / Who died and was Fidele. What think you?
One grain of sand isn't more like another than he is like that sweet rosy boy who died and was Fidele. What do you think?
Peace, peace! see further. He eyes us not; forbear. / Creatures may be alike; were't he, I am sure / He would have spoke to us.
Quiet, quiet! Let's see more. He's not looking at us; wait. People can look alike. If it were him, I'm sure he'd have spoken to us.
[Aside] It is my mistress. / Since she is living, let the time run on / To good or bad. [Cymbeline and Imogen advance]
(Aside) It's my mistress. Since she's alive, let time run on to good or bad.

Come, stand thou by our side; / Make thy demand aloud. [To Iachimo] Sir, step you forth; / Give answer to this boy, and do it freely, / Or, by our greatness and the grace of it, / Which is our honour, bitter torture shall / Winnow the truth from falsehood. On, speak to him.

Come, stand by our side and make your request aloud. (To Iachimo) Sir, step forward. Answer this boy, and do it frankly, or, by our greatness and the honour that goes with it, bitter torture will sift the truth from the lies. Go on, speak to him.
My boon is that this gentleman may render / Of whom he had this ring.
My request is that this gentleman tell us from whom he got this ring.
That diamond upon your finger, say / How came it yours?
That diamond on your finger: tell us how it came to be yours.
Thou'lt torture me to leave unspoken that / Which to be spoke would torture thee.
You'll torture me for leaving unspoken what would torture you if it were spoken.

I am glad to be constrain'd to utter that / Which torments me to conceal. By villainy / I got this ring; 'twas Leonatus' jewel, / Whom thou didst banish; and—which more may grieve thee, / As it doth me—a nobler sir ne'er liv'd / 'Twixt sky and ground. Wilt thou hear more, my lord?

I'm glad to be forced to say what it torments me to hide. I got this ring by villainy. It was the jewel of Leonatus, whom you banished; and (which may grieve you more, as it does me) a nobler gentleman never lived between sky and earth. Will you hear more, my lord?
That paragon, thy daughter, / For whom my heart drops blood and my false spirits / Quail to remember—Give me leave, I faint.
That model of perfection, your daughter, for whom my heart bleeds and my false spirit shrinks to remember... Give me a moment; I feel faint.
My daughter? What of her? Renew thy strength; / I had rather thou shouldst live while nature will / Than die ere I hear more. Strive, man, and speak.
My daughter? What about her? Pull yourself together. I'd rather you lived as long as nature allows than die before I hear more. Make an effort, man, and speak.

Upon a time—unhappy was the clock / That struck the hour!—was in Rome—accurs'd / The mansion where!—'twas at a feast—O, would / Our viands had been poison'd, or at least / Those which I heav'd to head!—the good Posthumus— / What should I say? he was too good to be / Where ill men were, and was the best of all / Amongst the rar'st of good ones—sitting sadly / Hearing us praise our loves of Italy / For beauty that made barren the swell'd boast / Of him that best could speak; for feature, laming / The shrine of Venus or straight-pight Minerva, / Postures beyond brief nature; for condition, / A shop of all the qualities that man / Loves woman for; besides that hook of wiving, / Fairness which strikes the eye—

Once (unlucky was the clock that struck that hour!) in Rome (cursed be the house where it happened!) at a feast (oh, I wish our food had been poisoned, or at least what I lifted to my mouth!), the good Posthumus (what can I say? He was too good to be among bad men, and the best of all among the rarest good ones) was sitting sadly, listening to us praise our Italian sweethearts: for beauty that left the boldest boasts of the best speaker empty; for figure, that put to shame the statue of Venus or upright Minerva, shapes beyond what short-lived nature can make; for character, a store of every quality men love women for; and besides that, the hook that catches husbands, beauty that strikes the eye...
I stand on fire. / Come to the matter.
I'm on fire. Get to the point.

All too soon I shall, / Unless thou wouldst grieve quickly. This Posthumus, / Most like a noble lord in love and one / That had a royal lover, took his hint; / And not dispraising whom we prais'd—therein / He was as calm as virtue—he began / His mistress' picture; which by his tongue being made, / And then a mind put in't, either our brags / Were crack'd of kitchen trulls, or his description / Prov'd us unspeaking sots.

I'll get there all too soon, unless you want to grieve quickly. This Posthumus, like a noble lord in love and one who had a royal sweetheart, took his cue, and without criticising those we praised (in that he was as calm as virtue itself), he began to paint a picture of his lady. Once his words had drawn it and given it a mind, either our boasts were about kitchen sluts, or his description proved us tongue-tied fools.
No, no, get to the point.

Your daughter's chastity—there it begins. / He spake of her as Dian had hot dreams / And she alone were cold; whereat I, wretch, / Made scruple of his praise, and wager'd with him / Pieces of gold 'gainst this which then he wore / Upon his honour'd finger, to attain / In suit the place of's bed, and win this ring / By hers and mine adultery. He, true knight, / No lesser of her honour confident / Than I did truly find her, stakes this ring; / And would so, had it been a carbuncle / Of Phoebus' wheel; and might so safely, had it / Been all the worth of's car. Away to Britain / Post I in this design. Well may you, sir, / Remember me at court, where I was taught / Of your chaste daughter the wide difference / 'Twixt amorous and villainous. Being thus quench'd / Of hope, not longing, mine Italian brain / Gan in your duller Britain operate / Most vilely; for my vantage, excellent; / And, to be brief, my practice so prevail'd / That I return'd with simular proof enough / To make the noble Leonatus mad, / By wounding his belief in her renown / With tokens thus and thus; averring notes / Of chamber-hanging, pictures, this her bracelet— / O cunning, how I got it!—nay, some marks / Of secret on her person, that he could not / But think her bond of chastity quite crack'd, / I having ta'en the forfeit. Whereupon— / Methinks I see him now—

Your daughter's chastity: that's where it begins. He spoke of her as if Diana had hot dreams and she alone were cold. At that I, wretch that I am, doubted his praise, and bet him gold against this ring, which he wore then on his honoured finger, that I would win my way into her bed and win this ring through her adultery and mine. He, a true knight, no less confident of her honour than I truly found her, staked this ring; and he would have done so if it had been a jewel from the sun god's chariot wheel, and could have done so safely if it had been worth the whole chariot. Off to Britain I hurried with this plan. You may well remember me at court, sir, where your chaste daughter taught me the wide difference between a lover and a villain. My hope put out, though not my desire, my Italian brain began to work in your duller Britain, most vilely, but to my great advantage. To be brief, my scheme succeeded so well that I came back with enough fake proof to drive the noble Leonatus mad, wounding his faith in her good name with such and such tokens: a detailed description of the hangings and pictures in her room, this bracelet of hers (oh, the trick by which I got it!), yes, even secret marks on her body, so that he couldn't help thinking her bond of chastity quite broken and that I'd taken the forfeit. Whereupon (I think I see him now)...

[Coming forward] Ay, so thou dost, / Italian fiend! Ay me, most credulous fool, / Egregious murderer, thief, anything / That's due to all the villains past, in being, / To come! O, give me cord, or knife, or poison, / Some upright justicer! Thou, King, send out / For torturers ingenious. It is I / That all th' abhorred things o' th' earth amend / By being worse than they. I am Posthumus, / That kill'd thy daughter; villain-like, I lie— / That caus'd a lesser villain than myself, / A sacrilegious thief, to do't. The temple / Of virtue was she; yea, and she herself. / Spit, and throw stones, cast mire upon me, set / The dogs o' th' street to bay me. Every villain / Be call'd Posthumus Leonatus, and / Be villainy less than 'twas! O Imogen! / My queen, my life, my wife! O Imogen, / Imogen, Imogen!

(Stepping forward) Yes, so you do, Italian devil! Oh, I'm the most gullible fool, a monstrous murderer, thief, anything that's due to all villains past, present and to come! Oh, give me a rope, or a knife, or poison, some honest judge! You, King, send for ingenious torturers. I'm the one who makes all the hateful things on earth look better by being worse than they are. I am Posthumus, who killed your daughter. No, I lie like a villain: who made a lesser villain than myself, a sacrilegious thief, do it. She was the temple of virtue; yes, and virtue herself. Spit on me, throw stones, throw mud at me, set the street dogs barking at me. Let every villain be called Posthumus Leonatus, and let villainy be less than it was! Oh, Imogen! My queen, my life, my wife! Oh, Imogen, Imogen, Imogen!
Shall's have a play of this? Thou scornful page, / There lies thy part. [Strikes her. She falls]
Are we to have a comedy about this? You scornful page, there's your part. (He strikes her and she falls.)
O gentlemen, help! / Mine and your mistress! O, my lord Posthumus! / You ne'er kill'd Imogen till now. Help, help! / Mine honour'd lady!
Oh, gentlemen, help! My mistress and yours! Oh, my lord Posthumus! You never killed Imogen until now. Help, help! My honoured lady!
How comes these staggers on me?
Why am I reeling like this?
If this be so, the gods do mean to strike me / To death with mortal joy.
If this is so, the gods mean to strike me dead with deadly joy.
O, get thee from my sight; / Thou gav'st me poison. Dangerous fellow, hence! / Breathe not where princes are.
Oh, get out of my sight. You gave me poison. Dangerous man, go! Don't breathe where princes are.
Lady, / The gods throw stones of sulphur on me, if / That box I gave you was not thought by me / A precious thing! I had it from the Queen.
Lady, may the gods throw burning sulphur stones at me if I didn't think that box I gave you was a precious thing! I got it from the Queen.

O gods! / I left out one thing which the Queen confess'd, / Which must approve thee honest. 'If Pisanio / Have' said she 'given his mistress that confection / Which I gave him for cordial, she is serv'd / As I would serve a rat.'

Oh, gods! I left out one thing the Queen confessed, which must prove you honest. "If Pisanio," she said, "has given his mistress that mixture which I gave him as a restorative, she's been treated as I'd treat a rat."

The Queen, sir, very oft importun'd me / To temper poisons for her; still pretending / The satisfaction of her knowledge only / In killing creatures vile, as cats and dogs, / Of no esteem. I, dreading that her purpose / Was of more danger, did compound for her / A certain stuff, which, being ta'en would cease / The present pow'r of life, but in short time / All offices of nature should again / Do their due functions. Have you ta'en of it?

The Queen, sir, very often pestered me to mix poisons for her, always claiming she only wanted to increase her knowledge by killing worthless creatures like cats and dogs. I was afraid her purpose was more dangerous, so I made her a certain substance which, when taken, would stop the powers of life for a while, but in a short time all the body's functions would work again as normal. Did you take any of it?
Most like I did, for I was dead.
Most likely I did, because I was dead.
My boys, / There was our error.
My boys, that's where we went wrong.
Why did you throw your wedded lady from you? / Think that you are upon a rock, and now / Throw me again. [Embracing him]
Why did you throw your wife away from you? Imagine you're on a cliff, and now throw me again. (She embraces him.)
Hang there like fruit, my soul, / Till the tree die!
Hang there like fruit, my soul, until the tree dies!
How now, my flesh? my child? / What, mak'st thou me a dullard in this act? / Wilt thou not speak to me?
What's this, my flesh, my child? What, are you making me a fool in this scene? Won't you speak to me?
[To Guiderius and Arviragus] Though you did love this / youth, I blame ye not; / You had a motive for't.
(To Guiderius and Arviragus) Though you loved this boy, I don't blame you; you had a reason.
My tears that fall / Prove holy water on thee! Imogen, / Thy mother's dead.
May my falling tears be holy water on you! Imogen, your stepmother's dead.
I am sorry for't, my lord.
I'm sorry for it, my lord.
O, she was naught, and long of her it was / That we meet here so strangely; but her son / Is gone, we know not how nor where.
Oh, she was wicked, and it's because of her that we meet here so strangely. But her son is gone, we don't know how or where.

My lord, / Now fear is from me, I'll speak troth. Lord Cloten, / Upon my lady's missing, came to me / With his sword drawn, foam'd at the mouth, and swore, / If I discover'd not which way she was gone, / It was my instant death. By accident / I had a feigned letter of my master's / Then in my pocket, which directed him / To seek her on the mountains near to Milford; / Where, in a frenzy, in my master's garments, / Which he enforc'd from me, away he posts / With unchaste purpose, and with oath to violate / My lady's honour. What became of him / I further know not.

My lord, now that I've no fear, I'll tell the truth. When my lady went missing, Lord Cloten came to me with his sword drawn, foaming at the mouth, and swore that if I didn't reveal which way she'd gone, I'd die on the spot. By chance I had in my pocket a false letter from my master, which sent him to look for her in the mountains near Milford. And there he rushed off in a frenzy, wearing my master's clothes, which he forced me to give him, with a lustful purpose and an oath to rape my lady. What happened to him after that I don't know.
Let me end the story: / I slew him there.
Let me finish the story: I killed him there.
Marry, the gods forfend! / I would not thy good deeds should from my lips / Pluck a hard sentence. Prithee, valiant youth, / Deny't again.
The gods forbid! I wouldn't want your good deeds to drag a harsh sentence from my lips. Please, brave young man, deny it.
I have spoke it, and I did it.
I've said it, and I did it.

A most incivil one. The wrongs he did me / Were nothing prince-like; for he did provoke me / With language that would make me spurn the sea, / If it could so roar to me. I cut off's head, / And am right glad he is not standing here / To tell this tale of mine.

A very uncivil one. The wrongs he did me were nothing like a prince's. He provoked me with language that would have made me kick the sea, if it roared at me like that. I cut off his head, and I'm very glad he isn't standing here to tell this story about me.
I am sorry for thee. / By thine own tongue thou art condemn'd, and must / Endure our law. Thou'rt dead.
I'm sorry for you. You're condemned by your own tongue and must suffer our law. You're a dead man.
That headless man / I thought had been my lord.
That headless man I thought was my lord.
Bind the offender, / And take him from our presence.
Tie up the offender and take him out of our sight.

Stay, sir King. / This man is better than the man he slew, / As well descended as thyself, and hath / More of thee merited than a band of Clotens / Had ever scar for. [To the guard] Let his arms alone; / They were not born for bondage.

Wait, King. This man is better than the man he killed, as well born as you, and has deserved more from you than a troop of Clotens ever earned by their scars. (To the guards) Leave his arms alone; they weren't born to be tied.
Why, old soldier, / Wilt thou undo the worth thou art unpaid for / By tasting of our wrath? How of descent / As good as we?
Why, old soldier, will you undo the reward you haven't yet been paid by bringing on our anger? How can he be as well born as we are?
In that he spake too far.
In that he went too far.
We will die all three; / But I will prove that two on's are as good / As I have given out him. My sons, I must / For mine own part unfold a dangerous speech, / Though haply well for you.
We'll all three die; but I'll prove that two of us are as good as I said he was. My sons, for my own part I must tell a dangerous story, though perhaps it will be good for you.
Have at it then by leave! / Thou hadst, great King, a subject who / Was call'd Belarius.
Here goes, then, with your permission! Great King, you once had a subject called Belarius.
What of him? He is / A banish'd traitor.
What of him? He's a banished traitor.
He it is that hath / Assum'd this age; indeed a banish'd man; / I know not how a traitor.
He's the one who has reached this old age: a banished man, certainly; how a traitor, I don't know.
Take him hence, / The whole world shall not save him.
Take him away. The whole world won't save him.
Not too hot. / First pay me for the nursing of thy sons, / And let it be confiscate all, so soon / As I have receiv'd it.
Not so fast. First pay me for bringing up your sons, and then confiscate it all as soon as I've received it.

I am too blunt and saucy: here's my knee. / Ere I arise I will prefer my sons; / Then spare not the old father. Mighty sir, / These two young gentlemen that call me father, / And think they are my sons, are none of mine; / They are the issue of your loins, my liege, / And blood of your begetting.

I'm too blunt and rude. Here, I kneel. Before I get up I'll present my sons, and then don't spare the old father. Mighty sir, these two young gentlemen who call me father and think they're my sons are not mine. They are the children of your body, my king, and of your blood.

So sure as you your father's. I, old Morgan, / Am that Belarius whom you sometime banish'd. / Your pleasure was my mere offence, my punishment / Itself, and all my treason; that I suffer'd / Was all the harm I did. These gentle princes— / For such and so they are—these twenty years / Have I train'd up; those arts they have as / Could put into them. My breeding was, sir, as / Your Highness knows. Their nurse, Euriphile, / Whom for the theft I wedded, stole these children / Upon my banishment; I mov'd her to't, / Having receiv'd the punishment before / For that which I did then. Beaten for loyalty / Excited me to treason. Their dear loss, / The more of you 'twas felt, the more it shap'd / Unto my end of stealing them. But, gracious sir, / Here are your sons again, and I must lose / Two of the sweet'st companions in the world. / The benediction of these covering heavens / Fall on their heads like dew! for they are worthy / To inlay heaven with stars.

As surely as you are your father's. I, old Morgan, am that Belarius you once banished. Your whim was my only offence, my punishment, and all my treason; what I suffered was all the harm I did. These gentle princes (for that's what they are) I've brought up for twenty years. They have all the skills I could teach them, and you know, sir, how I was brought up myself. Their nurse, Euriphile, whom I married for the theft, stole these children when I was banished. I put her up to it, having already been punished for what I then did. Being beaten for loyalty drove me to treason. The more you felt their loss, the better it served my purpose in stealing them. But, gracious sir, here are your sons again, and I must lose two of the sweetest companions in the world. May the blessing of the heavens above fall on their heads like dew, because they're worthy to set the sky with stars.
Thou weep'st and speak'st. / The service that you three have done is more / Unlike than this thou tell'st. I lost my children. / If these be they, I know not how to wish / A pair of worthier sons.
You weep as you speak. The service you three have done is more incredible than what you're telling me. I lost my children. If these are they, I couldn't wish for a worthier pair of sons.

Be pleas'd awhile. / This gentleman, whom I call Polydore, / Most worthy prince, as yours, is true Guiderius; / This gentleman, my Cadwal, Arviragus, / Your younger princely son; he, sir, was lapp'd / In a most curious mantle, wrought by th' hand / Of his queen mother, which for more probation / I can with ease produce.

Bear with me a little. This gentleman, whom I call Polydore, most worthy prince, is your true Guiderius. This gentleman, my Cadwal, is Arviragus, your younger royal son. He, sir, was wrapped in a beautifully made cloak, worked by the hand of his mother the queen, which I can easily produce for further proof.
Guiderius had / Upon his neck a mole, a sanguine star; / It was a mark of wonder.
Guiderius had a mole on his neck, a red star. It was a remarkable mark.
This is he, / Who hath upon him still that natural stamp. / It was wise nature's end in the donation, / To be his evidence now.
This is he, who still has that natural stamp on him. It was wise nature's purpose in giving it to be his proof now.

O, what am I? / A mother to the birth of three? Ne'er mother / Rejoic'd deliverance more. Blest pray you be, / That, after this strange starting from your orbs, / You may reign in them now! O Imogen, / Thou hast lost by this a kingdom.

Oh, what am I? A mother who's given birth to three? No mother ever rejoiced more in a delivery. Be blessed, I pray, so that after this strange wandering from your spheres you may reign in them now! Oh, Imogen, you've lost a kingdom by this.

No, my lord; / I have got two worlds by't. O my gentle brothers, / Have we thus met? O, never say hereafter / But I am truest speaker! You call'd me brother, / When I was but your sister: I you brothers, / When we were so indeed.

No, my lord, I've gained two worlds by it. Oh, my gentle brothers, have we met like this? Oh, never say after this that I'm not the truest speaker! You called me brother when I was only your sister; I called you brothers when you really were.
And at first meeting lov'd, / Continu'd so until we thought he died.
And loved at first meeting, and went on loving until we thought he died.
By the Queen's dram she swallow'd.
From the Queen's drug, which she swallowed.

O rare instinct! / When shall I hear all through? This fierce abridgment / Hath to it circumstantial branches, which / Distinction should be rich in. Where? how liv'd you? / And when came you to serve our Roman captive? / How parted with your brothers? how first met them? / Why fled you from the court? and whither? These, / And your three motives to the battle, with / I know not how much more, should be demanded, / And all the other by-dependences, / From chance to chance; but nor the time nor place / Will serve our long interrogatories. See, / Posthumus anchors upon Imogen; / And she, like harmless lightning, throws her eye / On him, her brothers, me, her master, hitting / Each object with a joy; the counterchange / Is severally in all. Let's quit this ground, / And smoke the temple with our sacrifices. / [To Belarius] Thou art my brother; so we'll hold thee ever.

Oh, wonderful instinct! When will I hear it all? This rapid summary has branching details that should be told fully. Where? How did you live? And when did you come to serve our Roman prisoner? How did you part from your brothers? How did you first meet them? Why did you run away from court? And where to? These, and the reasons all three of you went to the battle, and I don't know how much more, should be asked, and all the other connected events, one chance after another. But neither the time nor the place suits our long questioning. Look, Posthumus anchors himself to Imogen, and she, like harmless lightning, throws her eye at him, her brothers, me, her master, striking each with joy, and each returns it. Let's leave this ground and fill the temple with the smoke of our sacrifices. (To Belarius) You're my brother; we'll always think of you so.
You are my father too, and did relieve me / To see this gracious season.
You're my father too, and you helped me live to see this happy time.
All o'erjoy'd / Save these in bonds. Let them be joyful too, / For they shall taste our comfort.
Everyone overjoyed except these prisoners. Let them be joyful too, because they'll share our happiness.
My good master, / I will yet do you service.
My good master, I'll still serve you.
The forlorn soldier, that so nobly fought, / He would have well becom'd this place and grac'd / The thankings of a king.
The lost soldier who fought so nobly would have suited this place well and honoured a king's thanks.

I am, sir, / The soldier that did company these three / In poor beseeming; 'twas a fitment for / The purpose I then follow'd. That I was he, / Speak, Iachimo. I had you down, and might / Have made you finish.
I am, sir, the soldier who fought with these three, dressed poorly, as suited the purpose I had then. Say that it was me, Iachimo. I had you down and could have finished you.

[Kneeling] I am down again; / But now my heavy conscience sinks my knee, / As then your force did. Take that life, beseech you, / Which I so often owe; but your ring first, / And here the bracelet of the truest princess / That ever swore her faith.

(Kneeling) I'm down again; but now my heavy conscience bends my knee, as your strength did then. Take my life, I beg you, which I owe you so many times over; but first your ring, and here's the bracelet of the most faithful princess who ever swore her loyalty.
Kneel not to me. / The pow'r that I have on you is to spare you; / The malice towards you to forgive you. Live, / And deal with others better.
Don't kneel to me. The power I have over you is to spare you; my spite against you is to forgive you. Live, and treat others better.
Nobly doom'd! / We'll learn our freeness of a son-in-law; / Pardon's the word to all.
A noble judgment! We'll learn generosity from a son-in-law. Pardon is the word for all.
You holp us, sir, / As you did mean indeed to be our brother; / Joy'd are we that you are.
You helped us, sir, as if you really meant to be our brother. We're glad that you are.

Your servant, Princes. Good my lord of Rome, / Call forth your soothsayer. As I slept, methought / Great Jupiter, upon his eagle back'd, / Appear'd to me, with other spritely shows / Of mine own kindred. When I wak'd, I found / This label on my bosom; whose containing / Is so from sense in hardness that I can / Make no collection of it. Let him show / His skill in the construction.

Your servant, princes. My good lord of Rome, call your soothsayer. As I slept I thought great Jupiter, riding on his eagle, appeared to me, along with other ghostly visions of my own family. When I woke I found this tablet on my chest. What it says is so hard to make sense of that I can't understand it. Let him show his skill in interpreting it.
Read it and tell us what it means.

[Reads] 'When as a lion's whelp shall, to himself / unknown, without seeking find, and be embrac'd by / a piece of tender air; and when from a stately cedar shall / be lopp'd branches which, being dead many years, shall / after revive, be jointed to the old stock, and freshly grow; / then shall Posthumus end his miseries, Britain be fortunate / and flourish in peace and plenty.' / Thou, Leonatus, art the lion's whelp; / The fit and apt construction of thy name, / Being Leo-natus, doth import so much. / [To Cymbeline] The piece of tender air, thy virtuous daughter, / Which we call 'mollis aer,' and 'mollis aer' / We term it 'mulier'; which 'mulier' I divine / Is this most constant wife, who even now / Answering the letter of the oracle, / Unknown to you, unsought, were clipp'd about / With this most tender air.

(Reading) "When a lion's cub, unknown to himself, shall find without searching, and be embraced by a piece of tender air; and when from a stately cedar branches are cut which, after being dead for many years, revive, are joined to the old trunk, and grow fresh again; then Posthumus will end his miseries, and Britain will be fortunate and flourish in peace and plenty." You, Leonatus, are the lion's cub. The proper meaning of your name, Leo-natus, "lion-born", says as much. (To Cymbeline) The piece of tender air is your virtuous daughter. In Latin we call tender air "mollis aer", and from "mollis aer" we get "mulier", woman. That woman, I believe, is this most faithful wife, who just now, fulfilling the words of the oracle, embraced him, unknown to you and unsought, as tender air.

The lofty cedar, royal Cymbeline, / Personates thee; and thy lopp'd branches point / Thy two sons forth, who, by Belarius stol'n, / For many years thought dead, are now reviv'd, / To the majestic cedar join'd, whose issue / Promises Britain peace and plenty.

The tall cedar, royal Cymbeline, stands for you, and your lopped branches point to your two sons, who were stolen by Belarius and thought dead for many years, and are now revived and joined to the majestic cedar, whose children promise Britain peace and plenty.

Well, / My peace we will begin. And, Caius Lucius, / Although the victor, we submit to Caesar / And to the Roman empire, promising / To pay our wonted tribute, from the which / We were dissuaded by our wicked queen, / Whom heavens in justice, both on her and hers, / Have laid most heavy hand.

Well, I'll begin my peace. And, Caius Lucius, although we're the victors, we submit to Caesar and the Roman Empire, and promise to pay our usual tribute, which we were talked out of by our wicked queen, on whom, and on whose son, the heavens have justly laid a very heavy hand.

The fingers of the pow'rs above do tune / The harmony of this peace. The vision / Which I made known to Lucius ere the stroke / Of yet this scarce-cold battle, at this instant / Is full accomplish'd; for the Roman eagle, / From south to west on wing soaring aloft, / Lessen'd herself and in the beams o' th' sun / So vanish'd; which foreshow'd our princely eagle, / Th'imperial Caesar, Caesar, should again unite / His favour with the radiant Cymbeline, / Which shines here in the west.

The fingers of the powers above are tuning the harmony of this peace. The vision I told Lucius before this barely cooled battle began is fulfilled at this moment. For the Roman eagle, soaring high on the wing from south to west, grew smaller and vanished in the sun's beams; which foretold that our princely eagle, imperial Caesar, would unite his favour again with the radiant Cymbeline, who shines here in the west.

Laud we the gods; / And let our crooked smokes climb to their nostrils / From our bless'd altars. Publish we this peace / To all our subjects. Set we forward; let / A Roman and a British ensign wave / Friendly together. So through Lud's Town march; / And in the temple of great Jupiter / Our peace we'll ratify; seal it with feasts. / Set on there! Never was a war did cease, / Ere bloody hands were wash'd, with such a peace.

Let's praise the gods, and let the curling smoke from our blessed altars climb to their nostrils. Let's announce this peace to all our subjects. Let's set out, with a Roman and a British flag waving together in friendship. So we'll march through London, and in the temple of great Jupiter we'll confirm our peace and seal it with feasts. Set off! Never did a war end, before the bloody hands were even washed, with such a peace.
